DIALOGUE 1. QUESTION 1. Those who sail the great and wide sea pay little attention to the shores along their way as long as they are voyaging pleasantly with a fair wind. But when a violent contrary wind blows against them, stirring up a storm and threatening death to those who a little before were sailing without fear, then indeed they long for a calm harbour. They scan the whole coast lying opposite them, and when they can find no anchorage anywhere, they then steer the ship with the rudders toward the nearest island, if there happens to be one,

striving by every means to secure their own safety. When they draw near to it and take refuge under the shelter of its headlands, rescued from a dreaded death, they send up voices of thanksgiving to God, the Saviour of all. So we too, O Father who love your children, as we sail the storm-tossed sea of life, variously drenched by the waves of the heresies and finding no harbour for the mind anywhere, have come to your love, asking to hear from you about the worshipful and holy Trinity and about other chapters of holy Scripture, so that we may not go astray with the vain-minded, but, strengthened by your instruction, may little by little quietly withdraw ourselves from the surge of the world and make haste to bring the vessel of our soul into the waveless harbour of Christ, following your honey-flowing counsel.

ANSWER. The most exact interpretation of the divine Scriptures far exceeds and surpasses my understanding, which is not yet purified and has not yet put off the much-suffering garment of matter. For I do not recline at table with God as a righteous man with the Righteous One, since I lie sunk in sloth; nor do I approach him as Creator and Guide and Ruler of all, to be taught the principles of bodies, of judgment and of providence; nor do I, wretch that I am, stand before him as King and Master. For even until now I cannot entreat him with uncovered head, since I carry about the idols of the world and am weighed down in the head by its treacherous [?], and am dashed against the earth. In short, whenever [I turn] toward the loftiness of divine things, I grow dizzy and tremble again, like those who stoop from some high mountain ridge to look down into a yawning sea; or again like those whose eyes are struck when, at the steady height of noon as the sun rides across the heaven, they try to gaze at it fixedly, and their sight is darkened by the excess of its flashing and the brilliance that comes from it. I therefore thought it necessary to take silence as my helper. But lest by complete muteness I should with good reason become suspected by you of grudging, rebuffing your eager and obedient disposition with idle silence—when the divine David sings: "Many, O Lord my God, are the wonders you have done, and in your thoughts no one shall be likened to you; I declared and spoke of them, they were multiplied beyond number." And again: "I proclaimed righteousness in the great assembly; behold, I will not restrain my lips, O Lord; you know it. I did not hide your righteousness in my heart; I spoke of your truth and your salvation; I did not hide your mercy and your truth from the great congregation. But you, O Lord, do not withhold your compassions from us." And when the chief of the apostles, in a written catholic epistle, charges us to be ready ¹ Ps. 32:6.

to make a defence to everyone who asks about the hope that is in us; and when Paul the lofty cries out [?] that we should walk in his footsteps and imitate Christ; and, more than that, when Christ himself speaks divinely, telling us that, having received freely, we should give likewise, and with all our strength double the divine talents he has entrusted to us for this very purpose, lest, burying them in idle silence as if in dry ground, we be cast together with the wicked and lazy servant of the Gospels into the outer darkness—here, then, it is better to take fear rather than silence as my helper. For "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom," says David, the singer of divine things. For it is good to keep silent with discernment and sounder reasoning, and to be as it were mute and crucified to the world, yet clear and [?] in voice as an instrument of divine things. For thus the lovely muteness and the unceasing converse of the divinely inspired will come to be ours, when we entreat the Deity, crying out, concerning things that destroy the soul: "Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a fortified door about my lips, and do not incline my heart to paths of wickedness"; and concerning things divine and life-giving: "O Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise." With good reason, then, I will strip once more for the contest of your questions, making God the guide of my discourse and leaning on your prayers to him. It is like those who are keen supporters in the chariot races: even though the racers lack nothing in eagerness for speed, the spectators nevertheless, in their zeal for victory, shout from up in the seats and benches out of sheer heartfelt feeling, and, turning their eyes to follow the race, rouse the charioteer, as they think, to a sharper charge, yelling along with the horses, stretching out their hand at them in place of a whip, jabbing with their forefinger at those close by [?], scratching their cheeks, grinding [?] their teeth, and making threats, rising up wholeheartedly with their gaze at the racers and signalling to them with their hands whatever seems best for winning the prize—not because what they do contributes anything to the victory, but out of goodwill toward the contestants, expressing their love for them by voice and gesture. This is what I too am compelled to do out of my longing for you, most honoured of my friends and brothers, as you run swift-footed the course of virtue, straining toward the prize of the upward call with frequent and nimble leaps. I say nothing of my own or improvised, but only what I have gathered from the rose-garden of the celebrated and blessed Fathers, having walked through their meadows—whose roses are watered by the water from the side of God the Word made flesh, and reddened by the blood that flowed with it; who shine and bear torches over the whole world, above the luminaries of the firma- [?] Philip[?]

ment, holding fast the word of life; whose wick never falls, whose lamp is never broken; their oil is not spent, their lampstand is not shaken, their torch does not die down. They carry the cross as their staff, the Gospels as their wallet, and love as their crook and pipe, pasturing in them the rational flock of Christ. Ask, then, admirable friends, about the things you have come for, gleaning their divine seeds from my weakness.

Since we hear certain irrational and blasphemous utterances from some people about the only-begotten Son of God and the Spirit—who say that the Son is created and unlike the Father, and that the Spirit has been assigned the rank of a servant and messenger, and who hold still more irrational and debased opinions about them—we ask your love, which cherishes its children, to tell us concisely how matters stand concerning the divine and worshipful Trinity.

"Every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights," says the divine James. But you will rightly ask: of what lights? Properly and primarily, the true light is the Father, as John the Theologian says: "And this is the promise which we have heard from him"—that is, from the Son—"and declare to you, that God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all." But the Son too is light, as the same writer says: "For he was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world." And the immaterial and nightless light itself, which enlightens every intelligent and rational nature, says in the Gospels: "I am the light of the world." And I say that the divine Spirit is also light, in harmony with the divine David: "In your light we shall see light." For in God the Father we see the Son, who is also God; in the Son, the Father; and in both, the Spirit, as the Son says: "The Father is in me, and I in the Father," and, "He who has seen me has seen the Father." And concerning the Spirit he says: "The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father." So in the light that is the Father we see the light that is his Child and Word, and in the light that is the Son we see the light that is the Spirit. Let them rightly be understood, then, as three lights in one another, united without confusion and without separation. But the God who is over all, the Father almighty, is not begotten and not caused; he is the begetter and cause of his Son, as a spring is of a river, as the sun is of a ray, as fire is of a flame—a cause, yet not prior in origin. Likewise, what comes from them is caused, yet not later in origin. So also

the Son, having been ineffably begotten from the Father, his cause and begetter, [?]—not later in time, not lesser in power, not unlike in glory; being always in the Father, and from the Father, and with the Father, dwelling with the [?] without confusion, without separation, without change.

[QUESTION.] And how, having been begotten from the Father and having gone forth, can he be with the Father and in the Father? What has once been begotten and has gone forth from the one who possessed it—how is it again in the one who begot it? ANSWER. The Son and the Spirit did not go forth from the Father as mortals do, by flowing off, or cutting, or separation, but as rivers from a spring, being from it and in it and with it; and as the rays from the sun, in it and with it and from it; and as the flame and the light from the fire, with it and from it. I have spoken using an image that is faint, yet apt. So, being in the Father, he went forth, and he exists with the Father and will exist to the ages, as he himself says: "I am in the Father, and the Father in me"—showing by these words the sameness of essence and the identity and equal power of the Godhead. And again: "I came forth from the Father and have come into the world"—presenting the distinctness and particularity of the person. And the divine and all-holy Spirit is not begotten but proceeding, and caused, proceeding from the Father as cause. David too, the interpreter of the divine Trinity, says: "By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host." And Zechariah, in agreement with these, says: "Let the hands of Zerubbabel be strong, and the hands of Jozadak the priest, and the hands of the people; for I am with you, and my Word and my Spirit, says the Lord Almighty." The Father, then, is unbegotten, the Son begotten, the Spirit proceeding: lights in one another, not confused, of one light, ever-light, distinguished indivisibly by hypostases or persons, and united without confusion in the essence beyond essence, in a conjunction beyond understanding, and in a distinction without separation. Neither do the three hypostases cut the one essence of the Godhead into as many natures, nor has the one essence been fused into one person and one hypostasis, abolishing the three-mouthed and thrice-ever-flowing spring of the Godhead. Light, therefore, is the Father, light is the Son, light is the divine Spirit; but the three are one light, beyond time, before the ages, without beginning, in three persons, in three hypostases, three-lorded, three-throned, thrice-shining, thrice-radiant, equal in brightness, unchanging, undiminished, nightless, unconquered, uncapturable: one essence, one shared might, one glory, one kingdom, one Godhead, one will, one act[ion]

and command—identity in the Trinity, except for unbegottenness, begetting and procession, each hypostasis existing and continuing to exist in its own distinct way, not having begun, not ceasing, but always remaining the same and unchanging. For God the Father always existed, being always the Father of an only-begotten Child, a Voice existing as a hypostasis and doing all things, with the divine Spirit always present with them and worshipped together with them by every intelligent and rational nature. Among them there is no forebear and no descendant; they do not wax or wane like the light we perceive with our senses, or like the powers above the world. These all are the same in essence (as likewise the rational souls of mortals are all the same in essence), yet some hold one rank, others another station, and others a place of attendance and ministry; by their own choices, alterations and changes they incline freely toward the worse or the better, not falling into greater or lesser by any natural necessity—and it is in these things that they differ in eminence. A mortal is also called light; the sun and the moon are also called light; the varied dance of the stars has also been named light. But of the many material and various lights just mentioned, the Maker and Creator, in many parts and in many ways, is the true and immaterial light, the God and Father over all, with his only-begotten Child and the divine Spirit: the incorporeal, the invisible, the one beyond essence and beyond knowing, begetter of the Son and emitter of the Spirit by nature, ineffably, timelessly, before the ages. For there is nothing earlier or later, nothing pre-existent or introduced afterwards, in the divine Trinity; nothing before the ages, nothing of today, nothing beyond. For the three exist always: three co-holy, three co-unoriginate, three active, three co-active, three having form, three of the same form, three operative, three co-operative, three existing as hypostases, three co-existing as hypostases—not changing or passing over into one another, or mingling with one another. For the Father is always Father, and only Father, not also Son; the Son is always Son, and only Son, but not also Father. Likewise the divine Spirit is neither Father nor Son, but proceeding, without alteration. Unchangeably they always possess what is stable, distinctive and more than perfect, each according to his own hypostasis. Father and Son and Holy Spirit: a Trinity in a Monad, as it both exists and is understood, and is confessed and worshipped by those who worship in truth, and not in mere outward show and blasphemy—like Arius, who divides and weighs them in the balance, imagining greater and lesser in the divine Trinity; or like Sabellius, who confuses and mixes them together, madly teaching a Son-Fatherhood. The divine Trinity, then, is equal in power, equal in glory, equal in greatness—or rather beyond glory, beyond greatness, and higher than all comprehension—in one Godhead and kingdom, in one might and authority, having brought all things into being out of no underlying matter. As for how, let us leave that precise knowledge aside; for no one has seen the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father, and the divine Spirit reveals them to mortals. These, then, being three, not waxing, not waning, not [?], not gather-

ed, [are] from him or by him or toward him [?], understood piously and rightly believed—as the light reveals itself: light, fire, spirit—and, I think, by other comparisons and likenesses of expression, as one who is worthy and ministers to divine things might say.

[QUESTION.] And how is it that Moses writes, "The Lord your God, the Lord is one"; and Hannah in her song, "For there is none holy like the Lord, and there is none righteous like our God, and there is none holy besides you"; and Christ himself says, "That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent"—and he did not say "God"? ANSWER. Christ does not say these things to withdraw himself from the Godhead, but rather to lead us up to the monarchy and [?] to the knowledge of God, so that we may no longer be suppliants of the elements of the world, worshipping fellow servants instead of God and slipping into the polytheism of idols. So he says: "And Jesus Christ whom you have sent." Who is this, if not God? As John says: "The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known." And in agreement with these, Paul writes about Christ: "Theirs are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all."
If, then, the Son is equal to the Father, why is he not worshipped [?] in the writings of John and Paul as "the true light," as the Father is? [?]

[ANSWER.] Are you then able to suppress the catholic Epistle of John, which cries out toward its end that Jesus Christ is the true God and eternal life? And elsewhere, concerning the Father, he says that God is light, and the word "true" is not added. Must one then dare to say that the Father is not true light? [QUESTION.] You have sufficiently demonstrated the equality of the Father and the Son. Now, concerning the Holy Spirit, we [seek] the true harmony (2).
ANSWER. The Son himself is a sufficient teacher on this point. "For if I go away," he says, "he will come, the Spirit of
QUESTION 2 [?]. But Scripture also shows that the Spirit is created, when it says: "The Lord who makes firm the thunder and creates spirit."

[ANSWER.] But the text here is not speaking of the divine Spirit. For the word "holy" is not attached to what is created; it says simply, "creating spirit"—that is, the wind that blows to move the clouds and bring about [?] rain, by which the sound of thunder is naturally produced: the wind is trapped in the hollows of the clouds, and by bursting out and blowing it strikes with a crash on what lies below. It is like the thin, transparent membrane of a bladder found in birds or cattle, which unruly and ill-bred boys get hold of, dry in the air, and inflate with their own breath; then, secretly striking someone with it, they startle the bystanders with the noise of its bursting, out of [?] and from the depths of their hearts.
[QUESTION.] And how is it that in winter, when the same winds are present, and even more violent ones, the claps of thunder do not occur

[ANSWER.] Because the clouds become moist and softened by the thickness of the air, and by the misty dampness of the spring and river waters mingled with the land, the sound of bursting is not produced. This does not happen over the whole land, however, but only in its wintry regions. It is like a leather strap or a parchment: when they are puffed up and dried in the sun, they do not even take a touch without a sound, but when they are damp, they give no sign of bursting or contracting. So when the air around the earth turns muddy and thick, I think the moist [?] sound of thunder is not heard. Let it rightly be understood, then, that Scripture says the spirit of the wind is created; that is why it is placed alongside the thunder.

[QUESTION.] Having been well taught about the Spirit, we ask you to add what concerns the Son. For some teach that the saying of Scripture, "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works," was spoken about him, meaning that he is created and [?].

[ANSWER.] I too say that the saying refers to the Son—not, however, to his Godhead, but to his flesh from Mary. For he is uncreated in his Godhead, but created in what he assumed. For divine Scripture does not say of the Father, "creating his Christ for men," but

"announcing his Christ to men"—the true and immutable God, unchanging, uncreated and co-eternal with the Father, coexisting with him before the ages, as John cries out: "He who is in the bosom of the Father." He himself commands Moses to say to Pharaoh, not "He who was once created" (as the rash and vain-minded say), but: "You shall say, He Who Is has sent me." And he himself says of himself through Paul: "Christ, who is God over all."
[QUESTION.] But Moses wrote "He Who Is has sent me" about the Father, not about Christ.

[ANSWER.] I beg your love not to falsify the Gospels, in which the Lord speaks divinely: "Moses wrote about me," and "he himself bears witness about me." The Father, then, is He Who Is, and the Son is He Who Is with the Father, begotten from him, not fused with the Father, not having begun to exist, but being with the Father as his true Son. For there was never an age, or a time, or a moment when the Son was not. Was the Father himself, then, born of another Father before him? So as soon as you confess the Father, you confess along with him his only-begotten and most beloved Child. For those who think they honour the Father by giving him prior existence are utterly impious, placing time or a moment before Christ, the Maker of the ages. For with God there is no age, no time, no cycles of days, no [?], no indivisible instants, no twinkling of an eye; nor is it possible for the mind to imagine the timelessness of the ineffable Trinity. For if you say that there was once a Father when there was no Son, of whom then was he Father, if there was no Son? And if, again, you suppose that the Father himself did not exist, you take away his existence altogether. Believe, then, that the Son is of one essence with the Father (homoousios), not merged in essence with him (synousios), as in the drunken raving of Sabellius. For the first term indicates a hypostasis, while the second expresses a blasphemy against the Father, in which the Son and the Spirit are blended together and the Trinity is dissolved into a monad—something wholly alien to the divine laws.

But by saying God the Father, and God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit, you are plainly teaching tritheism.

Answer. I speak of a Trinity of the same essence, of the same might and Godhead. It does not increase, or diminish and cease, and it takes no addition to its number. For even though the Word was pleased to be united with flesh, he introduced nothing into the number of the Trinity. There is therefore one seal and one salvation in the Trinity, and nothing in it is created. For if the Father is uncreated but the Son and the Spirit are created, as the Arian fables and the rest of the vain-minded hold, on what reasoning is the uncreated joined and bound together with created things, mingled and glorified together with them, in the seal of the mystical perfection? Is it because the Father was unable to save, and took the two created ones to help him?

If, then, the Trinity has three persons and three hypostases, then each hypostasis would surely be one person, and each person subsistent. From this three Gods are shown. The Apostle refutes this when he writes, "One Lord, one faith, one baptism"; and before him Moses said to Israel, "The Lord your God, the Lord [?]"

But along with Moses and Paul, let us also hear the voice of the Cherubim and Seraphim as they cry without ceasing, "Holy, holy, holy." Those spiritual and God-bearing living creatures do not say this twice or four times. Nor do they say it only once, or say "Holies, holies," for that would make the singular many-named. Instead they cry out the sanctification three times without ceasing, yet they declare it in the singular, so as not to sow polytheism among the childish-minded.

What, then, is meant by the text "The Spirit searches the depths of God"? If the Trinity is consubstantial, with one knowledge, one will and one Godhead, and if nothing in it is created or unlike, how can the Spirit be said to search the depths of God, as though he did not know them? For if he knows, he has no need to search, since searching belongs to ignorance.

But he does not search out of ignorance or curiosity, as the madman Macedonius holds. He searches out of genuine kinship. For when the divine and all-holy Spirit comes to dwell in the virtuous and holy among mortals, he prepares them to search the depths of God. From the plain examination of the letter

he leads them up to the loftier sense through the search into more divine things. It is as though the mind had gone down into some deep, and the hook of the Spirit draws up out of the deep of worldly life the fish of the soul, holding in its mouth the precious stater, Christ, the Savior of all. For in the same way the chief of the apostles too is commanded to give the fish of the soul to those who demand payment for himself and for Christ. It holds in its mouth the stater, Christ, and the word of faith, and the praise lifted up from the depth of the heart. The lofty Apostle too says, "But we have received the Spirit of God, so that we may see the things freely given to us by God." And again the same Apostle says, "But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit." And again David, the singer of divine things, says, "I opened my mouth and drew in spirit." He means not the spirit of the air but the divine Spirit. Through this Spirit he declared a thousand years in advance the hidden things of God's divine-human coming, proclaiming plainly to God, "The uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom you have made plain to me."

And if the Son is God and equal to the Father, how can he not know what the Father knows? For he himself says in the Gospels, "No one knows the day or the hour of the consummation, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone."

Divine Scripture is accustomed to use human examples, and often illustrations from nature. Speaking divinely in the Gospels, the Lord says, "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, and like a grain of mustard seed." Paul, lofty in understanding, says, "There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies." Writing to the Corinthians, he also draws illustrations from the trumpet, the flute and the harp. So I too shall use a faint image drawn from our own life. Is my word, then, ignorant of my counsels? No one with any education at all will say so. How then could the Word of God the Father be ignorant of the Father's counsels, when he says, "All that the Father has is mine"? That is: being God, life, light, immortality and incomprehensibility. And again: "And all that is mine is yours, Father, and what is yours is mine." If, then, all that belongs to the Father is his, the knowledge of the Father is surely his too, and the Spirit's as well, as will be explained more fully shortly.
What then? Since I say, "All that the Father has is mine," do I too have the knowledge of the Father and know his counsel?
The Father, clearly, since he is without beginning, before the ages, incomprehensible, and the maker of all things.

If, then, the Father is greater than the hour, the day and all things, how can the Son know the greater and not know the lesser? And if he knows the maker and works with him in all things, how could he be ignorant of the things the maker has made? For he says, "As the Father knows me, so I know the Father." How then could he who knows the greater be ignorant of the lesser?
But we think the Father is also greater than the Son, as the Son himself says: "My Father is greater than I."

It is not pious to suppose that the Father is greater than the Son in circumference, bulk, time, season, rank, might, Godhead, size or appearance. None of these exists in the divine Trinity. Rather, because the Father is Father, the Son honors the Father as his true Son. The Divine is not a thing of bulk, and the Father is not bulkier than the Child. He is not subject to time, so as to make the begetter prior in time to the begotten. Nor again does the Father occupy some part of the heights. He contains all things and is contained by nothing, being without magnitude and without quantity.

If, then, the Son is equal to God the Father, and good as the Father is good, how can he himself say, "No one is good but one, God"?

Answer. When he says that God the Father alone is good, he is not denying his own goodness or withdrawing from the Godhead. Not to take the honor for himself but to refer it to the Father is clear proof of the highest affection and goodness, and it teaches us to love the Father. Humbling himself of his own free will, he does not seek glory [?]. Nor is he puffed up by his rank, like the haughty and boastful who have laid hold of some faint office. Swollen by the herald's voice, such people turn sullen and unapproachable and are transformed into untamed beasts. Since they do not exercise the authority of unending glory with gentleness and kindness, they will rightly be brought to account. But if you are quick to make a god of everything good, we shall have a great many gods on this score. In many places divine Scripture proclaims that there are other good things besides God. In one place it calls Samuel a good child, poor and wise; in another it says, "Saul son of Kish was good," the first king of Israel. And to Hannah, lamenting her childlessness and barrenness, Elkanah says,

"Why are you grieved? Am I not better to you than ten children?" And Solomon, wise in divine things, says, "It is good to go to a house of mourning." And, "May he open the heaven, his good treasury." And, "A good word is better than a gift." And, "A living dog is better than a dead lion." But even if the lion were alive, it would not be God, any more than the living dog is, except perhaps among the Greeks, who in their madness deify springs, onions and the winds of the stomach.

Earlier you promised to speak more fully about Christ's knowledge of the day and the hour of the consummation. Give us that account, so that our opponents may not find some other way to get the better of us when we debate them.

This has already been discussed briefly, but I admire your many-sided inquiry into it. I speak, then, of the holy Word: the living and subsistent Word, the King of all creation, the true Son of the Father, the radiance of his glory and the imprint of his hypostasis, coeternal and co-enthroned with the Father, the impartial judge of the living and the dead. He is life from life, light from light, wisdom from wisdom, the ever-flowing spring from the divine fountain. He is the river that pours out his divine gifts without suffering diminution and gladdens the city of God with its streams, as the divine song says. He is the root of Jesse, the scepter of David, the rod and the divine flower that springs from it, according to the inspired Isaiah. He is the lion, the king from the tribe of Judah, according to Moses the hierophant. He is the rational sheep, according to Isaiah, and the innocent lamb sacrificed for the salvation of the world, according to Jeremiah, who faced many dangers. He is the stone rejected by the Jews and set as the head of the corner of the Church of the Gentiles, holding together the whole building of the fellowship, according to David the singer. He is the angel of the greatest counsel and mighty God, as Isaiah says. He became mortal while remaining God, unchanged in nature and unaltered in Godhead. He is the Word incarnate and born in the flesh, the Word made flesh, who remained what he was and did not change by nature into flesh. (For after John had thundered, "In the beginning was the Word," and struck the whole creation with awe, he then added, "And the Word became flesh." The first phrase shows that the Word is God before the ages and beyond time, co-enthroned with the Father. The word "became" shows his later divine-human coming forth from the ever-virgin Mary.) This living, holy and subsistent Word, who speaks and hears, says divinely in the Gospels, "No one knows that day or that hour, neither the angels of hea[ven]

For, as I said earlier, if he knows the Father, who is above all magnitude and comprehension, how can he be ignorant of that day and hour, which are mere vapor or dust, and still more feeble and faint compared with the Divine? He plainly declares, "No one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father." For as the Father in his greatness knows the Son, so the Child in his supreme greatness knows the Begetter. And the divine Spirit, being equal in greatness, knows the Father and the Son and is known by both. Divine Scripture teaches us two kinds of knowledge, a twofold knowing and perceiving: one by action, the other by sight. I shall show this with faint examples, and so snap the cable of the heresies, if anyone is unaware of it [?], and draw you away from the blasphemous phalanx. For in this way Christ, lifted up on the cross, takes captive in his turn the mortals whom the wily Belial had taken captive, according to David the divine singer. For the inspired David foresaw the saving passion and our captivity when he said, "Ascending on high, you led captivity captive; you gave gifts among men." What are these gifts? Faith in the Trinity, the celebration of the mysteries, and the hope of the resurrection. And the song of divine things goes on to add, "Even the disobedient, that they might dwell there." Who are they, then, and where do they dwell? They are those from among the Jews and the Greeks, dwelling in the divine tent of the Church. Paul was once disobedient, a wolf that struck and tore the Christians. Now he is the pillar of the Church, the lofty-minded trumpet of the faith. He who once persecuted wickedly turned for the good, and he is willingly scourged for those who are persecuted. He who struck others is beaten with rods. He who killed is voluntarily beheaded for the sake of the slain. The voice from heaven and the blow to his eyes changed him to this, and Christ, who had purchased him, renamed him Paul instead of Saul, so that he might give the Gentiles the name of Christians. But let us return to the subject of our discourse and use the sharper eye of the mind to understand the twofold knowledge and perception. After Adam and Eve had been driven out of paradise, ashamed because of the forbidden fruit, divine Scripture says of them, "Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore a child." What shall we say, then? That he did not know her in paradise, though he said of her, "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh"? No, he knew her there by sight alone, but here by sight and bodily action. Likewise Abraham knew Sarah his wife, though she was not unknown to him before they came together. And concerning David the book of Kings says, "David grew old, and they covered him with garments, but he did not get warm. And they sought a virgin

to sleep beside him and keep him warm. And there was found," it says, "Abishag the Shunammite, and David did not know her, though she slept beside him." Shall we say, then, that in his case he did not know her even by sight and touch? We ourselves, too, often answer those who bring accusations about women by calling curses down on ourselves and swearing that we have not known her, whoever it is, woman or man. Clearly in this we speak the truth with respect to the act, though from voice and sight we plainly know who is male and who is female. The Son, then, is not ignorant of that day and hour. He reveals in advance all its signs and terrors, and describes it by its marks as though it were already present. But he did not wish to answer the idle question, and he fittingly arranges for the day to remain unknown to all. In this way, thinking that each day and hour may be that one, they will prepare for it and soberly await his coming to repay the rewards of this life. Away, then, with such folly! Stop babbling that the maker of the ages is ignorant of a single day and hour, he in whom are all the treasures of wisdom, as the holy Apostle says.
What then? Does the Father know that day in one way and the Son in another?

We do not say that the Father has one knowledge and the Child and the Spirit another. Rather, one part has been done and the other is held in reserve. The Father knows that day by a twofold knowledge and action: in one respect he created it, and in the other he decided to judge all people through his true Child. The Son too knows it, equally with the Begetter, by perception and by the action of creating, but not yet by the action of judging. For he has not yet judged, separating some to unquenchable fire and others to unending delight. This is not due to ignorance but to long-suffering, which grants the wicked a time to amend. Lamenting in a dirge those who are not cleansed of their shame and do not come to their senses, David says, "The sinner borrows and will not repay." By the loan he means the time of divine long-suffering, and by repayment he means repentance. And the divine singer goes on to add, "But the righteous has compassion and gives." The giver is God, and what is given is the time for repentance. For when God lends to mortals, he rarely or barely or never gets it back, waiting for the debtor's repayment until the very end. But when mercy is lent to him through our neighbors, he repays it many times over, since his habit is to be quick to do good and slow to punish. Even now the impious hate God, and the unbelieving stumble over the divine works, [?] the footing of their minds. Injustice prevails, and the Judge is long-suffering until his second
coming to us. That coming is his practical knowledge of that day and hour, the knowledge that belongs to judgment.
And how can he say, "To my God and your God, and to my Father and your Father"? Does he not show by this that he is not equal to the Father, when he says, "I go to my God"?

Do not let your mind fall into thinking that the Child is less than the Father because it stumbles over a word spoken in his divine-human dispensation. In the Old Book, while he was still bodiless, before the incarnation, he will not be found saying, "I go to my God." And even after he was united with flesh, the prophets proclaim him God no less. Isaiah cries out, "A child is born to us and given to us, whose government is upon his shoulder, and his name is called Angel of great counsel, Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Ruler, Prince of peace, Father of the age to come." David sings of his second divine-human coming, which gathers everyone for judgment and recompense: "Our God will come openly, our God, and will not keep silence. Fire will go before him, and round about him a mighty tempest." That tempest drives the guilty together to punishment and sets them before the dread and unswerving judgment seat of our God and Savior over all, Jesus Christ. Fittingly, then, he says, "I go to my God" because of his bodily dispensation, and he says, "I go to my Father" because of his natural, divine birth from the Father. So the Father is God of the disciples and Father of the Child by nature, but God of the Son according to the flesh, and Father of the disciples by grace.

And how is it that Scripture says of the Father, "He will not hunger, he will not thirst, and his understanding cannot be searched out," but says of the Son that he hungered after forty days of temptation in the desert, and that when he was thirsty he asked the Samaritan woman for a drink? Again, it says of the Father, "He who keeps Israel will not grow weary, will not slumber or sleep." Yet Jesus grew weary from his journey and sleeps in the boat. Do not these things fall outside what belongs to God?

Put away your childishness, man! The subsistent, living and holy Word, when he came, not only consented to hunger but also suffered in the humanity he assumed from us, and went to burial in it. First he was scourged on the back, and Pilate sent him bound to Herod, in that union. Then he was struck on the cheeks and spat upon. He also wept, and in his agony he sweated; and his

sweat became like clots of blood, and an angel appeared, strengthening him, as the divine Luke says. And as though he did not know, he asked about Lazarus, "Where have you laid him?" About the woman with the flow of blood, who stole healing through the fringe of his garment, he says, "Who touched me?" To the Jews who were seeking to arrest him he says, "Whom are you looking for?" To the disciples he says, "Who do people say that I am?" and "How many loaves do you have?" Yet he was ignorant of none of these things, as the outcome of what happened shows. In Lazarus's case, his prediction of the death shows it. I shall speak of this more clearly a little later, since the hour is pressing the discourse toward its close. In the case of the woman with the flow of blood, it is shown by his awareness of her touch and the generous help of his power. In the case of those who arrested him, it is shown by the pretext for their attack, the nearness of that hour, and his saying "I am he" to the murderers. In the case of what people said of him [?], it is shown by the blessing bestowed on Peter for his most exact and steadfast confession. In the case of the loaves, it is shown by the boundless abundance of leftovers from slight and meager means. The loaves were only five, yet they fed five thousand to the full and filled twelve baskets with fragments after the crowd had eaten. They multiplied at the touch and breaking of him who in the beginning commanded the dry land to sprout wheat and the waters to bring forth [?] every kind of swimming creature, and everything whatever that grows from them.

And if Christ is perfect God, how can the evangelist say, "The child Jesus grew and became strong in spirit, and advanced in wisdom and stature"? God does not grow or advance in wisdom, nor does he become strong as though he were weak.

He is the wisdom and power of God the Father, as the holy Apostle says. In his dispensation he passes through life as we do, and by a voluntary humility he who planted Adam's ear teaches mortals wisdom. Taking up briefly what has been said, I shall show more clearly that my God, without turning or change, became a babe for the sake of mortals, and that the growth he received was of the body, not of the Godhead. Jeremiah, the prophet who faced many dangers, says, "He is a man, and who will know him?" By this he shows that he is God, hidden from those whose minds are dull. Through unbelief they cannot grasp the knowledge, just as those with weak eyes cannot bear the sight of the sun because of their weakness. But if he was a man, how was he not known as we are known? Every man is certainly known, whether through his parents, his relatives and kin, or those who share his house and table. So the prophet presents him as coming from none of our kind when he says, "He is a man, and who will know him?" This is because, being God, he was pleased to become man. Hunger
…and he also accepts thirst for water, the blameless passions of the body, refuting the folly of the Manichaeans, who make the incarnation a mere seeming and a phantom.
Do you say that the body of the Word had a soul, or that the Godhead acted in place of a soul? For many say this, and it seems plausible,

It is simple-minded and childish to think that the body of God the Word was without a soul. For the Word was united, in a way beyond reason, to both of the things that make up mortal nature, I mean soul and body, and gave strength to each part. If one of them had been lacking to him, our salvation would be incomplete: either the body would remain in corruption, or the soul would be held fast in Hades.

And why does John not say this? Having said, "In the beginning was the Word," and, "The Word became flesh," he does not add that he also became soul, or that he took a soul.

Answer. If we suppose that the Lord's body had no soul, it will certainly follow that we declare the Godhead capable of suffering, since it would pervade the flesh as a soul does and would by nature give way to hunger and thirst, to sleep and tears, to agony and sweat. But we must listen to the inspired David, who sings of the divine-human soul, speaking in the person of Christ himself: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor let your holy one see corruption." And the Savior himself says in the Gospels: "I have authority to lay down my soul, and to take it up again"; and, "I am the good shepherd, who lays down his soul for the sheep."

Does the Father also have a soul, then? For Isaiah, speaking in his person, says of Christ: "Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased." If, then, you think the Son has a soul because of what he said, surely we must also say that the Father has a soul because of what he said. But if the Father has none, then neither, surely, does the Son; and if he does have one, this shows that he is unlike the Father.

But the Father has no soul, since he did not take on mortal flesh as the Son did, nor did he come to the cross and death. It was for these that the Word needed flesh: to be held by it and to suffer, and to make mortals, instead of mortal, immortal and blessed forever.
And why did John not say plainly that he also took a soul, as you say he did about the flesh?

Well then: Scripture says that God made man, taking dust from the earth, and does not add that he made a head or a brain, a liver or a spleen or lungs, or any other of the mysteries of our nature. Shall we therefore suppose that we lack them and do not possess them, because Scripture does not list our natural organs in detail? Just as in our own case the whole is recognized from a part, so let us believe that the holy God the Word was united to both soul and body, lest by thinking the divine body soulless we attach passions to God by nature.

And how is Christ equal to the Father in Godhead, when he was gripped by agony and sweat and was strengthened by an angel, as Luke says of him? For when these matters were raised earlier, you passed over the explanation.

From these things we are clearly taught that the living and subsistent holy God the Word united what is ours to himself not in phantom and seeming but in truth, except only unholy wickedness, for the Divine cannot admit it. Agony, we say, belongs to the soul, and sweating to the body. As for the clots of blood that burst from the flesh, I think they show that, through the moisture poured out, the serpent's venom, which was poured into us through the ear when the divine commandment was transgressed in paradise, is being sucked out of our nature by the union of God the Word; so that the arch-evil demon is no longer worshiped by us with the reek of sacrifices, with blood and the slaughter of children. Nor does it seem to me that the angel strengthened him in the sense of reinforcing him and making his own Maker strong. For how could a servant strengthen a master, or a spirit make a rock firm [?]? "For the rock was Christ," says the divine Apostle. And again: "Who makes his angels spirits"; and again: "Beyond all dispute the lesser is blessed and strengthened by the greater." From this let it reasonably be understood that the angel was making a kind of victory gesture over the marvelous victory of Christ that was to come, enacting in deed the words of Moses the lawgiver, who more than a thousand years before cried out plainly: "Rejoice, O heavens, together with him"—because he has raised up on high the things below—"and let all the angels of God worship him," as they see their own ranks increased by the addition of mortals; "Rejoice, O nations, with his people"—you from among the nations who are added to Enoch, to Abraham, to Isaac, to Joseph, to David, to Christ, to the Church—"for the blood of his sons," he says, "is avenged, and he will avenge it, and he will repay justice to his enemies, and to those who hate

him he will repay, and the Lord will cleanse the land of his people." Moreover, the lofty Apostle too, as it were strengthening Christ with a victory acclamation, says: "Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God." And again, teaching all creation to make supplication to him as victor, he says: "At the name of Jesus Christ every knee shall bow, of things in heaven and on earth, and every tongue shall confess him." In agreement with him John, the son of thunder, proclaiming Christ as God in a victory acclamation, says: "And we beheld his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth." And we too, following the angel, as it were strengthen Christ with a victory acclamation at the time of the divine celebration of the mysteries, crying out: "For yours is the might and the kingdom and the power and the glory." See here the oneness of the divine nature of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. This is also the custom in athletic contests, whether in gymnastic exercises or in the pankration: brave and robust athletes are cheered on and anointed by certain boys, quite young, whose cheeks are not yet shadowed by down, so that, swelling with vigor, they may advance more firmly against their opponents. This is not because strength and might are instilled into the brave by the weaker, but because law and custom come before every performance. It is certainly the law of mastership to be anointed and flattered by servants; and Christ, the Master of all alike, is the fulfillment of the law. And it is the law for angels to flatter and fawn upon their wise Maker and Master, being helped, not helping. For if he needed strength from them, he would have needed it far more in the wilderness when he was tempted by the devil for forty days. But this is nowhere said in Scripture: for angels, it says, came, not to help him, but they ministered to him; which clearly shows his mastership and their servitude. So let what concerns the angel be understood according to the account given. For neither do the holy Cherubim in heaven impart holiness to the divine Trinity when they cry out unceasingly, "Holy, holy, holy"; nor again, when we cry out in the Trisagion, "Holy God, holy Mighty, holy Immortal," do we instill holiness or strength or immortality into the Divine.

Having been sufficiently taught by us about the divine questions you set us, we ask next that the voices of the senseless be refuted. For they say that the Savior did not know where Lazarus's tomb was, nor who the woman with the issue of blood was who touched his hem, and that he was not

[?] BROTHER [?]

perfect God; for he advanced and grew strong in wisdom and stature and grace, as the Gospel says.

But do not let the things he said by way of the dispensation become a pretext for blasphemy for you: "Where have you laid him?" or, "Who touched me?" or, "Whom do you seek?" or, "Who do people say that I am?" or that "The child grew and became strong and advanced in wisdom and stature." For none of these convicts of ignorance God the Word, who became like us for our sake; rather, they show him to be equal to the Father. "For my Father," he says, "is working until now, and I am working"—not as though something were lacking in our fashioning of the universe, as if creation were seen to be incomplete, but we are working out the life of virtue, setting before mortals the life lived with God our Father, through those whom he has already changed from worse to better. The Father asked our forefather Adam, when he had transgressed, "Where are you?"—not because he did not know that he was trying to hide, and that the transgressor must be made to tremble, but as though laughing at and mocking his evasion and the folly of his ill counsel, as he tried once again to hide after [?] the forbidden thing. To him the One who forgets nothing says: "Where are you, you who thought to be made divine by the serpent's counsel? Where are you, who disobeyed God and trusted the enemy? Do not hide," he says, "for you will not escape notice, now that you have stripped off the pure and blessed life." In the same way, then, the Son was not ignorant of where Lazarus was shut in. Two days before he reached Bethany, which had borne Lazarus, he said to his followers, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, and I am going to wake him"—Lazarus who was already four days dead and stinking, a corpse. How, then, could he who knew what happens in places before he reached them be ignorant, once he set foot there in the body, of what he had foreknown by the Godhead with which he fills all things? Rather, he asked by way of the dispensation, so that the Jews, gathering at the tomb on the pretext of showing it to him, might themselves become witnesses of the dead man's resurrection: how, though his head was bound with a cloth, his face covered by the wrapping of linen, and his feet fettered with grave-bands, though his skull had already [?] and he had rotted with gaping mouth, and his tongue and eyes had melted away—how by the voice of the Creator his soul was drawn from afar and entered the body it had left; how, with his feet bound, he leapt from the tomb and was driven out, seen unharmed and whole, strengthened by the voice of the Word and using it as a helper for his exit. And it seems to me that death too was prodded to a very swift raising, lest, if it delayed and a second call came from the Word, he should release all who were there at once; which (10) "How with a cloth . . . how by the voice . . . using [?]"

and six days later the wretch suffered it, when he who calls the dead back to life came to him, according to the prophecy of Job and Isaiah, those inspired men, who a thousand years before had cried out plainly. The one said: "You came upon the sea, and walked in the tracks of the abyss; the gates of death open to you in fear, and the gatekeepers of Hades cowered when they saw you." In agreement with these the divine David, the singer of divine things, says: "Sing to God, sing praise to his name; make a way for him who rides upon the west: the Lord is his name." We are taught to make ourselves a way for the Lord, and to make a dwelling for him through a virtuous way of life, establishing the Divine within us and becoming his abode and temple, as he himself declared in the Gospels and, speaking divinely, in Paul. By the west is understood our nature, and the toilsome region of the world darkened by the pleasures of the passions. Hades too is understood. Into these the immaterial and shadowless light flashed and transformed everything for the better: it renewed our nature, brightened the world, and despoiled Hades for gentleness [?] and the release of those held there. What comes from David I have treated only dimly; the passages of Job and Isaiah we shall explain shortly, putting them off for now because the hour is short. Both of them proclaimed the future firmly as though it were already done, knowing how their prediction would turn out. So, by way of the dispensation, he pretended ignorance, though he knew all the secrets of the whole creation, so that by his question a crowd might be roused to show him the place, and the marvel might be attested all the more by his enemies.

And from this we are taught that the Son is equal to God the Father, and that, like the Father, he asked not out of ignorance but by way of the dispensation. For the Father said to Cain, the first murderer, who killed his brother out of envy because his gifts were preferred, with jealousy lurking within him and whetting the sword of murder: "Where is Abel your brother?"—not because he did not know, but offering the bloodstained man an occasion for repentance. But Cain, going on to madness, said, "Am I my brother's keeper?" And again the divine voice convicted him: "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me." From this it is shown that the question was put by God not out of ignorance but out of love for humanity [?] Job [?]; [?] 14:9; Ps. [?]:5.

and applied like a physician to the murderer. In the same way the Son also asked, not out of ignorance, but so that he would not seem puffed up to those of duller mind by announcing the miracle himself, and so that, if he kept silent, we would not be deprived of the marvel. He used the question by way of the dispensation, so that she might come forward and proclaim the release from her affliction that had come to her through touching his hem. For the divine evangelist says: "When the woman saw that she had not escaped notice, she came trembling and worshiped him," and so on. Moreover, at his first coming to us in the flesh, he pretended ignorance and said to Abraham, "Where is Sarah your wife?" But if he had not known, he would not have exposed her as being inside the tent and smiling. For "Sarah laughed within herself" shows that she was smiling. And suddenly, when he was entertained by the patriarch as a guest, one of three, he asked for the hostess by name and promised that she, though barren, would bear a child. The fulfillment of the promise was Isaac, born of her. For no creature, no name, nothing past, present or future, nothing at all that is spoken or thought, escapes the knowledge of Christ.

Let us not attach those things to the Godhead. For according to the Godhead he does not grow, nor cease, nor diminish, nor is he glorified, nor raised to a height, nor does he come into being [?], nor is he contracted. But he advances, growing strong and increasing, in the form of a servant which is like ours. For the fullness of the Godhead was not diminished, nor did he become God by advancement from being a man

And how did we say that the Son is not created, when the Apostle writes about him, "Consider the high priest of our faith, who was faithful to him who made him"? And, "Let all the house of Israel know that God has made this Jesus whom you crucified both Lord and Christ." And Solomon too says, speaking in the person of Christ to God the Father: "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works."

I have dealt with these matters earlier, and to go round and round the same things again would be absurd, or childish. "He made him" and "he created me" I take to be meant of the flesh. We also see that parables are not identical with the things they are compared to. We know that "The Lord created me" is placed in the book of Proverbs. Proverbs are, so to speak, wayside sayings, for in secular learning oimos means "way"; so that parables are by-paths and images of things. "For the kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed," says the Lord. How, then, could countless multitudes, peoples of angels and archangels, find room in a seed that is the least of all seeds? But surely the all-wise Lord uses this image either because of the humble condescension of his voluntary poverty to our littleness, through which we gain shade and relief from the pains of the present life; or because of the small size of the gospel flock at the beginning; or because of the sharpness of the Word's Godhead, by which showers of tears are stirred in those who sweetly and delicately partake, through virtue, of the spiritual mustard of repentance—filled with which the inspired David sings: "Every night I will wash my bed, I will drench my couch with my tears"; and again, "My eyes have run down with streams of water"; or because of the sharp divine judgment that will be brought upon those overcome by evil, as divine Scripture everywhere testifies, and as secular learning, through Plato, threatens wailing in fire; or because of the uncut and undivided union and single hypostasis of the Word and the flesh, which no reasoning or conception can divide. For the divine seed of the kingdom slips once again through the fingers of the minds of those who divide, and will not in any way allow itself to be enclosed in the palms of blasphemers. Yet no one knows clearly whether Solomon, the writer of proverbs, says "The Lord created me" of God. But if the Sage's saying is to be taken by us in this way, it seems to me to signify the Lord's divine-human coming, when he says: "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works; before the age he founded me; before all the hills he begets me." How, then, is what is begotten founded, and how is what is created be-

-gotten? For what is created is not begotten, and what is begotten is not created; the one is one thing, the other another. But we see that the Son is both: uncreated in his Godhead, created in his humanity. It is often the custom of divine Scripture to mention first what is nearest to us, and what is ancient second. So the divine Matthew does too: beginning from what is nearer and easier to grasp, he proclaims Christ to us: "The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham." On the one hand he draws in the Jews, who falsely claimed to be children of Abraham and vainly prided themselves on those inspired men whose way of life they did not imitate; on the other, while the company [?] was still in its infancy, he guides us from the nearer things toward the knowledge of God. And going on in the Gospel he begins to speak of Christ as God, leading our minds up to the more divine things as if by a ladder. So Solomon, wise in divine things, says: "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways"; for the beginning of the way of the righteousness of the Gospel is that God the Word was born for us according to the flesh from Mary, ever-virgin; he who "before the age founded me." Before the cycle of the week of the present age came to be, on the sixth day, the soul was founded in Adam by the builder of our nature; and so after the sixth day the seventh day of the age was created, which revolves upon itself in sevens throughout the whole present age. Then, advancing to things more divine and more primordial, he says: "Before all the hills he begets me," meaning by hills here the heavens, or the powers above them. For neither the heavens, nor angels, nor archangels, nor season, nor time, nor age, nor anything else that can be thought or spoken is older than the Son. For he is the maker of the ages and of all things together, as Paul cries out plainly: "Through whom he also made the ages," and, "In him all things were created, visible and invisible," for "all things came into being through him." So he is created from Mary in what he assumed; the soul is founded in the body that is created; and the Word, united to both, the one with the other, is seen as a created mortal but understood as uncreated God, from an uncreated Father, not [?] a father

QUESTION. [?] And how does the Son himself show that he is created, when he says, "I am the door of the sheep, and the way"? Likewise he is represented by the prophets through created things: by Isaiah as a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; by David as a pillar of fire; by others as a lion, a sheep, and other things
But let us not fall asleep over the letter and so shut ourselves out of the more divine things. For according to the lofty Apostle, "The letter kills, but the spirit

[?] the luminary undergoes no cutting, no flowing away, no swelling, no contraction; and passing through clear glass into houses, and as it were begetting its rays over every land, it is seen everywhere undiminished and undivided. Likewise a torch that kindles countless lamps suffers no flowing away, no cutting [?]. If, then, these things remain unharmed, we shall believe that the Divine surpasses them infinitely and altogether [?]; for all things together are but a vapor compared with it. So the Father begot the Son not through cutting or [?], not through swelling and contraction; but being incorporeal, [he begot] an incorporeal, subsistent Word, hearing and

…speaking. So let those who honour the Father in a way that dishonours him, rash in counsel and vain in mind, not dare to declare the Son a creature. For if, as he says, the Father suffers in begetting, then I say he grows weary in creating. Where, then, shall we find the source of the Son without blaspheming the Father as one who suffers or grows weary? Away with you, then, who honour the Divine in a way that dishonours it! For whoever blasphemes the Child stones the Father, as the Son himself declares in the Gospels: "Whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father either."

And how is it that some say Christ became Son of God by election and grace? For the Father does not say, "This is my beloved Son, whom I begot," but "in whom I am well pleased." And Isaiah, speaking in the person of God the Father, says of Christ: "Behold my Child whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased." Likewise Solomon says: "Chosen out of ten thousand."

It seems you belong to the drunken raving of Arius, since you argue so contentiously against the truth. Show me, then, those who were like Christ, from among whom the Father tested and chose Christ alone. For if he alone is the only-begotten Son, he has no brother to be set beside him. For the divine David sang of him: "Who among the sons of God shall be likened to the Lord?" and further on: "He is great and terrible over all who are round about him." So no one who advanced by grace or by progress can be compared with God the Word, who became man for the sake of mortals and was fittingly chosen. For though there were many myriads of women still uncorrupted, he set apart Mary alone out of them all, and in her he ineffably united and wove together what is ours with himself. As the divine tragedian says: "He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob, which he loved." By this he means the ever-virgin Mary, who had not yet come to birth but had been conceived in her mother's womb. And the Father, delighting in the Word's taking flesh from her, cries from above: "Behold my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." In this way he makes known to us one Child, God, born of him and of the Ever-Virgin, of one substance with him and with us: with him in divinity, with her in what he assumed. For the immortal, having of his own will become visible like mortals, remained what he was, while being seen as what I am.
And how does the Apostle show him to be Son of God by advancement and by being loved, when he says of the Father: [?]…
…: "He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love."

But these words do not show him to be Son of God by advancement. For elsewhere the same holy Apostle says that God loved us in Christ, which indicates that Christ is the love of God the Father, just as he is his wisdom and power. The Father, then, is love, and so is the Son: as he is light from light and God from God, so he is love from love. For "God is love," says John. So let the followers of Arius's madness stop thinking the Creator a creature, since neither of the Testaments means this. We have four Gospels, containing one thousand one hundred and sixty-two chapters. From beginning to end the Son in them speaks of God the Father and the Father of the Child, yet neither of them says, "I created a Son for myself," or, "He created me."

What, then, do you hold the Virgin Mary to be, created or uncreated? And the body of Christ that came from her? And how do you worship Christ? For if you say created, as you absolutely must, then clearly you worship a creature; but if you do not worship him, you deny the Son of God. I do not depict an image of the Godhead, for it is simple, invisible and without form. But when I portray the image of the flesh, I worship it as befits God because of the hypostatic union.

By my health, I shall not worship Christ as a creature, but as the maker of creatures and as God. It is just as I honour the emperor together with his purple robe in a single act of homage, without separating him from it. Or do you think anyone would say to the sovereign, "Get up from your throne so that I may do you homage"? Or, "Come out of the temple so that I may sing your praises without the lifeless [?]"? If, then, lifeless things are honoured along with the living one, and cheap things along with the Master of the whole world under the sun, then the Word too will rightly be worshipped in a single act of worship together with the temple of his body, which I call his purple robe, his tunic and his throne.
And if he is God with a body, how can he himself say, "No one has ever seen God"? If he was God, then everyone alive at that time saw him.

The Son says of the Father that no one has ever seen God. He did not say, "No one has ever seen the Son, who is God the Word and became man." Prophets and apostles and each of the righteous did see God, but no one can see him as he is in his nature. No nature can take in that sight. He appears to each of the worthy, but not without some ve-

-il, suited to the measure of each one's purification. So Job saw him, but through a whirlwind and clouds. Before him Abraham saw him speaking through angels. Jacob saw him as a man wrestling with him, and Moses saw him in the midst of the thick darkness. Likewise the rest of the company of inspired men saw him through riddles and veils. The apostles too saw God the Word made man through the flesh, the Child of God and of man, each according to the measure of his own virtue and strength of soul. It is like people whose bodily eyes are strong or dim: some can gaze at the sun for a long time, while others, seeing faintly, cannot bear the luminary's lightning or the impact of its flashing rays. We see the sea from a mountaintop or some hill, and we speak truly when we say we have seen it, yet we see only the surface of the open sea, and only part of that. From this shore or bank the eye cannot reach the lookout on the far side, but fades out into the air. Nor can the mind find its hollow depths or its lowest floor, for we always suppose something beyond what we conceive, holding in its edges so that it does not pour out or flow away downward, and our thought quite naturally gives up in helplessness. We also see the heaven, but not all alike: each sees according to the strength of his eye. The mind does not reach (12) its limit, nor can it attain with precision to the solid resistance of its vault. So we see our fellow servants not as they are by nature, but as far as we can take them in. For both visible and invisible things lie before us, the former partially and the latter wholly. In the same way the Divine is both visible and invisible to mortals: visible through the veil of a body, by condescension; invisible because by nature it cannot be grasped. Stalk and chaff cannot endure the nearness of fire, but are burnt up and fall to the ground. When Christ briefly unveiled his divinity (13) on the mount of the Transfiguration, he sent the pillars of the Church reeling. Peter, James and John fell down shaking with fear and were very nearly melted by the fire of the divinity. With this in view the divine Apostle also cries out plainly: "From the greatness and beauty of created things he is correspondingly perceived." If we cannot see the whole nature of heaven, earth and sea, how shall we be able to see their maker in his nature?
(12) Ἀφικνεῖται: perhaps ἐφικνεῖται. Ed.
(13) Ἑαυτῷ: perhaps ἑαυτοῦ, or ἐν ἑαυτῷ.

Hear, then, my admirable friend, the Spirit commanding with authority and sovereign power, and acting equally with the Father and the Son. "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them," he says to the apostles. In harmony with this the Son says to Paul: "Go into the city, and there you will be told what you must do." Elsewhere the Acts of the Apostles say: "So these, sent out by the Spirit, went down to Seleucia." Likewise the Son says, "Go and make disciples of all nations," and likewise the apostles say, "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you nothing beyond what is necessary." Likewise Paul says: "I say, yet not I but the Lord, that a wife should not separate from her husband." "They went through Phrygia and the region of Galatia," it says, "having been forbidden by the Spirit to speak the word in Asia." Likewise the Son says to the apostles: "Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans." The divine David too, showing that all things are the work of the divine Trinity, sings in the Psalms: "By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their host." By "Lord" he means the Father, by "Word" the Child, and by "breath" the divine Spirit. In agreement with this Paul, the divine teacher of all under heaven (15′), says: "There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and varieties of workings, but the same God, who works all things in all." He presents three persons, but one Godhead, one authority and one kingdom.
We ask you to add to what has been said why Scripture compares the Holy Spirit to water and fire.

It is not idly (14) or without purpose that the divine Spirit is compared to these. The water that rains from heaven makes things green, gives life and nourishes. It enriches all things and penetrates all things, and though it is of one form, it works in many ways: from a single spring different kinds of plants are watered. The same rain, one in nature and appearance, does good in many ways. In the lily it is seen as white, in the rose as red, purple in violets and yellow in the crocus. It falls on the fig tree in one form but turns out in different forms: sweet in the fruit, sharp in the milky sap drawn from it. The same rain comes to the vine in one form and thickens into tendrils, shoots, sour grapes, clusters, wine and drink. In short, it becomes all things in all. Being one in form,
(15′) ὑπ’ οὐρανῶν: perhaps ὑπ’ οὐρανόν or ὑπ’ οὐρανούς. Ed.
(14) Οὐκ εἰκῆ, etc. These things almost word for word de-

it unites itself with the nature of those that receive it and gives each what suits it. Fire, again, is one in form but works in many ways: it warms, purifies, cooks, tests, gives light and burns. In the same way the divine Spirit is one, of one form, of one manner and of one substance, indivisible and unharmed, and distributes grace to each as it wills. It is like what naturally happens to plants. As long as the gloom of winter holds sway over them, they remain fruitless; but when they are moistened by rain and warmed by the sun, they come back to life and sprout. So too with the souls of mortals. As long as they are gripped by the winter of wickedness and show gloom and unsociability toward their neighbours, they are dead and fruitless. But once they receive the divine rain of the Spirit through the word of instruction, rub off the shame of wickedness and lay aside the much-suffering garment of matter, their rational part is rekindled. They come back to life, as it were, through the divine moisture and warmth of the Spirit and bear fruit, as the divine saying has it, "one thirty, another sixty, another a hundred." The Spirit uses the tongue of one for wisdom, of another for prophecy, of another for putting demons to flight, of another for making divine matters clear. It teaches one to be temperate and another to be merciful. It strengthens one for self-control, and anoints and prompts another for martyrdom. It appears differently in different people, yet is not itself different. As that sublime Apostle, great in understanding, writes: "To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each individually as it wills." Just as it belongs to water both to make things green and to make them rot, and to fire both to burn and to give light, so it belongs to the divine Spirit both to do good and to punish.

QUESTION 44. Since we have found in you a physician of souls, who amply heals our souls through your proofs and rescues us from error, we ask you to add to what has been said something about angels: whether they have orders, how many (14) there are, what their nature is, and whether they [know] the future…

The angels are created and changeable. They are rational spirits sent out to serve, as the singer of divine things says, and Paul after him, in agreement: "He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire." In this they indicate both their nature and their dignity. There are seven
(14) Πόσαι: perhaps πόσα or πόσοι. Ed.

orders, as Jude wrote and as the sublime Apostle lists them. Following him, the priests of the divine rite also cry aloud to God: "You are hymned by angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, authorities and powers." That they are changeable is plainly shown by the devil, the author of evil. He turned to the worse and drew a good number of angels away with him. They were turned not by nature but by choice, at the prompting of their leader, who received a name fitting his deed. He is aptly called "devil" from slandering his own kind, and "Satan" from opposing God and men. For this reason he was cast down from the realms above the world, and Ezekiel (15), the inspired interpreter of the cherubim, reproaches him: "How you have fallen from heaven, morning star, who rose at dawn!" By the image of the luminary he shows both the fiery and shining quality of his nature and the leading place of his rank. In agreement with this, Daniel denounces his wickedness and speaks of how he leads his followers astray.

Angels, like mortals, do not know the future, for it belongs to the divine Trinity alone to know what is and to foreknow what will be. They serve the Trinity and they serve us: the Trinity as servants, in a manner befitting God; us by dispensation, carrying out for our salvation what the Trinity commands. Some people they remove because of incorrigible wickedness, so that those near them may not be infected by the contagion. They act like wise physicians, who stop the flow with cautery or the knife before the ravages of the disease spread through the whole body. Farmers too take care to uproot the tares as soon as they come up, lest they grow up together with the wheat and ruin it. Vinedressers pull up the choking weed while it is still green, before it twines round the vine, or cut it off with the pruning hook so that it does not spoil the grapes. The farmer of our nature and vinedresser of the Church does the same. He foreknows the deadly growth of the nursling, and as soon as it springs up he roots out and pulls up the one who would pull others up by deeds and doctrines of perdition. Or else he does it so that the scourge owed for that person's deeds may be lighter for the one who is removed. For those who undergo their reckoning here and pay in advance (15′) the penalty stored up there will not, in my view, be pursued again for what they have already answered for. They answer not for those whom the murderer killed on various occasions, but for the one for whose sake and through whom he now incurs the sentence of death. For the divine law commands an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, and that whoever sheds blood be put to death. And that they are not punished again for those things,
(15′) Προαποτινοῦντες: perhaps προαποτιννύντες.

it cries out plainly: "The Lord will not avenge twice for the same thing." Even among us it is not just for a condemned man to be punished by two judges. "When we are judged here, we are disciplined by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned along with the world." And the sublime Apostle says: "Whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives." It is not that he receives some and rejects others. Rather, some do this here and others there, receiving him or rejecting him through the commandments. The highway is not to blame for those who stumble or fall; they are to blame, because they turn their eyes away from it and walk with careless feet. So angels remove those who persist in wickedness, but preserve those who turn to virtue. "An angel of the Lord went out from the camp and killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand foreigners," says the divine book. An angel, it says, struck down the firstborn of Egypt.
