An angel barred the way of Balaam as he went to Balak to curse Israel. The beast that carried Balaam saw the angel, cowered in fear and sat down, and rebuked its rider with a human voice. Michael the archangel is sent to Joshua son of Nun. Gabriel is sent to Daniel to explain his dreams, to Zechariah to announce to him the birth of John, and to the ever-virgin mother Mary concerning the conception of God the Word. Raphael is sent to Tobit to carry his bag, to travel with him for fourteen days, and to join him to a lawful wife. He frees the woman who had been married to the man from the man-slaying demon, and he opens the eyes of the bride's father-in-law, which had been blinded by birds' droppings. You will find many other services of angels in the stories of Abraham, Moses and Manoah, at Bethlehem and with the shepherds, at the divine tomb and at the Ascension.

QUESTION 45 [?]. And if the angels do not know the future, how did Gabriel in Babylon foretell to Daniel that Christ would be born after [?] years? For the interpreters have explained that the sixty-nine weeks he told him of are [weeks] of seventy years [?].

But he did not declare this from his own foreknowledge. Angels say whatever they are taught by the wisdom on high. Angels are taught by the divine Trinity, human beings by angels, and the creatures below us by us.

If, then, they are taught, they must use tablets and papers as we do. For words and decrees that are not written down are quickly forgotten. If the words had stayed in memory, Moses would not have received them written
on tablets of stone on the mountain. And when these were broken, he would not have needed a second set if he remembered what was written on the first.

Moses received on the tablets the ten words of the divine decrees, engraved by the divine finger without chisel or stylus. But how did the same Moses write what he held in memory alone when God told him about the creation of the world? And how did he imprint on his memory the divine tabernacle shown to him on the mountaintop, and then instruct Bezalel by word of mouth to copy the immaterial in matter? And how did all the inspired prophets and apostles preach to the world? They did not learn through study; they kept in memory what the Word sounded within them. Galileans came as teachers to the Romans, their tongue transformed for each nation. Parthians, Medes, Elamites and the other nations each heard them speaking the mighty works of God in their own language. They proclaimed these things not by grammatical learning but by the working of the Spirit. "For there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire" (on the fiftieth day after the resurrection and the tenth after the ascension), "and it rested on each one of them," says the divine Luke, narrating their story.

If angels are incorporeal, how did they have intercourse with women, from whom the giants came forth? And how do they appear to the saints as men, if they are incorporeal? For divine Scripture says: "And the sons of God went in to the daughters of men," from whom, some say, the giants were born.

Angels are incorporeal compared with us, but in themselves they are body, like wind, fire, smoke or air. They are fine, immaterial bodies, free of our grossness. As the holy Apostle says: "There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies." But it is absurd and utterly foolish to think that they slept with women; on that view people would think that demons too sleep with women. For the demons abandoned not their nature but their rank; they were deprived not of their greatness but of their freedom to approach God. It is therefore blasphemous and childish to think that angels lust after women. Divine Scripture is not speaking of angels when it says that the sons of God went in to the daughters of men, for angels are nowhere yet called sons of God. It means the sons of Seth and Enosh, [so called] by the people of those times [?]. For Scripture says that he was the first to begin to call on God. And the Lord says to Moses: "I have made you a god to Pharaoh"; and of the divine judges he says: "You shall not speak ill of gods, nor of a ruler of your people." So the children of Seth and Enosh may rightly be understood as sons of God. They, overcome by licentiousness,

…went in to the daughters of Cain. From their incongruous and defiling intermarriage the giants were begotten: strong because of the righteous man, but wicked because of Cain. But how could women sleep with angels, when men were struck numb at the sight of them, and not ordinary men but outstanding ones? Daniel, for one, could not bear the sight of Gabriel. He fell straight to the ground and was in danger of melting away with fear. Zechariah too cowered before him. He was struck dumb the moment the angel appeared, and he trembled with fear, his tongue fettered until the birth of John, so that he could convey what he wanted to say only by nods. This seems to me to foreshadow that the law and the ancient rite of sacred things would be silenced at the coming of the Greater One; a little later we shall show more clearly what is meant. The women too, hurrying to the saving tomb, were struck numb at the sight of the angels and shrank back in fear, and they did not report to the apostles what they had been told. "For fear and amazement had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone," says the divine evangelist. If even the great could not bear the condescension of angels, how could lowly women endure their touch or share their bed? Straw has no strength at all near fire. Scripture says: "Adam lived 230 [?] years, and begot a son after his own form and after his own image." That is, the image [?] he had from the beginning when he was made by God, an image and a radiance upon his face. "And he called his name Seth," that is, "resurrection," because he saw renewed in him that ancient and wondrous form, and the grace and radiance of the all-holy Spirit. When the people of that time saw him, they called him God. That is why Scripture says that the sons of Seth, seeing the daughters of men, those of the race of Cain, took wives for themselves. For they too shared in the grace of the Holy Spirit, until God said: "My Spirit shall not remain in these men." Seth, however, kept this form for five hundred and five years.

If the devil turned to evil and fell from the heavens, with those who remained unchanged now above his head, how is he able to approach the heavens, stand before God with the angels, and ask for Job? For the story of Job says: "And the angels of God came, and the devil came among them," and so on.

It is not that the devil, who rushed out from there in his frenzy, is able to go up to the heavens, or to come before God with the angels, or to rise above the vault of heaven at all. Rather, the Divine has no quantity or magnitude and cannot be contained, and so it is present everywhere

and fills all things. "For our God is in heaven and on earth, in the seas and in all the deeps," says David, the singer of divine things. From this we learn that not only angels but also the devil, demons, human beings, beasts, and everything that exists are in his presence and are seen by him. Even while we are on earth we stand before God, as the divine Elijah says: "As the Lord lives, before whom I have stood today." If all things are contained in the air, much more is the fourfold order of the universe held within the air's Maker: the incorporeal, intelligent and rational; the perceptible and embodied; the brutish and irrational; and the lifeless and insensible. "For all things are naked and laid bare to his eyes, and no creature is hidden from his sight," says the divine [?]
Why did Moses not begin his account with the angels and the things above? Why did he pass over the hosts of angels and everything beyond the heavens and begin his work with heaven and earth?

He gave his writing a beginning that suited the times and helped the people. The Jews had only recently left Egypt, and the errors of the Egyptians still rang in their ears. Some of those godless people made a god of the heavens, others of the earth, although both are altered and changed by winds and clouds. Others gave their worship to the sun and moon, so that at the setting of these lights some were left without a god by night and others by day. Some deify what is darkened by night, mist and dust; others worship what wanes and shrinks to almost nothing. Others make gods of springs and rivers, so that their gods dwindle in summer and in winter swell, rise and overflow in flood. Still others tremble before fire as a god, a thing put out when water is thrown on it, or dying away when the fuel that feeds it runs short. What folly! These rash and empty-minded people deify things lowlier than themselves, led away by error from the true God. It was for their sake that Moses, the writer of divine things, set aside what lies beyond the world and began his account with the things here below. Through what can be perceived and seen, he guided them toward what is intelligible and toward the truly invisible God. In the same way the divine companions of Ananias trampled the god of Babylon, the fire, as if it were grain [?]. That fire was heaped up with naphtha, pitch and brushwood, yet water kills it. "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord," they say. In this way they led the godless Chaldeans to the immaterial God, who is not made with hands, and showed that all the gods of the Greeks are creatures and works of the truly real and uncreated God. For "Bless,"

they say, "all you works of the Lord, the Lord." Following the song, they present all things as servants of God, saying: "Bless him, angels, heavens, waters, sun, moon, stars, fire, earth, mountains, hills, cattle, wild beasts, creeping things, birds," and everything else the Greeks made into gods.

On the first day he brought forth matter out of nothing. As soon as he conceived what kind of matter each thing should have, he at once set before himself what he had conceived. Do not fall back on reasonings by asking how. He willed it and he was able, since he is the active power behind all things. From what was made on the first day he fashioned the rest of creation. First he made heaven, not the visible one but the one that lies above it, of which David sings: "The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord." Like someone building a two-storied house, he partitioned off what lies beyond the world from what is on earth, and kept it as an upper room.
Why did Moses not write that God made water, or fire, or air, as he did for heaven, earth, trees and the rest?

What then? Scripture says that God took dust from the earth and formed man. It does not add that he made eyes for him, or ears, or feet, or an arm. Must we suppose from this that the organs of our nature, inside and out, were not all created by God? No: with things that are composite and will one day be dissolved, divine Scripture usually presents the act through the more honorable part. So the singer of divine things says: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly." He did not shut women out of the blessing. Rather, since their nature is one, the song speaks from the more commanding part. Let the rest of creation be understood in the same way. Everything is included in the making of heaven and earth: air, darkness and abyss.
QUESTION [?]. Why then did Moses, as if he lacked the strength, choose not to write about the creation of darkness and the abyss?

Moses passed over it, not because he lacked the strength to write, but to leave us an exercise. Solomon, however, did write about it, speaking in the person of the Son to the Father: "Before you made the abysses, I was"
When did the air come into being? Surely you cannot say that Solomon wrote about this too?
Then listen to Moses: "And the Spirit of God was borne over the water." Amos agrees with him: "The Lord, who makes the thunder firm and creates
But he is not speaking about the air; the passage is rather about the Holy Spirit. For we hold that nothing else is, or is called, spirit except the Holy Spirit.

I am afraid to count the Uncreated among created things. Still, without rejecting what has been said, I accept this too, when it is understood fittingly and in a way worthy of God: he was borne over the waters to bring forth life, warming them like a brooding bird and releasing a life-giving power into the waters he warmed, so that they would swarm with countless kinds of fish. Besides this, we need to learn about the origin of fire. Scripture does not say that God said, "Let there be fire."

Fire is the most active of all natures, and it appears to have come into being together with the making of dry land and to lie hidden within it. Wherever you strike a stone, fire is born. When pieces of iron are rubbed together, the same thing happens. When pieces of wood are pressed together, fire likewise shows itself, as a wagon's axle makes clear when it smolders from the fire within it under the pressure of the load. And when millstones turn with nothing between them, you can see the fire leaping out. In the same way the friction of clouds driven by the winds commonly produces lightning. All things are mixed with fire, as Peter, who holds the keys of the kingdom of heaven, says somewhat as follows: "The present heavens and earth are stored up for fire, kept for the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly."

And how is it that in winter, when there are the same clouds and winds, there is no lightning and no thunder? Answer. What I think about thunder has been said above. As for lightning not appearing in winter, I think the cause is the thickness of the air and the moisture that runs through the clouds. In friction, what is dry and parched does not behave like what is soaked and muddy: the one catches fire, while the other slips past. (19) For ἀνιέντος ("releasing") perhaps read ἐνιέντος ("instilling"). Id.

Let the sun be our teacher, showing us the kinship between its own fire and ours. Goatherds, cowherds and horse-herders who live in tents in the wilderness often want to cook meat or bread. They fill a vessel of clear glass with water and hold it facing the sun's rays. If they hold some dry [?] to the water-glass, they kindle fire from the beacon above.
Who made the darkness? Was it primordial, or did the devil make it as the opposite of light? We think it was ancient, older than the world, since Moses does not say that anyone made the darkness.

Neither God nor the devil made it, and it did not exist before the visible world. All the incorporeal choirs of angels lived in light even before the world came into being. But when the body of the heavens was stretched out overhead, darkness arose as a by-product, a shadow cast by a kind of barrier. It is like someone at the height of noon who pitches around himself a tent of thick, watertight material. Sailors teach us the same thing when they stretch hides overhead in the rain and darken the ship. Or, if not this, it seems to me that darkness arises naturally from the misty vapor of the abyss, as the haze and steam grow thick. "And God said, Let there be light." God's first word created light, which he also called day (hēmera), honoring its mild and gentle (hēmeros) quality with a pleasing name. One could also tell of other lights made by him. There is the light of fire that appeared to Moses when the bush burned but was not consumed, so that he might show its nature and also make known his power. There is the light in the pillar of fire that went before Israel and tamed the desert. There is the light that shone around the shepherds. There is the light that snatched Elijah up in the chariot of fire without burning the one it carried off. There is the light that shone around the shepherds when the timeless Light, Christ, came into the world of time. There is the light of the star that ran its course to Bethlehem, to guide the Magi and to escort the Light above us that had come to be with us. The Godhead shown to the disciples on the mountain is light, almost too strong for their sight. The vision that shone around Paul is light, healing the darkness of his soul by striking his eyes. The splendor there for those who have been purified here is also light, when the righteous will shine like the sun. Among them God stands, in the midst of gods and kings, distinguishing and assigning to each, according to the worth of their lives, the prizes of the blessedness there. The commandment given to our forefather in paradise is also light: "For your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths," says David, the singer of divine things. The power of reason within us is also light, guiding our steps toward God. Light too is that which bore witness for God and, with the torch of the Godhead, trampled down the flame of error, like the companions of Ananias in Babylon, who danced in the middle of the furnace flame while not even their trousers were harmed. Besides these, the illumination of baptism is light in its own particular way. Above all, faith in the divine Trinity, equal in glory and without blemish, is light. "And God said, Let there be light, and there was light. And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night." QUESTION 62. What then? Is light one thing and day another? Is night one thing and darkness another?

Everything bright and cheerful is fittingly called gentle (hēmeron); its opposite is named night. In another way, the naming seems to me to signify their servitude and the orderly way they hand their course on to one another. For it belongs to a master to call by name, and to servants to obey and, as it were, to answer with a voice through the good order of their course.
How was the earth invisible and unformed? Was it made only half-finished by God, or how?

The earth was invisible and unformed, not in its nature but in its adornment and elevation [?]. The waters had not yet been separated into their own place, so that its substance could be seen, adorned with plants and crowned with flowers. Since the abyss was flooding over it, the earth was not yet girded with springs and rivers to feed the animals that were to be formed from it by divine command. Instead it wore the abyss like a mourning garment, as David, the singer of divine things, says: "The abyss like a garment is his covering." To this day it is plain that the Ocean lies around the earth like a ring.
And why did the Prophet not say "her covering" but "his"?

That makes no difference, since what is meant is the element of earth. Again, the souls of all people are called by a feminine name, yet we shall not grant that souls are female rather than male [?]. Christ, too, is called wisdom, power and rock, being himself God, Word and man. But let the passage be understood another way: the earth is invisible because its beholder, man, did not yet exist, nor the bleating kinds of animals that by nature bend toward the ground and gaze intently at it. QUESTION 65. What is the nature of the firmament that divides between the water and the water above the heavens and [?]
On the first day the heaven that lies above the firmament is brought forth. On the second day comes this visible firmament over our heads, which is of a different nature from the heavens above it.
And how can they have one and the same name and yet be of different natures?
Those who examine the text with care and not carelessly will find that they differ greatly even in name: heaven is one thing, firmament another. So from the very naming

we learn that the visible one is of a more solid nature than the invisible ones. Moses says: "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth." But here he speaks of solidity: "And God said, Let there be a firmament." Isaiah shows the fine and lighter nature of the one and the denser, thick body of the other. Of the first he says: "Who made the heaven firm like smoke, and stretched it out like a tent." And of the visible one he says: "Who fixed the heaven like a vault." Divine Scripture is likewise accustomed to call both man and woman "human being." Though the name is one, the one is enduring and bears burdens, while the other is softer, or lighter, in mind and reason. So, keeping silent as far as I can about the substance of the heavens above, I say that the visible one is by nature ice, frozen by divine command and strengthened to bear the things beyond the world. Those are lighter (22) than it and free of our thickness. Both are upheld by the divine [?] that holds together and bears all things.
QUESTION 67. And how can ice bear up and hold apart that vast and boundless water?

Christian beliefs are by nature made firm through faith. Where God wills, nature gives way and serves against its own nature. So water is changed into wine at Cana in Galilee; so the Nile turns blood-red in Egypt; so, against nature, the Red Sea becomes dry land. The divided halves of the water stand firm like walls, and the people cross on a dry bottom without getting wet. Let the God-hated Pharaoh, drowned in the sea, cure you of your unbelief. The one who buried him under the waves in that same crossing had long before spread out the heavens like a hide. He arched them over the dry land and founded them upon the waves of the abyss, as the singer of divine things teaches in his song: "Who stretches out the heaven like a hide, who roofs his upper chambers with waters." He came to us in the last days, it says, bearing flesh, and walked with dry feet upon the wet and restless sea.

And I very rightly ask your admirable sharpness of mind not to stumble or limp at all in the stride of your understanding when it comes to the truth. Let us give the argument an illustration. Suppose the water above the earth to be a hundred cubits deep. Suppose that God said, "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water and water," and that ice at once froze and held up half of the waters, as on the (22) For κουφότερον ("lighter," singular) perhaps read κουφότερα (plural). Ed.

[?]… we say that the things above [?]. We compare the king of the lights, the sun, to a tiny lamp shining in a vast house, when it is measured against the body of the heavens. Suppose someone placed a small coal on an enormous dish, or lit a lamp beneath it. Not only would he be unable to burn or melt (24) what lay above it; he would not even manage to warm the vessel. [How then could a faint lamp dissolve or scorch a frozen abyss? And when does a burning cup-lamp [?] manage to break the cold of winter, when winter strives to quench the wick with frost, to turn the water and oil inside it to stone, and to make the lamp wither with its excessive cold?] And how does the plant called "undefiled" remain entirely unburned? We also know of the salamander, a lowly animal but by nature superior to fire, which leaps through the middle of a fiery furnace and passes right through it, suffering no harm at all from the destructive nature of fire. So the sun, running its course beneath the heavens, would do them no harm. Describing its rising at dawn, the singer of divine things says: "And he, like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, will rejoice like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the end of heaven." Notice: "end" and "going forth"—not a sphere and a rolling ascent, as the idle talkers suppose. ["And his arrival," it says, "is at the end of heaven" (25)]: "arrival" and "end," not descent and setting below. But let us turn to the bridal beauty of this light. David says of it: "And he, like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber," portraying the brightness and well-measured warmth of its morning appearance. When it rides across the heavens at noon, we often try to escape it because we cannot bear its fiery heat. But as soon as it rises it delights everyone and is seen like a bridegroom. Generously making its way from east to west, it dispels the gloom of the air with its torchlight through the whirling of its rays. It keeps company with the earth to make it bear fruit, warming it and calling (26) the seeds to sprout.
And how is the ice not melted by the burning heat of the sun? It is so hot that we [?] (27) it, unable to bear its flame at noon.

When God wills, let the "how" be silent. I too might fairly ask you: how was the bush in Moses' day ablaze and yet not burned up, but instead seemed all the more to flourish, as if moistened by dew? And how were the hair and the trousers of Ananias' companions, in the furnace of the Chaldeans, at forty-nine cubits of the (24) For φλέξας ἢ χωνεύσας ("burning or melting") perhaps read φλέξει ἢ χω[νεύσει] ("would burn or melt"). Id. (26) For ἐγκαλούμενος perhaps read ἐκκαλούμενος ("calling forth"). Id. (27) For ἐμφαίνειν perhaps read ὡς φεύγειν ("so that we flee"). Id.

…the flame towering up, they remained untouched and undiminished, shining brighter than the fire itself. And so that they would not seem to have curbed the all-devouring power of the fire, heaped high with tow, pitch, naphtha and brushwood, by some magic or illusion, the Godhead that rejoiced with those inside arranged for the flame shooting upward through the mouth of the furnace to burst out onto the dry ground. It burned up the servants and spectators sitting forty-nine cubits from the blaze and reduced them to ash and dust. And how did Elijah, carried up to heaven on a fiery four-horse chariot, remain unburnt down to the last hair of his head? And how does a wick made from the asbestos plant, once placed in a lamp, last for twenty years? Only the oil is constantly consumed by the lamp's flame, while the wick itself remains undamaged. So let the 'how' rest with God. 'The voice of the Lord divides the flame of fire,' says the divine psalmist. With the bush in the desert, with the furnace in Babylon, with Elijah the prophet and with the others [?], the divine command cuts away the burning power of fire. In this way it fittingly divides what for us cannot be divided, and it points to the impartiality of the divine judgment to come: the illuminating property of the fire of Gehenna will be allotted to the righteous, and its burning property to their opposites. 'For that day is revealed in fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each person has done,' says the lofty Apostle. In agreement with him Peter, the leader of the company, says: 'But the heavens and the earth that now exist are stored up for fire, kept for the day of judgment and retribution.' And the Lord, setting his seal on the words of his servants, says in the Gospels: 'Then the Son of Man will send out his angels throughout the whole world, and they will gather the sinners from among the righteous and throw them into the furnace of

What then? Will the heavens never be dissolved, and those luminaries never disappear? Answer. There will be a dissolution of creation, but not a complete disappearance; rather, there will be a transformation for the better. This is what the inspired David teaches us when he sings: 'In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands; they will perish, but you remain.' And again, adding the regeneration, he says: 'And they will all grow old like a garment, and you will roll them up like a cloak, and they will be changed.' So when the waters above the heavens give out, then all things will be utterly melted down by the overwhelming fire. 'For the stars will fall like leaves from a vine,' says Isaiah, the loftiest of the prophets. And in the Catholic Epistles Peter says: 'The elements will be burned up and dissolved.' And that all things will be strengthened anew for the better, and from then on [?]
without ceasing, the divine psalmist of things present and to come declares: 'You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.'
Will the sea also come to an end at the consummation, then, vast as it is, and the waters above the heavens as well? God says: 'Let there be a firmament between water and water.'

The lofty Isaiah teaches us, and quite rightly, that the sea will come to an end and disappear at the consummation. For the inspired prophet says to God: 'Who says to the abyss, You shall be laid waste, and I will dry up your rivers.' This should be understood figuratively. The abyss of wickedness is the devil, and the rivers are the demons who flow out of him and back into him. He foams up deadly things against us, while they, like cresting waves, keep leaping at us through temptations. The Creator devised a quantity of water just sufficient for holding the universe together. The firmament is not only preserved by the cooling of the waters above the cosmos; it also sends the flame of the luminaries downward. With its compacted body it bends the upward thrust of the fire back down and spreads it out into rays by the pressure. Think of a torch in our hands: when its flame is pressed from above by a board or a pan, it breaks into rays and beams. For this reason Christ, the Sun before the sun, set the sun on high, rising on one side in summer and on the other in winter, so that it would not linger too long over one region and damage the vault of the firmament or scorch any part of the ordered world.
What then? Are the waters above the cosmos also bitter, salty and heavy, like the waters of the sea?

The water that was separated off amounts to one and a half times the whole of the remaining water, yet it is not extremely bitter, heavy or foul-smelling like the sea. The sun runs beneath that water and does not touch it. But it shines at length on the sea and evaporates it, drawing up whatever sweet, drinkable water has been mixed into the sea by rivers and torrents. We often see marshy land left dry and without moisture by evaporation in a single noonday. The water is separated out, rises and is absorbed into the clouds, and then it is squeezed out again onto the earth as if from sponges and dispensed as rain.
What then? Are the rains supplied to the clouds from the sea scattered again over the earth? And how… [Note 28: For 'pepēlēmmenō' it seems one should read 'pepilē-'.]

Listen to David singing of God: 'Bringing up clouds from the ends of the earth, he made lightnings for the rain.' And another of the prophets says: 'He who summons the water of the sea and pours it out on the face of the earth, the Lord God Almighty is his name.' For lightning occurs when the clouds, driven by the winds to dispense the rain, rub against one another. Question [?]. And how is it that the water of springs and of the sea has not been used up, though it has been drawn on for so many years, both as it rises to form rain and as all creatures use it?

[?] …to overflow, like torrents; so it cannot overflow either [?]… as Solomon teaches: 'All the rivers run into the sea, and the sea is not [filled].' [?] …And the sea water is not diminished [?], because it is repaid from above for what the sun evaporates, as the sky drips and sweats [?], or else for what is drawn up every day through the vapours of the air. It is like the domes of baths, where the air becomes moist and lets drops fall back onto the floor. Often one can see thick air breathed out from the sea or from springs, and this seems to me to be nothing other than water. [?] But how can spring or river water come from the sea, when the sea is bitter and salty, and these waters are sweet, drinkable and lighter?

None of these things can cast doubt on what has been said. As the water is squeezed through the pores and winds its way through [?], it sets aside its heaviness and bitterness, and its brine is thinned out. It is like wine mixed with water and poured over a sponge or clean bread. The wine, being thicker, is held back in the pores of whatever receives it, while the water, being thinner and clearer, is drawn through the pores. Oil and water poured over the same things show this too: the fatty, thicker part stays behind, while the thinner part passes through and is separated out.
[?] …we bring on no ordinary toil, often even [?]… bringing on a most pitiable death, being buried under [?]… Answer. One can very reasonably infer from wells

that spring waters come from the abyss and are sent up through the more porous flanks of the land. In their long ascent from the abyss they wind through the pores, boil off their bitterness, lay aside their saltiness and become sweet. Well water, by contrast, is naturally heavier, brackish and unpleasant to drink. This is because the bottom of a well lies close to the abyss and floats on it like a bucket or a jar. Since its ascent is nearer and its emergence quicker, it cannot [shed] the bitter saltiness of the sea. Instead it is in every respect in between: heavier than spring water, lighter than sea water.

How do the clouds draw up sea water? Once they have taken it up, why is it not poured out at once? And why does it rain in some places and not in others? Answer. Listen to David singing of God: 'Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin.' Another says: 'Binding up water in clouds of the air.' And before these, Job, the guide, tower and bulwark of those who contend for God, says: 'And the cloud did not burst beneath it', that is, beneath the water. This should also be understood of the Saviour's divine-human ascension. For a cloud came under his feet, not to help him ascend, but to show that he was the one who long ago spoke through whirlwind and clouds to Job, and after him to Moses. When the clouds are filled like wineskins or siphons, the divine command is laid on them in place of a cord, a finger, or whatever presses on the siphon to keep the water in. Think of today's merchants. They lower the siphon into a vessel as if into the deep, and once it is full they draw it up with the thumb pressed against it. They carry it full through the whole house, as the clouds are carried through the world, and they dispense what was drawn up as the one who drew it wishes, by placing and removing the finger.

Since all things had previously been surrounded by water and covered by the abyss, how was the water gathered together and made to give way when God said, 'Let the water be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear'?

When the divine power that brings about all things decided that the water should be separated into one gathering, it at once also produced the place that was to receive it. For the sea beyond Gadeira did not yet exist, nor the great ocean that sailors dare not venture on, which surrounds the island of Britain and the western Iberians. But when that region was then created by the divine command, the waters flowed together into it
'Binding up water in his clouds, and the cloud did not burst beneath it.'

The whole element has a single gathering, but there are very many separate bodies of water. There are the lakes in the north, and those seen along the Greek sea, which lie in Macedonia, Bithynia and Palestine. These are clearly gatherings of water. No one will deny that they hold a great quantity of water, yet we do not say that they are properly seas, even if, like the sea, they contain bitterness and salt. Examples are the Asphalt Lake in Judaea and the Serbonian Lake between Egypt and Palestine, which stretches along the Arabian desert. One might add the Hyrcanian and the Caspian, and some of these appear to be enclosed on every side. But we should pay attention to the geographies of those who have described them. For they are invisibly connected with one another and open into the one greatest sea, as the Red Sea shows, since it is invisibly joined to the sea beyond Gadeira.

The Lord called 'seas' the gulfs that are enclosed in a shape of their own by the surrounding land: the Northern Sea, the Southern Sea, the Eastern Sea, and again another, the Western. There are also particular names of seas: the Euxine Pontus and the Propontis, the Hellespont, the Aegean and the Ionian, the Sardinian Sea, the Sicilian, the Tyrrhenian, and countless other names of seas, which this is not the occasion for us to list.
Question 113 [?]. Why does he call it 'earth' at the beginning of Genesis, but here 'dry land'? Is the dry land not one thing and the earth another?

Question 114. What does Moses mean when he says, 'And God saw that it was good'? How could the one who foreknows all things see that the light was good only after he had made it? Even human beings know before they make something whether what they are making will be good or bad. So how could God see that it was good only after making it, as though he did not know in advance what he was going to make?
The passage does not mean that the sea had some pleasant appearance in God's sight. For the Maker does not see the beauties of creation with eyes

but contemplates them by his ineffable wisdom as they come into being. This is the one who says to Jeremiah: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came out of the womb I sanctified you.' To Nathanael he says: 'Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.' To Abraham he says: 'At this season Sarah will have a son.' And to the Jews: 'Before Abraham was, I am.' The sea is indeed a fine sight when it grows white in a steady calm. It is pleasant too when morning breezes ruffle its surface and it shows its viewers a purple or dark-blue face. It neither beats violently against the neighbouring shore nor lies completely still, but greets its shores with peaceful embraces and then springs back into itself. It is beautiful too in its fear of the divine command: 'This far you shall come, and you shall not pass beyond; your waves shall be broken within you.' It displays the fear that hangs over it, and this rebukes our ingratitude. Its waves run a little past the boundary and leave a visible line printed on the beaches, as though warning us with a tongue not to overstep the boundaries of the divine command. It is beautiful also because, as the mother of rivers, it receives them back again: on one side it gives birth to them, on the other it welcomes them as guests. It is beautiful also because it joins continents and cities that lie far apart. It carries merchant ships on its back and gives sailors, and through them everyone else, unhindered contact with one another. It grants knowledge of things that were unknown and supplies necessities to those in need, providing cities with export and exchange. Yet we should not think that the sea looked beautiful and pleasant to God in this way. Rather, 'good' in that passage is judged by the purpose of creation. And the same must be understood about the light and the rest.

Moses wrote that God said: 'Let the earth bring forth the green plant, sowing seed according to its kind and according to its likeness, and the fruit-bearing tree whose seed is in it according to its kind.' How is it, then, that we see many plants with no fruit at all and no seed? What fruit does the poplar have, or the fir, or the pine, or the reed? And what seed does garlic have, or the rose, the crocus, the vine, the tamarisk and the other fruitless plants?

Anyone who unfolds divine things with a love of learning and careful effort will find that all of them came forth according to the divine will, with nothing lacking. The poplar does provide fruit: shoots for each of our needs; its leaves, which are stored up to feed livestock in winter; and the oil from its buds, which is given to the sick and commonly called poplar oil. And in place of seed, the branches of the poplar take

root when they are planted in the ground. In the same way the fir and the pine increase their kind by shoots and cuttings. As for the rose, the garlic and the crocus, some of them provide fragrance, and they are mixed into adulterated wine for drinkers of strong drink [?]. Perfumers skilfully make it into incense, and physicians into eye-salves, and it is also eaten [?]. For water-drinkers it makes the water harmless. The reed bears fruit too: its tuft serves as sponges and the rest as pens. Both multiply their kind by offshoots of their roots.

Why do harmful things that destroy our life grow alongside good ones? Darnel and hemlock grow with the wheat, thistles with the roses, and hellebore, aconite, mandrake and poppy juice with the other edible plants, and these take our lives.

What then? Shall we abandon our thanksgiving for useful things and accuse the Creator over things that grew up to teach us discernment and to benefit some creatures? Shall we not consider that not everything was created for the sake of our stomachs? The foods assigned to us are ready to hand and well known to everyone, while each thing that comes into being fulfils its own particular purpose in creation. Because bull's blood is poisonous to you, should that animal never have been brought into being, or should it have been bloodless, when our life needs its strength for so many things? No, the reason implanted in you is enough to guard you against deadly things. Do not sheep and goats know how to avoid whatever would destroy their life, telling harmful things apart by smell alone? You have reason, and the art of medicine to supply what is useful, and the experience of those who went before you, which teaches you to avoid deadly things. Is it hard for you, then, to keep away from poisons? None of those plants grew without purpose or use; each was given for the benefit either of us or of the animals. Starlings feed on hemlock and quails on hellebore, and the constitution of their nature makes both immune to harm. With mandrake physicians induce sleep in illness, and with opium they soothe violent bodily pain. Some people have even quenched the frenzy of the appetites with hemlock, and with hellebore have rooted out many chronic ailments. So what we thought had grown up hostile to our nature has turned out to be one more reason for thanksgiving.

Question 117. Why does it say 'Let the earth sprout' for plants and trees, but 'Let it bring forth' for cattle and wild beasts? Is there some inconsistency here, since both come forth from the same womb?
Since the shoots and fruits were to sprout every year and to remain on the earth, they end up back in it, as in a mother's lap, when their flowers fall,
and are brought forth from it again. But once the animals had been cast forth from the earth, they were no longer born from it, but from those who came after them.

Why did he not adorn the heaven first, since it was the first thing he made, but instead gave precedence to the earth, which was created after it? The adorning ought to have followed the order of creation.

It was because of the polytheistic error that was going to arise, which even now holds many in its grip. They worship the sun instead of God and are godless at night when it sets. The earth was adorned first so that no one would think that the fruits, once brought forth from the earth, are ripened by the sun's heat, rather than each being brought to the size it has assigned by the divine might that governs all things. Or again, so that no one would think the sun the originator and father of light. For this reason the adorning of the earth is older than that of heaven.
And why, on the first day, while the abyss still covered the heavenly things and had not yet been gathered into one gathering, did he not make the sun and the moon and

Because the firmament in which the luminaries were to be set did not yet exist. For 'In the beginning,' it says, 'God made the heaven and the earth.' This means not the visible heaven, but the one above the visible.
What then? Do you also say that there is a multitude of heavens above the firmament?

None of the inspired writers has ever stated a number, except the lofty Apostle, who proclaims that he passed through as far as the third heaven. Yet he did not stop the count there. By saying that he was caught up 'as far as the third heaven', the words 'as far as' hint that there are other heavens beyond the three. David, the singer of divine things, says: 'Praise the Lord from the heavens.' And the inspired companions of Ananias say: 'Bless the Lord, you heavens of the Lord.' Both, guided by the Spirit, keep silent about the number. And what good would it do us to know the highest heaven, the one beyond all numbering? We do not even want to climb in thought to the first heaven, the one above our heads. Weighed down by [?] and passions, with our power of understanding darkened, we gape at the things below that lie on the ground.
What then? Do you think that the heaven above differs in nature from this visible one, which is also called the firmament?
I say that the upper heavens are of a finer substance than the lower one, since they are higher, and light

[?]…like bubbles formed on ice. But the visible heaven is more compact, because it carries the things above the world. “Praise God in the firmament of his power,” says David. In agreement with him, Ananias and his companions sing, “Blessed are you in the firmament of heaven.” Before them Moses showed that the heaven made at the beginning of the world on the first day is one thing, and the firmament made on the second day is another. There he says, “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth”; but here, “And God said, Let there be a firmament,” which is different in both nature and use.

And how is it that the waters above the firmament do not slide off its hardened, solid structure? Answer. Its back is not convex at all, but level and even. The roofs of baths and the buildings set in caves teach us this: seen from below they appear vaulted, but their upper surface is sloping[?], level and lived on. In the same way the divine vaults[?] look hollow from below as one gazes upward, but above they are flat and even and provide a bed [for the waters], as the earnest teachers of the Churches hold[?]. For God does not work as mortals do, nor does he lay foundations proportioned or matched to what he creates. He arched the heaviest thing over something soft, and with what is unstable and flowing he holds up what is thick and material. Under the heaven he spread the air and the heights[?] of the abyss, and under the dry land he set the waters, ordaining that the heavier should appear resting on the lighter. We are taught both points by the singer of divine things: “Who roofs his upper chambers with waters, who makes the clouds his chariot”; and further on, “Give thanks to the Lord, who established the earth upon the waters.” When builders raise great houses to a height, they lay foundations in proportion to that height. When shipwrights build a merchant ship that carries ten thousand measures, they fix a keel to match the weight of its cargo. But my God first stretched out the roof and only then laid the foundation. He first spread out the sails and then built beneath them the ship of creation. That ship sails through the surge of this world and its flowing life, in which neither bright things remain nor grievous things last, until it escapes the present storm into the calm harbor of the consummation. What a wonder! How does the dry land float on the perishable[?] element? How does the heavy not sink through the flowing? How do the mountains not go under in the soft? Without noticing, I have caught myself asking “how” about God. For who will know? By what wall is the abyss enclosed? What is its lowest bottom, the narrow place that holds it from beneath? When my mind ventures into these questions it falls into impossible and endless things, always imagining further supports beneath the foundations it has found.

But its worthlessness was held in check when Solomon cried out: “Do not seek what is higher than you, and do not examine what is deeper than you. Think about what has been commanded you.” So believe that the divine strength which holds the universe together controls and preserves all things, passes through all things, and governs the whole. [Question.] What were the luminaries made from: the sun, the moon and the chorus of the stars? We know that they are God's work, but we are asking about their substance.

It seems to me that the luminaries come from the firstborn light. When God brought forth the matter of light, he said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. Then, reshaping that matter into different appearances, he said, “Let there be luminaries.” Imagine someone who first produces a mass of gold and then cuts it up into coins. He makes two of them larger than the rest, glues them onto a huge disc and hangs it from the roof of his house, delighting the eyes of those who look at it and making the memory of his ingenuity immortal. In the same way God made the luminaries far from the firmament and then set them beneath it. Moses himself, the teacher of divine things, says: “And God made the two great luminaries.” Fix your hearing here, admirable friend, for from the wording I will make clear that the luminaries came into being outside the firmament. Moses says, “And he set them in the heaven,” which shows that he painted their panels below, or outside the roof, and only then were they placed beneath it. QUESTION [?]. Did he fix the two together, or did he set them apart from each other?

The sun was brought forth after the earth had been set in order, so that no one would call it the author of light or the maker of what grows from the earth. First the nature of light was brought forth. Then on the fourth day the sun's body was prepared as a vehicle for the firstborn light, like a lamp for the fire to be set in it. Whiteness is one thing and the whitened body another. In the same way these two are different, yet they are united, even though they are inseparable. Things that we can separate only in thought are separated in fact by the power of their Maker. He also separated fire's power to burn from its brightness, as we hear happened in the bush and in the furnace of the three youths. So too the fire at the fearful judgment will give light to the righteous and burn up sinners, as David testifies: “The voice of the Lord, who cleaves the flame of fire.” The phases of the moon help us grasp what we are seeking. When the moon wanes, its whole body is not consumed. Rather, by putting off the light that surrounds it and taking it up

again, it gives the appearance of decreasing and increasing. In clear air one can see its unlit part, outlined by an arc as large as at full moon. Think of the sun in the same way, except that the sun received its light once and holds it inseparably, while the moon is continually clothed with it and stripped of it. This confirms what was said about the sun. Let us learn their positions from the writing of Moses, for he says: “And God made the two great luminaries and set them in the firmament, the greater luminary to rule the day and the lesser luminary to rule the night.” So he set them opposite each other, the sun in the east and the moon in the west, the one to rule the day and the other the night. Running against each other, the sun through the day and then the night, the moon through the night and then the day, they would each reach the one east. As the day declined, the moon would come to the edge of the east like a queen holding sway[?] and brighten the night with her beams. As the darkness withdrew, the sun would drive to the same point and, like a king presiding, light up[?] the world under heaven. So his rising would be her setting, and her presiding his withdrawal, so that the words “Let them rule the day and the night” might be fulfilled. QUESTION [?]. How was it that the moon was then four days old and yet full, lighting up the whole world as a fifteen-day moon does? And how is it that today, when it is again four days old, it does not likewise shine through the night upon the [world]?

It is called four days old because its fellow servants were created before it. That does not mean that it was created later and appeared already four days old. When it was made it was complete, for God's work could not be maimed or half-finished. That it is not seen like this now on its fourth day is, I think, not even worth asking about, since our own image is seen in it. Our forefather Adam was created full-grown and received a full-grown companion for his life. Yet we see that their descendants do not match their stature when they come into being. They do so only when, with the passing of time, they reach that stature. Once they have reached it, they return to the earth again through death. Shortly afterward they are born again in the resurrection, putting off the body and putting it on again after the image of the moon. As for the eleven days by which the moon outdid the sun, not in existence but in nature, it pays them back to the sun. Each month it is reckoned at twenty-nine and a half days, and it completes three hundred and fifty-four days in the cycle of the year, according to the Hebrew reckoning. The Hebrews do not know our Roman months, for they follow the moon.
QUESTION [?]. What does “Let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years” mean? For some say that much about a person's birth can be inferred from the heavenly bodies.

The empty-minded attribute their birth to astrology. But Isaiah testifies that nothing about mortal life can be read from the stars when he says: “Let the astrologers of heaven stand up, those who gaze at the stars, and tell you what is going to happen to you.” A little later I will set out their myths at greater length. The signs of heaven and of the stars may fittingly be said to be rains, winds, storms and spring. We learn these from the stars, and this is God's love for humanity. The sailor sees the sign, steers his ship into harbor and escapes shipwreck. The farmer follows the yearly sign and digs his field. The traveler stays a little while at the inn and escapes the onset of rain or hail. There are also signs of war and of peace, and the Savior confirmed these when he spoke his divine words to the Jews. QUESTION [?]. What then do you take season, sign and time to be? And how does Scripture show the difference when it says, “And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years”?

Time is one thing and season another. The first signifies length, the second the right moment. We do not say, “The time of harvest or of vintage has come,” but “the season.” Nor do we say, “It is time to marry the girl,” but “It is the season.” Wise Solomon teaches this. By the signs of the stars I mean such things as these: the rising of the Pleiades marks the beginning of harvest and of sailing, and their setting the opposite. The one gathers the seed and the other scatters it on the fields. By “for days” I mean the day of Sabbath rest that comes round with the weekly cycle. Among the Hebrews every feast that brings rest from labor is called a Sabbath, and they observe this three times a year outside the weekly cycle, often in addition to the proper Sabbath. The Feast of Unleavened Bread is a Sabbath day, and so is Pentecost, and so is Tabernacles. And if in the course of the calendar a feast falls for them apart from the proper Sabbath, they call it a Sabbath day. The lofty Matthew makes this clear when he says, “On the second-first Sabbath,” meaning the day which, after the proper Sabbath, they counted as a Sabbath because of a feast. So the moon completes the months and the sun the years. The moon becomes full after a cycle of days. The sun, after a cycle of months, comes back to the same

point in the east, keeping its turnings and the equinoxes of summer and autumn. QUESTION [?]. Is heaven a sphere, or a hemisphere that rolls the sun round and carries it under the earth, or does it give it a course in some other way?

Let us both follow the lofty Isaiah, who cries out plainly: “He who set up the heaven like a vault and stretched it out like a tent.” What is set up does not roll, and what is stretched out is not carried round underneath. Heaven therefore has a beginning and an end. Scripture does not say, “The sun went up,” but “went out upon the earth, and Lot entered Zoar.” This confirms that heaven is not a sphere but a vault. David says in his songs: “His going out is from the end of heaven,” not his ascent; “and his course reaches to its end,” not his descent or his setting. He speaks this way so as not to make the sun run round like a rolling sphere. And again he says: “And he, like a bridegroom,” not going up but “coming out of his chamber.” The Lord himself said in his divine words: “He will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they will gather the elect from one end of heaven to the [other][?].”
How then does the sun set, if it is not carried under the earth? And what place shades its rays?

The sun races swiftly over the bounds of heaven and comes under a kind of wall, the northern region, which rises high above the land of Cappadocia. There the flash of its rays is shaded by thickets and waters and by the overbearing pressure of the firmament, so that its gleams are bent aside, and the height[?] of the dry land keeps them from touching us. It is like the image of our lamp given earlier: the fire is pressed down from above by an earthenware pan and shaded in front by something, so that its brightness can only escape freely at the sides. In this way the luminary reaches the east, running round the northern part in secret. Our admirable witness is Solomon, wise in divine things, who says: “The sun rises and the sun sets; rising, it goes toward the west[?], and circling it circles toward the north[?], and draws to its place.” See, then, how it runs through the south and circles round the north, so that it may arrive on time in the [east][?].
If the sun's course never stops, how does it make the days long for us in summer and shorter in winter?

When it comes near the south and travels not the high path but the slanting one, it makes the days shorter. Setting at the edge of the western region, it circles during the night through the whole west, the north and the east, so as to reach the edge of the south again, and from there it begins its swift daily course once more. That is why the night naturally grows longer and the day shorter. When it drives evenly through the middle of the sky, it makes the equinox. In summer it turns back toward the north and rises higher, taking from the night and adding to the day, because its circuit by night is shorter. The moon, for its part, is never caught wholly diminished. Rather, its disc is shaded in part, and one can see it waning and ending, shaded as if under a cloud, like a picture behind a silk curtain. Then it puts on its light again as the covering is drawn back, and it comes forth like a queen. It is a clear image of our nature: born, growing, filling out, waning, diminishing and setting, yet never wholly perishing. In the same way we are born, we grow, we reach our fullness in old age[?], and then the bloom of our looks ends. We wane in the good color and bloom of our cheeks as their red turns pale. Our bodily strength diminishes: we begin to walk bent over and to lean on a staff, bowed toward the earth, and by our posture we declare to it, “Here I come.” We die, and in body we end in the earth, but in spirit we do not perish. A little later the soul puts on again the garment of flesh it had laid aside. For I am not the body. I am the soul, and the body is mine, along with whatever grows out of the dry land; hence this too[?]. And after it has ended, the moon is born again, appearing to our sight as if it had come back to life. So we too, having ended in the tomb, shall rise again as though born anew, according to the divine words: “When the Son of Man comes in the regeneration.” By this he shows the time of our resurrection.

Yesterday we heard you tell those who asked you that the earth has no soul. If it has no soul, how does it bring forth living creatures with souls: the ox, the sheep, the lion, the serpent, and all the kinds of cattle, creeping things, wild beasts and the rest?

None of this proves to you that the earth has a soul. Otherwise we would certainly have to grant that the vine lay hidden with its clusters and was sent up all at once, and that the date palm grew under the earth full of fruit and sprang up all at once into view, or that the wheat, full of ears and ready for harvest, [Note 34: πυρόν: perhaps read πυρῶν. — Ed.]

had been buried and then rose up again at the divine command. But the saying makes no sense. If the dry land has a soul because it brought forth things with souls, then it left itself empty of soul. Whoever brings out a soul, whether his own or another's, is surely dead and soulless, having cast out the cause of life.

But a human being begets the bodily instrument, and God puts in the soul. Nowhere does Scripture say, “Let the woman bring forth a living soul,” nor that Eve or Sarah or Elizabeth conceived and brought forth a soul, but that she bore a child. Why then do so many mothers give birth only to bodies empty of soul, if they could bring forth an infant with a soul? And when they give birth to a dead child, why do they wail and lament instead of putting the soul back into the dead body, if it were in their power to produce a soul? When any creature with blood is cut or scratched with iron, the blood at once gushes out in streams and reddens what lies beneath. How is it, then, that the dry land is ploughed, split with the hoe and dug out for a well, yet does not cry out, does not bleed, is not stained red, and does not trouble[?] those who strike it, as all living things naturally do? And how is it that garlic, onions and the other plants do not bleed when they are cut with a knife or a sickle, if they have souls, as the Manichees say, those idle talkers and empty-minded men who carry their foul-smelling blasphemy about in their souls? Every creature with a soul, whether on land or in the sea, will certainly have blood. So the earth does not have a soul, nor do any of the plants or the luminaries. For nowhere does the divine Book say of these that he breathed into them the breath of life, as it says of man. Away, then, I beg you, with their drunken madness and frenzy. Every animal begets its like: ox begets ox, and horse horse, and so with the gazelle, the tiger, the beasts of burden and the bloodthirsty wild beasts. Each is able to beget its own nature and that alone. How then could the dry land, which is of one nature, bring forth so many souls of animals of other kinds and unlike one another, unless what sprang from it was given a soul by God's command? And how did the waters, yielding to the same decree and being of one nature, soft and flowing, produce in one moment of time, just as the earth did, countless kinds of swimming creatures with souls, sea monsters and cartilaginous fish? How did the soft and flowing element produce living bodies, hard and rocky, swimming in the abyss and equal to mountains in size: seals and whales, sawfish and gauroi[?], and the other creatures of the deep, dreadful in name and in size, which there is no time now to explain? If water is of one nature and has a soul, how did it pour forth countless kinds of swimming and flying creatures of different natures, and [?] amphibious ones that live now on the land and now in the

waters: the Nile crocodiles of Egypt, the river dogs of the Pishon in the west, the griffins of the Euphrates, the frogs of the marshes, our own hedgehogs, and swans? One could find countless kinds of amphibious creatures. At one time they pick up seeds or graze on meadows and fields alongside the land animals. At another they devour the smaller swimming creatures in the waters, as the bloodthirsty land animals naturally do. But let us turn the rudder of our discourse back to the subject before us and follow the teachings of the prophets. They nowhere declare the earth to have a soul. Rather, they say that what springs from it is given a soul by divine power and spirit. The inspired David sings: “You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created.” Isaiah, speaking as if in the person of God, cries out plainly: “I am God, who made heaven and earth, and who gives the breath of life to those who walk on it.”
We do not say that anything which bellows or roars has no soul. How then does the earth roar, if it has no soul, and bellow when it is shaken?

Like the sea, it swells with winds under the ground and gives off a kind of rushing or bellowing. The sea too is often stirred and swollen by exhalations from the deep and makes a roar as it dashes itself in great waves. Yet when the wind is still it has no soul; after its roaring it sleeps and enjoys a deep calm. Or do you think that water jars or wine casks have souls, because we hear them rush and bellow when air passes through them? When an ox is slaughtered and completely flayed, its hide clearly has no soul. Yet when it is worked into a skin bag, stretched with air and then emptied again by the squeeze of our hands, how does this soulless thing give off a kind of rushing or bellowing? And how again does it breathe into a musical instrument and, under the guidance of the player standing over it, pour every kind of melody, mournful and gentle, through the pipes? Shall we then say that the things blown through musical instruments by human skill have souls? Or the lyre strings and the drumskins that twang[?], boom and bellow at the touch and plectrum of the one who plays them? Think of the earth in the same way: it bellows and shakes through the action of something else.

How then do the three youths present the whole creation as having a soul when they sing in the furnace, “Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord; praise and [?]…”? [?] roars. [Note 36: ὠρυᾶται: read ὠρύεται. — Ed.] [Note 37: εἷ: perhaps read ἐστι.] [?]

If the stars contribute nothing to birth, and our affairs cannot be guessed from them, how did a star rise at the birth of Christ and become a guide to the Magi? And how did they recognize the star as royal and set out on their journey, urged on by the star to worship the child?

Since the Samaritans and Sadducees do not accept angels, the divine evangelist fittingly calls the angel a star. At the same time he draws the veneration of the stars toward Christ and leads mortals away from the error of many gods, and so he presents the angel as a star, the guide to worship. For the Magi were roused to worship in no other way than through the appearance of the thing they themselves venerated. Magic grew weaker and lost its power at the divine-human birth of the one who founded the stars and appointed their order. Those wandering Chaldeans perceived this and, setting out [?] to make supplication to the one who frees from error, they deserted to him, becoming evangelists and the first heralds to the nations of the divine-human advent. So they arose, heeding the prophecy of the lofty Isaiah, who cries: "A child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us, and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Sovereign, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come." What the inspired prophet had foretold five hundred years earlier they carried out in deed, even though they had not heard it, and so they went ahead in faith of the foolish Jews who spent their time on the law and the prophets. That the guide of the Magi was not a star but some intelligent and rational power we learn from the way it moved and stood still. For some stars are always moving and never rest from their motion, while others are fixed and do not move. But this one plainly did both: it moved and stood still, and it hid itself from those it was guiding. It did this so that, when they asked, "Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews?", Herod and all Jerusalem would be troubled, and the divine birth would be proclaimed and spread abroad by the Magi while their guide was hidden from them. Then it appeared again, and "it came and stood over the cave where the child was," says the lofty Matthew. For if it had not appeared at intervals, Jerusalem would not have been shaken by the Magi's question, and Herod would not have been enraged at hearing about a king. And unless the star had been recognized as some intelligent and rational power,

it would not have been shown to be a servant of the one who was born. As it is, it did what is customary with kings: the divine courier calls certain people and leads them to the king. When they reach the gate of the broad palace, he leaves those he has summoned standing in the forecourts until he has announced their arrival to the king. Then he appears to them again and leads them into the golden-roofed hall and to the king seated there. So it appeared as a star but is understood as an angel, the guide of the nations. Look at it another way: which do you think is greater, the star or the sun? You will surely say: the sun. When the sun is in mid-heaven, then, who can say which of the cities or villages it is pointing out precisely, or which house it is indicating, as if with a finger? Compare a star with the sun, then, as a gnat with an elephant, and compare the divine star with the greatest of all cities as a mosquito with a camel. If we cannot tell which of the greatest cities the king of the luminaries is pointing out when it stands overhead, how can we say that the faint star pointed out the cave, unless it was an angel travelling close to the earth and pointing out the Master? Let those who think that a star rises at the birth of each of us stop their drunken raving. They are tellers of fables, and they babble that the star dies out along with the person who dies. For when there were only two human beings in the world, I mean Adam and Eve, the heaven was already full of stars. And again, when every living creature was destroyed in the time of the giants, except the inspired Noah, who was saved as the eighth, the stars were not carried off along with those wiped out by the water, nor were they moved even slightly from their proper order. (Note 43: "of the broad squares": perhaps "of the broad palaces", or "of the broad pal[aces]". Editor. [?] … true, firm, strong, unchang[eable] [?] …)

but piety, he applied the sharpened iron of circumcision first to himself and then to his son Isaac. It was not astronomy but the word of God that made him believe in Isaac's birth from a barren and aged wife. From their youth and the vigour of their prime until grey hair and the deepest old age they slept together, and yet they never put their trust in astronomy. Again, when the Maker of the stars commanded him to sacrifice his son as a test, he did not follow the stars [?]. And it was not by following the stars but by obeying God that he exchanged Chaldea for Mesopotamia of Syria. I ask your sagacity, most lovable Constantius, while this divine assembly keeps silence for a little and listens, to explain to me our astronomical nativity as you understand it, and what its judgment and combinations are. Then the doctrines you have been tossed about by can be overthrown by divine strength and wisdom, and better ones can be raised up again by you through sober thought and learning, as also happened with the lofty Apostle, when the things of the law were overthrown and the things of the gospel were raised up in their place. When evil has been broken down and created anew for the better, and you are at peace with my doctrines, and those gathered to hear the discourse depart unharmed, taking with them nothing of the Hellenic evil, then David, the singer of divine things, adds: "This is the change of the right hand of the Most High". And the lofty Isaiah, foremost among the prophets, would also cry out in the person of God: "I am the one who makes peace and creates evils for the

Since your holiness permits me to speak, I begin my argument here. I do not wish to corrupt those present but to have them put the corruption away. To begin with, then, take Mars on a cardinal point, in its own house, in square aspect to Saturn, which is with Mercury on a cardinal point, with the Moon beginning to be full upon it, in a daytime birth. This produces murderers and murder victims, oath-swearers [?] and blood-drinkers, drunkards, lechers, the demon-possessed, initiates of secret mysteries, magicians, sacrificers and the like, especially when none of the beneficent stars is in aspect. Again, Mars in square aspect to Venus, exact to the degree, on a cardinal point, with no beneficent star in aspect, produces adulterers who have intercourse with their sisters and mothers. Venus with the Moon in the terms and houses of Saturn, together with Saturn, with Mars bearing witness, produces women who farm and build and are skilled in all manly work. They share themselves and sleep with whomever they wish, and their own husbands do not prevent them. So it makes women masculine (Note 45: "To begin with, then, Mars": before this [?] in the Question.)

in Capricorn, and [?] unfortunate in Venus. With men the opposite happens when she is with Mars in Aries. Hence neither fear nor anyone's threat nor any device can restrain the desires, because of the allotment of the stars. Answer. You have recounted the myths of the Hellenic error most expertly. So I in turn will strip boldly for the contest against what you have said. Using the word as a sling or a bow, I will try to bring down Mars and Venus, our stars, so that you may assign me a nativity of star-slaying. But first I ask you to learn that whoever wishes can either restrain his desires and actions or shake them off altogether. He shakes them off [?] when his conscience torments him and when he remembers the unswerving judgment and so is held back from evil. Moreover, the laws of rulers can bring the licentious to their senses and blunt the swelling vigour of youth before they ever experience racks and frying-pans and catapults, simply by making the fearful penalties for wickedness known. Such laws exist in every country, written or unwritten, among us and among the nations: among some it is the letter, among others custom. For those without law, ancestral customs count as law. First among these are the Seres, who live at the edge of the land. Their ancestral custom is their law: not to fornicate, not to rob, not to commit adultery, not to worship images or supplicate demons. Among them there is no idol at all, no prostitute or adulteress, no robber, no murderer, no thief. And yet the star of Mars, fiery-bright as you say, has compelled the free will of none of them. It has not forced any of them to kill his neighbour with a sword or strike him with a stone. Venus with Mars has not persuaded them to rage with lust for their neighbour's wife, though Mars stands in mid-heaven all day long. Even so, among the Seres the ancestral law is stronger than the necessity of the stars. Among the Bactrians too, that is, the Brahmans, the teaching handed down from their ancestors is law: not to get drunk, not to taste dead flesh, and not to drink wine, whether pure or adulterated, since they fear my God. Yet the Indians next to them commit murder and drink to excess, go mad for women like wild boars or swine, and are shaken by passion. And in the western regions, further inland than the Indians there, there are certain killers of strangers who kill newcomers and eat them, and none of the beneficent stars has been able to drive them away from their bloodshed to this day. The Chaldeans and Babylonians have another law: to marry their mothers, to defile their sisters and to rage with lust for their own children (Note 50: "pure or adulterated": the force of the word "adulterated" here [?]. Note 48: "unfortunate in Venus": I deny it, with Cotelier [?]; read therefore [?] "with Venus unfortunate". Note 49: "Brahmans": [?] read "Brachmans" [?] …)

and to commit defilement. Even if they go far from their native land, they also observe their own laws and enjoin them openly and in secret. Some of them are still found today among the Medes, Parthians, Elamites and Egyptians, and among the Phrygians and Galatians, defiling themselves in certain villages. Yet Venus with the Moon in the terms and houses of Saturn, with Mars bearing witness, could never be found in the nativities of all of them. The Gelae have a different law: the women farm and build and do men's work, and they even have intercourse with whichever newcomers they wish, and the leading men neither rebuke them nor are jealous of them. They do not wear perfume or falsify their faces with rouge, painting their cheeks, as the women among us do, putting on a mask that is not their own. The men adorn themselves with soft clothing and brightly dyed garments. Among them the women are also very warlike, and they hunt the less powerful wild beasts. How then did all the women of the Gelae not get Capricorn or Aquarius with Venus unfortunate? And again, how did their men not get Venus with Mars in Aries, where the Chaldeans in their theory say the brave and the luxurious are produced? In Susa of Babylon the women use every exquisite perfume and ornament. They are attended by servants and go out splendidly with boldness [?] and great merriment. They sleep fearlessly and shamelessly with all the Greeks, and they rule their own husbands rather than being ruled. Yet surely Venus is not in mid-heaven with Jupiter and Mars in the terms of Jupiter in the nativity of every woman of Susa. In the East, those who corrupt males, those among the Christians [?], are punished without mercy by their kin if they are found out. In Britain many men sleep with one woman, and likewise many women consort with one man. And the nations follow all their ancestral customs as a law, without pain and without effort. The Amazons have no husbands. Like irrational animals, once a year around the spring equinox they cross their borders and have intercourse with the neighbouring men, treating the time of intercourse as a kind of festival and feast. Once they have conceived by them, they all run back home together. When the time of birth comes, they destroy the males but keep the females alive and nurse them carefully. It is absurd to believe that Mars with Saturn happens to stand at the hour, in equal degree, at the conception of the males but never at that of the females. All were conceived in their wombs on the same day and night, and again they come out together as if from one womb. How then are some destroyed the moment they taste life, put to death by the murderers before they suck milk or utter a cry, while others are kept alive and cherished, frolicking among evils in lawless bosoms? How (Note 51: [?] Bardesanes [?] "among the Geli". Note 52: "are unfortunate": perhaps "with [Venus] unfortunate". Editor.)

But since seven stars govern our birth, we say that the earth is divided into seven climes. Each clime is ruled by one of the stars, and those it rules are guided by the stars' combinations and are shaped by them. Some call this influence of the star a law.

Then how is it, if the inhabited world is divided seven ways, that we find many different laws in one portion? There are not only seven, matching the stars, nor twice six, matching the signs of the zodiac, nor again thirty-six, matching the decans. Countless laws are recorded, some changed long ago and some in force now. How is it that in the same section we see both the man-eating Indians and the Brahmans, who abstain from living creatures and from every feast? How is it that the people of Babylon, wherever they go, run riot in defiled marriages with their own kin? And how is it that the Sclavenes and the Physonites, who are also called Danubians, live in another section, yet differ so widely?
