The one people eat women's breasts with pleasure because they are full of milk, and dash the infants against the rocks like mice. The other abstain even from the lawful and blameless eating of meat. The one are self-willed, a law to themselves and without leaders. They continually kill their own leader and ruler, whether eating together or travelling together. They eat foxes, forest wildcats and wild boars, and they call to one another with the howling of wolves. The other abstain even from gluttony, and submit and yield to whoever happens along. There is much to say, too, about the Lombards and the Norici and the western Gauls, who have no share in the Hermetic and Saturnian science of the stars. How many kings and rulers have abolished badly made laws and legislated as they themselves saw fit! Or again, their opponents have rejected the better laws, and the stars did not prevent them from what they chose! I wish to say one thing that stops the mouths of all unbelievers. All the Jews who received the law through Moses circumcise every male rational being born to them on the eighth day and shed his blood. Yet from all time no Greek or Christian has received circumcision. Many Jews, Greeks and Christians are born in the same months and weeks and days and hours, whatever Mars or Mercury or Venus or the rest of the Greek myth may be doing, since one circle encompasses everything, and none of them is forced by the stars. For not all Greeks or (Note 58: "zodical": perhaps "zodiacal". Editor. Note 59: "according to the decans": certainly [?].)

Jews or Christians were conceived in the womb on the same day or hour, nor again were they all born together. How then did most of them join themselves to Christ and renounce their ancestral error, when the star ruling that portion of the land could not prevent them from turning to piety? Question 111 [?]. But our argument about the stars is not about faith. It is about character, way of life and conduct, which are shaped by them, and also about the constitution of the body. Those born under Aries turn out curly-haired, bright-eyed and high-minded, since the ram is a leader. They are also generous, since the ram parts with its fleece without grief and nature clothes it again. The one born under Taurus is long-suffering and servile, for the bull is under the yoke. The one born under Scorpio is a striker, because he resembles that creature. And the one born under Libra is just, because our scales are equal.

O Hellenic [folly]! What could be more ridiculous than this? The ram, from which they babble that a man's birth is determined, is a twelfth part of heaven. When the sun reaches it, it touches the vernal [?] points. Likewise the balance, the bull and the scorpion are each a twelfth part of the heaven called the zodiac circle. How then can they say that the primary causes for mortals lie up there, and then characterize those causes by the bleating creatures here among us? For the ram is generous, not because that part of heaven produces such a character, but because the sheep received such a nature from its Creator. You hasten to explain our birth from the stars, but you try to prove it from bleatings. If the heaven has obtained such starting-points of character by taking them from the [sheep] [?], then it too is wholly subject to principles outside itself. We are subject to the stars, and the stars to the animals, and so their causes depend [?] on the animals. If this is ridiculous, it is still more ridiculous to bring in, from things that have nothing in common, (Note 60: "cheerful": perhaps "bright-eyed". Editor. [?] …)

[?] using [?] impulses. This is madness and the utmost folly: to blaspheme the Creator and to tell lies about soulless things. How are those born under Aries curly-haired, bright-eyed, generous and resourceful? We see many who are curly-haired but blind and poor. They are not generous but brazen, needy, filthy and ragged beggars, going from door to door for their daily bread. And how do the bald, or those with straight hair, or the dim-sighted have the opposite, wealth and abundance and quiet, and rarely gather with their friends and kin? How many times a day or night are the configurations of royal nativities formed? Why then are kings not born every time? Or again, how is it that the succession to the kingship passes from father to son? Surely no king watched for the royal configuration of the stars so that he could match it in his intercourse with his wife, for no one has control over such a thing. How then did King Uzziah beget King Jotham, Jotham beget Ahaz, Ahaz beget Hezekiah, he Manasseh, he Amon, he Josiah, and he Jehoahaz? Each king begot kings, and none of them happened on a servile hour of birth. Further, suppose the beginnings of vicious and virtuous deeds do not lie in what is in our power, but come from the necessities of birth. Then lawgivers who define for us what is to be chosen and what avoided are superfluous, and so are judges who honour virtue and punish vice. For the wrong would not belong to the thief or the murderer. Even if they wished, they could not control their hands, because the stars drive them to their deeds and the necessity of fate presses upon them. I will refute them also from the general change in human affairs. Before the divine-human advent all the nations were mad for idols and danced their way through every impiety. After the coming of the God-man, the preaching of the gospel brought about a move to piety. Error was removed and virtue honoured, while the aspect and position of the stars stayed the same. Many Greeks, Jews and other nations turned and joined themselves to Christ. Where then are the stars that once compelled them to supplicate idols? And where were the stars that now draw them to piety hiding before? If nothing has been taken away from or added to the position of the stars, they must admit, even against their will, that virtue or vice is lived out or chosen not because of some fate or necessity. It comes from the free choice of each person, who goes on to what he has chosen. The lofty Isaiah sets this out clearly, crying expressly in the person of (Note 64: [?] rewrites it as "filthy". Thus also [?] reads "filthy" in another form [?] for "filthy".)

And these godless and empty-minded people deified his children as well. In Hermopolis they deified Hermes, whose name "interprets" only for the worse, and who has been dissolved into dust. In Cyprus they deified Cypris, who lies in a tomb in dung. In Thrace they deified Ares, who takes his name from "curse". From there, as from the ill-fated Esau [?], Dionysius the Areopagite rose up for us and became a disciple of the divine apostles. By the Casian [?] mountains Kronos was worshipped, or rather an ass was worshipped by asses, braying and bellowing against the Greeks. In Thebes Dionysus is worshipped, who is an incurable and foul-smelling disease of soul and body to those who revere him. In Tyre Heracles, or rather "inglorious earth" [?], who was caught by fire because of his wickedness, is deified by the godless. In Epidaurus Asclepius, a child in his wits, was called a god by people more childish and foolish than he. The Syrians, rightly named "sweepings", wrongly deified Adonis, whose name recalls Hades. The Egyptians deified Osiris, the one dragged along and thrown to the ground. The pitiable Ilians deified Hector, or rather not even a decent cock. Those on the island of Leuke deified Achilles the [?]. The people of Pontus deified Patroclus the father-slayer. The Rhodians deified the Macedonian who fought rashly. And so on, each people its own: they revere dust lying in tombs and are utterly impious, for not one of these was torn from life while in God [?]. Explaining their drunken follies is not for the present occasion. If anyone wants to hear their nonsense, let him ask Orpheus and Hesiod, the authors of their mythmaking, and do me the favour of letting me keep silent from now on.

Question 113 [?]. I am not arguing with you as a champion of the Greeks, Father. I want to take up arms against them from your great learning. How then can you say that nothing comes about spontaneously, and nothing outside the divine power? Look at the rainbow we see. It has a precise curve, equal on every side, such as not even the mind could truly trace out. And yet we see that no one makes it; it forms spontaneously.

The formation of the rainbow cannot bring in spontaneity. It is stretched on the pattern of the firmament, like a scarlet cord on a disk. For even if the mould that imprints its own shape is [?] mind, yet at least [Note 72: "In Tyre Heracles", etc. In Cotelier's view, instead of Ἡρακλῆς it should rather be ... ἔρα ἀκλεής, "inglorious earth" [?] ... "In Tyre Heracles ... who was caught by fire because of his wickedness, by the godless" [?].]

the one who made the mould designed it intelligently, intending to pour onto it or press into it whatever he chose. Lead or wax or bronze melted by fire is poured onto a mould, takes its shape from it, and becomes what the craftsman wants. No one will think that it formed spontaneously; it is finished as the craftsman chose, by his hand working through the mould. So the formation of the rainbow should be understood in the same way. It appears in heavy rains and is given to the world as a sign of reassurance that the things under heaven will not be flooded and swamped again. For God says, "I set my bow in the cloud as a sign for you." The sun, like a cupping-glass, draws the moisture of the clouds by the casting of its rays, as if from a body, and draws up the rain like a stream flowing down to its base [?]. The rainbow has three colours: red, air-coloured, and grass-green. It foretells that peace and wisdom and power, the Word and God of all, would come to the world in blood, water and spirit. With water he would wash all creation clean of its shame through baptism in the streams of the Jordan, and with the divine Spirit he would drown the spiritual giants. After this worldwide drowning and washing away of idols and demons, the sign of salvation through blood is given to us. This is the true rainbow and peace of God the Word, stretched out through flesh as if on a mould. He became for us a clear sign, a rainbow assuring us that we need not fear a flood of demons, and he drew us out of their storm when he said, "When I am lifted up from the earth" (that is, on the cross), "I will draw all people to myself." And again he says, "Look, I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy." The sublime John says that there are three witnesses to this: "the blood, and the water, and the spirit, and the three are one." For about the ninth hour Jesus cried out and gave up the spirit of his soul. The divinity was united even with the body when it was without a soul, and in the same way remained blended with the soul in its sojourn [?]. If the breath of the air is present in both, much more will the divine be present with each part, since it is indivisible and without quantity. Someone pierced his side with a lance, "and blood and water came out. The one who has seen has borne witness, and his witness is true," says the sublime John. Blood and water poured from the divine, ever-flowing spring because of Pilate, who judged him, and those who shouted, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" Pilate threw off the blood of the Lord's murder, and they drew upon themselves the condemnation that came from it: "His blood be on us and on our children!" We say these same words with love, but not in the spirit they had. For they regarded as a mere mortal the one whom we worship as God of all. Wise physicians stop the flux that runs from the crown of the head to the eyes. In the same way [?], through the rainbow [God stops] the outpouring of waters [Note 78: For ἀποῤῥιψαμένου ("throwing off") perhaps read ἀπορρυψαμένου ("washing off"). Ed.]
stretched over what lies beneath it as if on a mould. The sun acts like a cupping-glass: it gathers the clouds with its rays and dries up the water-bearing veins with its heat, as if with a cautery.

Question 114. You said that the primordial darkness came about when the body of heaven was stretched out, and so it is. But how is it that we see night come about spontaneously, without being imprinted by any mould?

I have already given an account of night above. Now I will use a faint image to show again that night does not come about spontaneously or outside the divine hand. Builders raise towers, and a craftsman's hand carves sculpted or cast works. Their shadows, however, do not naturally come from the craftsman; they are produced by the things he has made. So even if some things come into being alongside others, imprinted by a mould, the moulds themselves were made in the beginning by a craftsman's hand. Night, then, likewise does not form spontaneously. It is the shadow of the land, as I will show a little later. Just now the hour is urging us to the divine celebration of the mysteries, and the congregation is waiting.

Question 115. Yesterday the hour was pressing. Today, give us the leftovers from that table: explain more fully about night, and why Scripture calls the first day not "first" but "one". That seems out of keeping with the days that follow. If the days after it are called second and third, it would have been more consistent to call the day that begins them "first" rather than "one".

Scripture calls a day and a night together one day, giving the whole span of twenty-four hours the name of its dominant part [?]. Divine Scripture often speaks this way: when it reckons time it counts days and does not count nights as well. Listen to the divine psalmist: "The days of our years, in them, are seventy years." Before him the patriarch Jacob says, "The days of my life are few and evil." Again the singer of divine things says, "And that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life." The divine evan- [Marginal note: Ps. [?]]

-gelist also says, "Six days before the Passover Jesus came to Bethany." And Jesus himself, speaking as God, says, "You know that after two days the Passover is coming." What is handed down here in the form of a narrative is a law for what follows: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." The day already existed. Then evening came; out of the evening came night, and out of the night came morning, where the one day ends. The one day holds the full measure of one day through twenty-four hours, and the night is understood to be included with the day within those hours. This is why at the solstices one of them happens to exceed the other in length. At the fixed time of the equinox, however, the two must be exactly equal, each taking back from the other what it had lacked. When the face of the heaven returns to the same position, it is fittingly called one day. The same thing happens with the land: from one flowering to the same flowering again is called a year. So whenever evening and morning come upon the world in the sun's circuit, the day and night together, and the return of the luminaries to the same position, are signified not as a longer time but as the span of one day. Or rather, the explanation handed down in secret teaching seems to me more authoritative. God, who constructed the nature of time, set the spans of the days as measures and signs for it. He measured it out by the week and commands the week always to revolve back on itself, numbering the movement of time. As the week revolves on itself, it again completes the one day, turning back into itself seven times. This is the figure of a circle: to begin from itself and end in itself. That is also the property of the age, to turn back on itself and never come to an end. So he called the head of time not the first of days but one, so that by its name it might be akin to the age. Since it displays the character of what is single and shares nothing with anything else, it was properly and fittingly called "one", as it revolves in itself through every age into

Question 116. Then how does Scripture indicate many ages when it says "ages of ages"? And David says near the end of the psalm, "Give thanks to the Lord of heaven, for his mercy endures for all the ages." Again the same David says, "I will exalt you, my God, my King, and I will bless your name for the age, and for the age of the age." There you have three ages in the hundred and forty-fourth psalm. We also hear the priests offering thanksgiving to God and ascribing to him power over all things, when they say: "The power, and the [Note 80: For ἀνακυκλοῦσθαι πάλιν ("to revolve again"), therefore, read ἀνακυκλουμένην πάλιν [?].]
kingdom, and the might, and the glory are of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen."

But these passages do not teach us to count many ages. They teach changes of circumstances and conditions, not limits and ends, nor ages succeeding one another. "For the day of the Lord is great and glorious," says the prophet. And again: "Why do you want the day of the Lord? It is darkness and not light": darkness, clearly, for those who deserve it, since Scripture knows that day as one without evening and without anything to follow it. The divine psalmist also called it the eighth day when he gave one of his psalms the title "For the eighth". He titled another "For the one who inherits", since this day alone inherits [?] all the other days in boundless and undivided spans. It has taken up authority over all things because it surpasses this seven-day cycle and lies outside it. So whether I say "day" or "age", I mean the same thing. If it is a day, it will be one and not many; if you call it an age, it will be single and without end. To lift our minds to the life to come, Moses the revealer of sacred things wrote "one" as the image of the whole age. This is the first-fruits of the days, the same age as the light, the divine and venerable Lord's Day, honoured by the Lord's resurrection. Question 117. Some people say that the moon is drawn down from heaven by incantations and sorcery. Most of humanity has been gripped by this rumour. They beat on iron and bronze, thinking that the noise will bring the moon back from its wandering, as if it had fallen into a trance.

Drunken old women babble ridiculous myths that have spread everywhere: that sorcery moves the moon from its own seat, carries it down to earth, and lets people handle it [?]. This is utterly irrational and the height of madness, and I think it contradicts the divine psalmist when he sings, "The moon and the stars, which you founded." And what place could have received the moon once it had been dragged down? I will use a faint image to show its size to those who think so rashly. Cities throughout the world lie very far apart, some in the east and some in the west, in various stretches and on various shores of the land. Yet all of them receive the moonlight equally. For sensible people this is enough to show that the moon faces all of them and is enormous. If it were not, it would surely light only those directly beneath it. To those lying beyond its breadth it would cast slanting rays as it ran past along the sides [Note 81′: For τῶν ... ψαλμῶν ("of the psalms"), perhaps read τὸν ... ψαλμόν ("the psalm")?]

Nonetheless, the matter can be made clear in another way as well. Have you ever looked from a high ridge over a wide, level plain? How big did the oxen look to you then? How big were the ploughmen, or the herdsman with his herd of a thousand cattle, or the flock of ten thousand sheep bleating in the marsh? How big was the herd of horses, prancing and leaping in the meadows? Did they not seem fainter to you than ants? Or have you stood on a lookout or a hill facing a vast sea and cast your eyes over the water? How big did the greatest islands seem to you? How big did one of the huge merchant ships look, sailing with white sails over the dark-blue sea? Did it not seem fainter to you than any dove? Your sight was spent in the air and faded over the distance, so that you could not perceive it exactly. And the greatest mountains, broken by deep ravines and gullies, look rounded and smooth. The eye falls only on the peaks and surfaces; it is too weak to enter and look into the hollows between them. Square towers as high as the clouds also look low and [?] to many people because of the distance. So if the body of the moon were not immense, it would not appear equally bright to everyone from every place. It is no smaller in breadth than the whole land, and it shows its size clearly and shines at once even on those who sail far away from it. [Note 82′: For μέσαι, perhaps read μέν σοι. Ed. Note 83: For ἐρριγμένα, perhaps read ἐρρηγμένα or ἐρρηγμέναις. Ed. Note 83′: For ἐμπερεῖς, perhaps read ἐμφερεῖς [?].]

[?] and pierced by a spear. I think the moon, the shining one, sees this as she imitates her brother on her nightly course above them. She sees sorcerers flocking to tombs and altars and the murders and child-slaughter they dare there, as they cut up their own offspring. These murderers stain themselves with blood over the quivering livers. The inspired David rightly laments their godlessness and says, "And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons, and shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan." And after other things he tells what harvest they reaped from their own seed: "And the Lord was furiously angry with his people, and he abhorred his inheritance." Even now very many are darkened by the gloom of paganism and secretly bow to the error of their ancestors and the ancient bloodthirstiness of their thoughts. They spend their nights on hills or at tombs and monuments, serving the demons with the smell of burnt sacrifice and with blood, and lamenting at home over what [?] ... So the moon, being lowered [?], grows dizzy, cowers and veils herself. She slips into a cloud and will not cast her light on the unworthy, after the example of her brother. It is as if she cries out from heaven by her change, as from a hidden ridge [?], and strikes the murderers of this godless drama with darkness and holds them back. Question 119. If the Son of God is not unlike the Father and God, but equal to him in all things, of equal honour and of the same nature, how can he say, "I am the vine, and my Father is the vinedresser"? A vinedresser and a vine are not of the same nature. One is rational and has a soul; the other is irrational and has no soul.

I do not approve of your restless cleverness. It often wanders away from the subject, and it throws me off with this odd question. If you do it on purpose, know that you have been found out. If you are simply bringing out whatever springs up in your mind, then forgive, and grant me forgiveness too. The things of Christians are made firm by faith, not by syllogisms; syllogisms have shaken most people out of their wits. Were Paul and Apollos of a different nature from the Church? The one with lofty understanding writes to the congregation of the Church, "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth." Is the Church, then, without soul or reason, because Paul planted it and Apollos watered it with the irrigation of the commandments and
Why did God hand Job over to the devil, when he himself bore witness to his righteousness and to his true
and blameless way of life? Forgive this question that does not follow from what came before; I am not asking it to test you.

He handed over not Job himself but what belonged to him. And he did not hand it over; he permitted it. He was training Job for courage, and he set the righteous man, made of clay, against his bodiless adversary. [Note 85′.]

Question 121. You were right to say that it was not Job himself but what belonged to him that was handed over. What then? Was it not Job himself who was nailed down [?] with worms and eaten by them, and

[?] forsaken [?]. "I will ascend above the stars, I will set my throne upon the clouds, and I will be like the Most High." It is as if God laughed at the devil's arrogance and said: "Why do you boast, you foul devil? Look at one of my servants. He is made of clay and earth; he is lowly, a mortal by nature, not an angel. It would be an insult to an angel to have to contend with you, since you will not get the better even of clay. Look," he says, "we hand him over into your hand," as though he were bound and lying on the ground. "See whether you can overcome his lofty mind as you besiege him and shoot arrows at his body." And what happened then? Like an arrow striking something harder, the braggart who thought himself a god bounced off without effect, defeated by flesh and blood. He besieged the divine city of the body and shot arrows at it, but he could not conquer a single one of its citizens, the thoughts, or kill any of the guards at the gates of the mouth. "In all these things that happened to him, Job did not sin even with his lips before the Lord." The enemy tried to force him to blaspheme, but he did the opposite and said, "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. As it seemed good to the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord for ever." So Job was not betrayed. He was put forward as a contestant, a teacher of courage and of giving thanks in the painful things of life. We know of four kinds of discipline. The first is brought on us because of sin, to correct us: "Many are the scourges of the sinner," says David. The second casts down pride and conceit and represses the swelling or puffing-up of the soul, "for the Lord opposes the proud." In the third, people whose virtue and courage are hidden [are brought into view] so that those who see them may imitate them. "No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel or under the bed, but on the lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house," says the Lord. It is as if he said, "This is why I lit Job like a torch and set him outside the town on the lampstand of the dunghill, to shine for all who are in the world." The fourth is complete abandonment by God, because of utter wickedness with no trace of anything good, so that a person is handed over to destruction for wickedness that will not change. This is what happened to Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar and Judas. "For I will turn my face away from them and show what will become of them in the last days," says God through the tongue of Moses. Yet when Nebuchadnezzar came to his senses through discipline and sobered up from his drunken madness, God, whom he had rejected, did not reject him. He gave him back his kingdom and made him splendid again with purple and diadems.
Question 122. How many days did Adam spend in paradise? Many have written about him. Some say six days: that is why, they say, on the sixth day he came

…the Saviour. Others say that it was only six hours; and that is why the Saviour was crucified at the sixth hour. Others again say that he lived in paradise for forty days, enjoying its delights, and was then driven out for his transgression. To set against these days and make up for them, they say, Christ neither ate nor drank for forty days in the desert, while he was tempted by the devil as a man.

I myself have already set out this account of the forty days, and it does not seem unreasonable to me. Following it, the divine assembly of our Church fasts once in the whole cycle of the year, with the strictest abstinence from food and from worldly affairs, seeking the ancient homeland of paradise and the life there that it longs for. For Christ took on himself, in exchange, all the debts of our forefather. Adam disobeyed; Christ in return obeys, even to the cross and to death. Adam was tempted through Eve, who had already been defeated by the tempter, and tasted what was forbidden; Christ, when tempted, fasts, setting his fast against the forty days that our forefather Adam spent in paradise, and raising up want against luxury. Adam wished to become a god and was changed from what he was, becoming mortal instead of immortal and condemned instead of blessed; Christ for Adam's sake becomes mortal while remaining God, unchanged in nature and unaltered in his Godhead. Adam was banished from paradise to this place of passion and toil; Christ came down from heaven for his sake and took up Adam's life. Instead of unapproachable light he lived in a dark and lightless cave; instead of intelligent and rational beings, he was surrounded by irrational animals; instead of all the powers that bear him up, he was carried in the arms of a woman, holy indeed, spotless and ever-virgin, yet sharing our common nature; instead of angelic hymns and songs, he was slandered as having a demon, as casting out demons by the ruler of demons, and as leading the crowds astray; and he was hymned by the children of the Hebrews crying out, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” In place of the virgin Eve he raised up his holy mother, ever-virgin; in place of Eve's sentence, he sent to Mary the greeting “Hail” through his own servant Gabriel, healing in her what Eve had done. In place of the tree of transgression, he planted a tree of resurrection in the midst of the earth, his own saving cross, as David, the singer of divine things, says: “But God, our King before the ages, has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.” In place of the eating that brought death, not by its nature but through disobedience, he united his own divine nature with ours and is set forth in the air as life-giving food, partaken of by all, while he himself remains unconsumed: he who was willingly condemned for the condemned, being himself both God and mortal. Just as he was fed gall and given vinegar to drink in return for the eating of Adam, who had willed it but was disappointed in his hope, [?]

paying off his debts in a divine-human way, so too, it seems to me, the forty days are set against just as many days. But rather than their six hours or my forty days, I prefer the account of this that has come down to us from certain elders of no small repute, confirmed by the words of the lofty Apostle: that our forefather lived blessedly in paradise for a longer time. For the divine Apostle, speaking in Adam's person, cries out plainly, “I was once alive apart from the law.” Now Paul did not exist before the law, since he was the last of all the law's students; nor was he ever without this law. Indeed, in preaching the Gospel he cites the testimonies of the law everywhere. But speaking in Adam's person, with fitting lament, he says, “I was once alive apart from the law.” He shows still more clearly that he is crying this out in Adam's person, and makes the meaning plain, when he no longer says “law” but “commandment”, evidently the one given to Adam: “But when the commandment came”, that is, when it was given, “sin revived, and I died”, he says, by falling from the blessed life through disobedience. So it is evident that the commandment was not given as soon as Adam was made, but after some time, though how long is not stated. The commandment that God gave Adam in paradise concerned eating from every tree and abstaining from the forbidden tree. This “every tree” is the tree that comprises every good; its name is “the All”. It is the truly existing good, of which David says, “Delight yourself in the Lord”, and which Solomon calls a tree of life when he speaks of Wisdom, who is the Lord. The tree of life, then, is the same as “every tree”, from which God urges us to eat. Against it he sets the other tree, whose fruit is not distinctly good or evil but mixed. The author of life forbids it, but the serpent recommends it, in order to prepare the way for death. The fruit of the forbidden tree is mixed of opposites for this reason: evil does not lie before us bare, showing itself in its own nature. Wickedness would be ineffective if it were not colored with some good that draws the person deceived into desiring it. As it is, it is mixed: it has ruin hidden in its depths, while by deceptive appearance it displays some semblance of good. So sins, whose corruption is hidden, become desirable to the unwary, who pursue them as good because they are deceived. Most people judge the good to lie in what pleases the senses, and there is a confusion of names

between the true good and the apparent good. For this reason the desire that arises for evil as if for good was called the knowledge of good and evil: it is not simply evil, because it is decked out with good, nor purely good, because evil lies hidden beneath it. For what is truly good is simple, but evil is manifold: it is taken for one thing and turns out by experience to be another. That is why the serpent displays the evil fruit of sin without showing openly the evil it had by nature, for the man would not have been deceived by an obvious evil. Instead he embellished its appearance with a certain beauty, and so seemed persuasive to the woman. “And the woman saw,” it says, “that the tree was good for food.” Yet that eating became the mother of death. So that tree was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, like the malice of poisons mixed with honey: insofar as it sweetens the senses it seems good, but insofar as it destroys whoever touches it, it is the worst of all evils.

Disobedience and every kind of wickedness are called sin, but before Adam no human being sinned, for none existed. By whom, then, was sin committed, that it existed beforehand as dead and revived when the commandment came? For it must be one of two things: either we suppose that sin has a nature of its own, or that it was committed by someone before Adam.

Away with calling evil a nature! Rather, it seems to me that all sin is resistance and battle against what is better. And this, I say, is the devil, who turned to the worse not by nature but by his own choice. He was an archangel, but because he slandered the angelic choirs to God, he was fittingly named “devil”, that is, “slanderer”. Cast down from the realms above the world, he became an enemy in his actions before this visible world had come into being, and before the man he would subdue existed. Then, once man was made, he in turn slandered God to Adam, prattling to him about God's envy. Passing over Adam, he first approached the weaker Eve and said, “Why is it that God said you are not to eat from every tree in paradise?” The wretch put his questions slyly, so that she would teach him which plant it was whose fruit the Lord had forbidden; for he did not know to which of the plants the commandment was attached, or why. And she, a most simple nature, as yet unspoiled, not knowing what he was aiming at, dealt herself a fatal blow. For she said, “From every tree in paradise you may eat, but from the tree in the middle of paradise you shall not eat.” And he, slandering God, said, “God knew that on whatever day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil; and that is why he forbade it.” So he persuaded the

wretched woman to eat what was forbidden, and through her he overpowered the man, both of them longing for divinity. Having thus stripped them of the immortality, incorruption and blessedness they possessed, the God-hater and murderer of men revived in his deeds, and in turn slandered to God the man who had transgressed. Moses, who saw God, the divine lawgiver, records the words of his slander, depicting the deceiver in tragic colors. The devil, slandering Adam to God, says: “And Jacob ate and was filled, and the beloved kicked. He grew fat, he grew thick, he grew broad, and he forsook God who made him and turned away from God his Saviour.” For he did the same to Jacob too, rolling him into meat-eating and drunkenness and then dashing them down into idolatry; against them Moses armed Levi and in a single day in the wilderness mowed down twenty-three thousand of Jacob like grass. Nevertheless, God, who loves mankind, without change became like the one who had been slandered, and came to us to overpower the enemy. He truly appeared in the form of the one who had been deceived, so that the enemy could not say, “I fought against mortals, but I was defeated by God.” He himself became mortal while remaining God, and came to fight for mortals. David, the singer of divine things, already prophesied this five hundred years beforehand: “Blessed,” he says, “is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Who is this, inspired one? “The Lord is God, and he has appeared to us.” And why does God become mortal, David? “To destroy the enemy and avenger,” he says, that is, the devil. For he slanders everyone to God, and God to others, and prompts both to take vengeance. He did this with double malice in the case of Job and God. To God he said, “Does Job worship God for nothing? Is he not flattered and pampered with great wealth?” To Job he said, “Fire fell from heaven and consumed all you have.” Again he said to God, “But stretch out your hand and touch his bones and his flesh”; and again to Job, through his wife, “How long will you hold out in the open on the dunghill? Say some word against the Lord, and die, and be rid of the evils that grip you.” Destroying this enemy and avenger by his divine-human coming, the Lord says, “Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy.”

QUESTION 121. And if the Lord destroyed the enemy, who is it that fights against each of us and besets us with unexpected temptations and sins?

Answer. Although he was able to bring about his complete obliteration and destruction, he did not wish to, so that we would not [?: “But say some word against the Lord, and die.”] [?]

be left without reward in the eternal life to come, having no adversary here in this present life to contend against, as in a stadium, and so win crowns in exchange for it. When he struck the dragon's head, he deadened along with it the whole trailing body, but left in it some faint movement, to exercise us and to display our virtue. For we too often strike a snake on the head and then let children beat the body as it crawls on, teaching them at the same time to be bold and to hunt wild beasts. For the demons do not have authority even over pigs, as the divine book of the Gospels teaches. Before Christ's divine permission they did not dare to touch the herd of pigs of the Gergesenes. And the Lord permits them, not to drown the herd together with the swineherds, but to let the swineherds take flight and to go against the irrational animals only. In this he clearly teaches us that, if we were not guarded by his divine power which encompasses all things, the demons would treat us like the pigs, or worse, when we are sailing or [at] sea [?].

But if he had not set up the commandment as a kind of prize and wrestling match, and left the antagonist free, man would not have been crowned or proclaimed victor. If he had not charged him to keep it and threatened death for the transgression, you would reasonably blame the one who gave it. But if, after the charge had been given, man slipped and fell by disobeying, blame the one who was defeated, not the one who set up the contest. Besides, just as he foreknew that Adam would transgress, so he also knew beforehand that Adam's descendants would be proclaimed victors by keeping the commandments and would be crowned by him: some in times of peace by displaying a virtuous life, others in times of persecution by standing firm for him even to death. For he foreknew that Abel would be justified, and Seth likewise; that Enoch would be taken up so as not to see death; that Noah would be justified; that Abraham would become the root of faith and the father of many nations. He foreknew that Isaac would be shown to be his virtuous servant; that Jacob would prevail against him in wrestling as against a mortal, and that the broad sinew of his thigh would go numb when it was touched; that Joseph would live in prison for his chastity, and that by his deeds he would hold royal power; that Moses would grow up fit to be a general and lawgiver; that Joshua son of Nun would win trophies over his enemies and enslave the Gibeonites; that David, with a single stone from his sling, would dash to the ground the champion of the foreigners, fully armored, wearing greaves, carrying a giant's club, holding shield and spear, and clad entirely in iron,

and that shortly afterward he would reign and would prophesy much about him. He foreknew that from Adam would spring the company of apostles, prophets, martyrs, teachers and the rest of the Church. In short, it was not right that through the simplicity and fall of one man the stadium should be closed to all, the contests be [?], courage be hidden [?], and [?] lie idle.

QUESTION 126. The Saviour says, “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wishes.” How is it, then, that when he came to Lazarus he did not raise him by his own authority, but entreated the Father, saying, “Father, glorify your Son,” and only then called Lazarus from the dead?

None of this takes away his power or authority. For he says, “I said it for the sake of the crowd standing by, so that they may believe.” And why does he add, “so that your Son also may glorify you”? Does the Father then need glory from the Son? Not at all. Rather, the Father glorified the Son and the Son the Father, showing us that they are of one mind and equal in glory. And how could the Son, who exercises full authority in greater matters, need the Father's permission or help in lesser ones, as you suggest? For whether he punishes or blesses, he nowhere calls upon the Father: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” And to those on the other side: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire.” To the paralytic he says, “Get up, take up your bed, and go to your house.” Elsewhere again: “Young man, I say to you, rise from the dead.” Likewise to the dead daughter of the synagogue leader he says, “Little girl, get up.” And to the leper, covered with sores from head to foot, he stretches out his hand and says, “I will it; be cleansed”; and at once the disease runs off, put to flight by the divine will. Rebuking the evil demon, he says, “I say to you, come out of him.” Again, with a rebuke he calms the swelling deep. Condemning cities along with their inhabitants, he says with authority, “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! And you, Capernaum, exalted to heaven, you will go down to Hades.” And pronouncing the destruction of the old Jerusalem, he says, “Not one stone will be left upon another in it,” which we see has come to pass. How, then, could he who in these greater matters nowhere called upon the Father or needed strength from him, heal the sick in lesser matters by borrowing the benefits from the Father? Away, then, my admirable friend, with such a notion about Christ! For it is not from any lack of authority or strength that in certain

[?] places he speaks to the Father. Rather, his aim [?] is always to teach us humility, to wear down the height of our pride, and never to entrust what is to be done to ourselves before he leads the way, but to make him the beginning of every word and deed.

QUESTION 127. [?] “…when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him.” How, then, can he be equal to the Father? For it is clear that the lesser is subject to the greater.

We must consider that lofty sacred herald himself. Here he speaks in more fleshly terms to those who are more childish, whose spiritual senses are not yet trained to discern loftier doctrines. “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ,” he says, “have put on Christ”; and these are the assembly of the Church, which wears Christ. At present, while the nations are being subjected to him in faith, it is as if he has not received the complete subjection of the nations of the Church [?]; for the fullness of the nations has not yet come in, as the Apostle himself says. But every day the company receives subjection through the addition of those who believe, as if it were Christ who received it. And when the fullness of the nations comes in, and the Church, which is Christ according to the flesh, has complete subjection with nothing left over, then it too, with its whole host, will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to it, that is, as if to Christ himself according to the flesh. So in what he writes to the more childish, he does not wholly veil the authority and divinity of Christ himself, lest Christ be thought to be against God or acting in opposition to the Father. But when he speaks to those more mature in perception, he sets before the nurslings, as it were, more solid food in place of milky, infant fare, drawing his teaching from the more divine truths. He gently draws aside the curtains that veil Christ's authority and shows him to be equal in glory and equal in power, God by his own authority, crying out plainly: “We await the Saviour from heaven, who will transform the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory, by the working of the power by which he is able even to subject all things to himself.” And elsewhere he says, “That God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.” See: in both passages it is said that he subjects things to himself. Keep yourself, then, from childishness, since the Apostle interprets himself: he does not teach everything with the same letter, but writes to each as suits them, as if leading them by the hand toward perfection.
QUESTION 128. If, then, Christ is God and equal to the Father, why does this same Apostle write of the Father as God and of the Son as Lord? It [?] me not a little…

For my part, I say that Christ God is above every power and lordship, since he is equal in glory to God the Father. His being called Lord by the lofty Apostle does not deprive him of divinity. Nor, again, does the phrase “God in Christ” show him to be merely indwelt, as we are taught by the Apostle himself and by the lofty Isaiah before him. For Isaiah, prophesying of Christ long ago, says: “And the Sabaeans, tall men, will cross over to you and will be your slaves; they will follow behind you, bound in fetters, for God is in you.” And refuting the idea of indwelling as you understand it, he goes on: “And there is no God besides you; for you are our God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel, the Saviour.” And again the same prophet [?] says: “A child has been born to us, and his name is called Mighty God, Ruler.” And Paul, lofty in mind, says: “Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.” As for the title “Lord”, David the sacred psalmist shows that it is not outside divinity. For foretelling in song the divine-human coming of God the Word in the flesh, he says: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has appeared to us.” Throughout the Old Testament the inspired prophets call the Father Lord: the lofty Isaiah, “Thus says the Lord of Hosts”; Jeremiah, who faced many dangers, “Thus says the Lord Almighty”; Ezekiel, the expounder of the Cherubim, “Thus says the Lord Adonai, the Lord”; and likewise Daniel and the rest of the prophets. Nor does Paul, when he says, “one God, the Father,” place the Father outside lordship; nor again, when he says, “one Lord, Jesus Christ,” does he show the Son to be outside divinity. Nor, again, does the Son, when he speaks divinely, “On this rock I will build my Church,” show the Father to have no share in the Church. For he says, “All that is mine is yours, Father, and what is yours is mine.” Everywhere in divine Scripture the titles “God” and “Lord” are united. And that the divine and all-holy Spirit too bears the same name and the same glory, we are taught by the sacred Apostle when he writes, “For the Lord is the Spirit.” To those, then, who look sharply into divine Scripture, it will never seem to disagree or be at war with itself, when it proclaims now the more divine truths and now the condescension, adapting itself to the understanding of the hearer. It is like a mother who loves her children and feeds each of them suitably: to the nurslings who are still tender she gives milk, as it were, to drink; those who have left infancy behind she feeds with vegetables; and to the more mature she gives bread. For the lofty Apostle says to both, “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet [?]”

…for you were not able; indeed, even now you are not able.” And turning to others he says, “The one who is weak eats vegetables.” By this he means teachings of a middling kind, since such a person cannot yet be fed on bread like those already mature in instruction, because his mind is still simple and unsteady.

QUESTION 122. How is it that the Apostle puts limits on the kingdom of Christ when he writes, “For he must reign until he has put his enemies under his feet”? The interpreters have explained this to mean that after the end of this world Christ's kingdom will be completed, and when he returns to the Father, God will be all in all, as the Apostle says.

I think it is of such people that Jeremiah speaks in his lament: “Who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes, and I will weep day and night for the wounded of my people?” He means those who have shut their ears and pay no attention to the divine word, which cries out plainly, “The Son abides forever.” Daniel, the man of desires, will stand against them as a bitter refutation of their drunken folly. He says, “I beheld in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man coming on the clouds of heaven.” And shortly after he says, “His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.” David, the singer of divine things, says the same: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.” And further on: “In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands; they will perish, but you remain; you are the same, and your years will not fail.” Paul, lofty of mind, interprets this of the Lord, and everywhere in his letters he proclaims him creator, king and God before the ages and to the ages. Moses too, who saw God and gave the divine law, writes this at the end of the song of Miriam: “The Lord reigns over the ages, and to the ages, and beyond.” And “the Lord” is Christ, as we have already confessed. So let them stop babbling, on the strength of the word “until,” that the kingdom of Christ will one day come to an end. They misunderstand what was rightly said. The very words of the Apostle expose their rashness. “For death reigned from Adam until Moses,” he says. Did it reign only until Moses, or beyond him as well? It stretched its power over many generations. It ran its course through every age of rational beings until Christ tripped it up, crowned mortals with power over it, and himself became death to death. The Apostle was also refuting the Jews, who thought great things of Moses

and despised Christ. They even supposed Moses to be God, because his tomb has not been found to this day, and because he stood with the prophet Elijah beside the transfigured Christ on the mountaintop. So they thought he was still alive, carried away in the flesh as Elijah was. The Apostle puts down their arrogance and the swelling of their empty opinion about the man. He shows that Moses was mortal and of the same nature as we are, as though pointing at it with his finger and saying, “Moses was mortal and he died; why do you boast, O Jews?” And again he refutes them: “For to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart.” Are the Jews blind only until Paul's day, or until the very end of the age? Again, writing to the Corinthians, he says, “We came even as far as you with the gospel of Christ.” Did he reach only as far as Corinth? Did he not run swiftly from the east to the west, around as far as Illyricum, and preach when he arrived even at Rome itself? And again he says, “Exhort one another every day, as long as it is called Today.” The inspired David also foretold, “Today, if you hear his voice” (God's voice, that is), “do not harden your hearts as in the provocation, on the day of testing in the wilderness.” Was obedience to the divine voice necessary, then, only for people up to David's time? O the drunken folly of the vainly wise! We, who are creatures of Christ, will rise after the present age incorruptible and immortal and abide forever. Will he himself, the architect and ruler of the universe, then cease to be once he has returned to the Father? And how can he promise mortals that they will reign with him eternally and immortally, if, as these empty-minded people say, he is deprived of that reign and gives up his kingdom when it reaches its limit? Away with such absurdity, I beg you. In the Old Testament David will refute them when he sings of the kingdom of Christ: “Let all your works confess you, O Lord.” And all things are the work of Christ. As the lofty John says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” that is, Christ; and “all things came into being through him.” And again David says, “Your kingdom is a kingdom of all the ages, and your dominion is in every generation.” Gabriel, the minister of Christ's boundless kingdom, agrees with him and says plainly, “And he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” So the words “until” and “today,” which are commonly used in many places of divine Scripture, do not set limits of time. For with God the whole age is one day without evening. The same is true for all the intellectual and rational powers, since the light above the world is never followed by night.
[QUESTION.] If he is equal to the Father, how can he himself say, “The Son can do nothing of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it”?

It is utter folly to think this way about the Child of God, the only-begotten God. For it would really follow that the whole creation must be twofold. One creation would be the Father's, already complete. The other would be the Son's, still being made, brought in piece by piece and fashioned in imitation of the Father's. So let the followers of Arius's madness show us two suns and two luminaries[?], and tell us which belongs to the Father and which to the Son; and which moon is the Father's and which the Child's. I will reasonably ask the same about the dry land and the sea. And how will John, the son of thunder, be telling the truth? He drew his account of the incarnate Word from Christ's bosom, where he reclined, and like a divine bowl he was filled from an ever-flowing spring. He set “All things came into being through him” as the rule for everything under the sun, meaning that the Son made all things without looking to any archetype or model. And who is this? The one who was united to our nature in the womb of the Ever-Virgin can only be the only-begotten Child of God, sent by the Father to be born of a woman, as the divine Apostle teaches. Where, then, or when did the Son see the Father become flesh, be born, be crucified, be buried and rise again, so that he could do these things after his example? Where did he hear the Begetter say anything like “I have authority to lay down my life and to take it up again,” and “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself”? Where did he see the Father riding on a beast of burden, so that he too came into Jerusalem seated on a donkey in imitation of him? In short, the Son did all the things mentioned without looking to anyone. When he formed Adam and fashioned Eve from him, he did not see some other rational male or female made by the Father and fashion his own after that pattern. He is creator by his own authority and the self-determining God of all. He was so before the incarnation and remains the same after it, able to do all things simply by willing them. Why, then, does he say, “The Son can do nothing of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it”? So that people whose sight is dim where he is concerned would not think him an opponent of God or a parricide. At the same time he teaches us to love our father.
QUESTION 131. When James and John, the sons of Zebedee, asked to sit with him, how could he say, “To sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to give”?

He did not refuse because he was unable to grant it. With a well-reasoned refusal he checked their pride and their attempt to rise above their fellow disciples. Through them he also brought the others to their senses, and the sting of his refusal withered the improper desire for first place that was smoldering in them. He does not say, “The Father will certainly grant it to you,” but “to those for whom it has been prepared,” meaning those who toil. He is spurring them on to virtue and courage: they must first show their devotion and strip for the contests, standing firm for him even to the point of death. It is as if he said: “You have not yet preached my message. How can you long to proclaim the words[?] when you have not yet been beaten for my sake? So strip for the contests in the stadium. Go down into the arena, come forward willingly, and stay unconquered. As soon as the theater of this present age is broken up, I will give you the thrones as prizes. For now, however, I am right to shake you off by saying that the Father grants them to those people. There is no other way to fend off you and your mother when you pester me.” Or he is acting like people who do not want to give something to those who ask before the proper time, and so pretend that the authority belongs to someone else. They do this so that the askers will not grow slack in devotion and courage once they have received it, content with what they were given and no longer willing to toil. Earthly kings commonly do the same when people press them for high office or a military command. They have the power to give it but do not wish to do so before the time. So they refer the authority from one official to another, and the hope of advancement rouses the petitioners to zeal for the realm. In this way the kings get them to compete with one another and to be vigorous and sharpened against the enemy. There is another explanation too. Because they thought he would reign over an earthly, temporary kingdom, he says to them, “You do not know what you are asking.” It is as if he said: “Sober up, my disciples. Lift your minds up to my kingdom. Do not delight in things that flit past like a phantom in the night, or in things that cling to the ground. Otherwise you may hear from my Father as well: It is not mine simply to give; it is mine to demand of you the repayment of contests and sweat. I would rather be in your debt for your devotion than accuse you of slackness. It is not mine to give, nor is it my Father's to give simply to those who ask. If it were, murderers and adulterers and every wicked and dissolute person could ask and sit beside me. It is not for us to give at random and debase justice. A just judge assigns to each according to merit; he does not pass over those who sweat and reward the slack. So if you long for the thrones, you know the contests for which you must strip. Do not pride yourselves only on the philosopher's cloak, the beard and the staff, but buy the thrones with toil and win the favor of the judgment seat.”
QUESTION 132. If the Son is as powerful and self-determining as the Father,

how can he fear the cross and plead with the Father, saying, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”? Fleeing to another in time of need and asking for his help is not a sign of sovereign authority or free will.

I think the divine hand deals the empty-minded a mortal blow from this passage too. Here also he is shown to be equal in power to the Begetter, and the words he spoke while playing a part do nothing to take away his authority. His coming as God and man was hard to accept, and people could not believe it because of his extreme humility and love for humankind. His aim was not to drive off the avenging fiend by the might of his Godhead or to destroy his ranks by sheer authority. He meant rather to condemn the adversary through gentleness and patience. If he had come using his natural strength, he would not have seemed to be doing anything remarkable: God fighting an apostate angel. Worse, it would have puffed the devil up even further into madness, since he would have been known as God's opponent. So he fittingly took on the lowliness of mortals to bring down the devil's arrogance and win the trophy of victory for us. Man had been subdued in the beginning. If the destroyer had been overcome by God, perceived as God, and not through the man who was seen, the victory would have seemed foreign to our race. But the holy Word came in a nature both divine and human. He defeated the enemy through the exaltation of the very one who had been captured, and as God he gave us power over him, declaring: “Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy.”

QUESTION 131[?]. QUESTION 133. Who, then, is the one crucified, or rather the one who begs to be spared and says, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”? ANSWER. Neither nature on its own. A mere mortal cannot save, and God alone is not of a nature to suffer. It is the one person made of both through the union and joining of the natures: the God-man born of the Ever-Virgin, who kept her unharmed. He is the same God and the same mortal, and neither nature is separated from the other as he mounts the cross. So he speaks at one time as God and at another as man, adapting himself to the occasion. At one point, while the enemy is held off at a distance, he shows himself to be God before his hearers through words and signs. At another, when the enemy approaches and looks closely to see whether the one who hints at this is truly God, and . . . to the contests and the arena, he again plays the part of a mortal. He does this so that the adversary will not take fright and run away from the fight to the end, to the cross and death, on which the whole divine-human victory depended.

QUESTION 134. Why, when he came, was he not crucified openly, relying on his own strength? Why does he appear poor at some times and glorious at others? And why does he even pretend to be afraid, when he is God?

Because the enemy did not attack our forefathers openly in paradise either, since then they would have been on guard against his scheme and their fall. Instead he hid his own nature in the serpent, uniting himself with it, and said to the wretched woman, “On the day you eat of the forbidden tree, you will be like gods.” In short, by what followed he cunningly led them away from the blessed life. So the wretched enemy, who deceived with deceitful words, was deceived with divine words. There it was neither a mere serpent nor the devil on his own; here it is neither a mere mortal nor God on his own. Nor is he actually afraid; he plainly undoes the fool's trick. Notice how willing and how strong his pretended fear was. When the Jews came to arrest him, he blinded them and said, “Whom are you looking for?” When they said they were looking for Jesus, he again showed that he was acting willingly. He said to them, “Here I am,” and promptly went along with those who were looking for him. Who could have stopped him from flying past the vultures? Who could have kept him from walking away from the blinded men, when he says, “I have authority to lay down my life and to take it up again”? And why did he rebuke Peter so sharply[?] when Peter prayed that the cross might be kept from him? He says to his beloved disciple, “Get behind me, Satan, for you are not thinking the things of God, but the things of men.” It is as if he said: “Follow me and do not rush ahead. You do not understand the divine plan, and the sight of my flesh has broken your spirit. How could I, the immortal Life, fear death? How could I, who free people from suffering, pray to escape suffering? I healed the blind with the touch of my hand. With a bare word I gave strength to the paralyzed and made those who had been carried on pallets carry them. I dried up fountains of blood through the fringe of my garment and stripped lepers of their disfigurement. I drove out legions of demons with a command. I walked on the deep as on dry land, and I made it fall silent and be muzzled as it rose and crashed. I stretched out my hand to the winds and calmed them, the winds that had made the disciples endure the swell and the tossing. With five loaves I fed five thousand until they were full, and filled twelve baskets with the leftovers. I called Lazarus back to life from the tomb unharmed after he had been dead four days and was stinking. I am the creator and God of all, and I myself am the life and the resurrection. I pretend fear and humility by exposing my flesh, because I want to catch the dragon. That devil mocks mortals, but he is being mocked by me. I am a fisherman, and I have let myself down as a hook into the depths of this life. For bait I have put on the captured flesh of mortals, and by my own act I have become Adam like them, without change. Like a fisherman, I sometimes tease and tug the hook that has been let down into the deep, and sometimes I hold it

still as the man-killing fish I am watching for comes near, so that it does not take fright and dart away. That is why I say through my servant David, ‘But I am a worm and not a man.’ For just as the worm takes flesh and comes to life from the earth without any mating, so I too took flesh from the Ever-Virgin without any intercourse or union with a man. By my own act I became mortal while remaining God.” That is why Jeremiah, the prophet who faced the most dangers, saw with prophetic eye that the deceiver would be deceived. As if laughing at his arrogance and folly, he spoke of me more than five hundred years beforehand: “He is a man, and who will know him?” He means that this man is God, who became man for our sake in his saving plan, choosing in his wisdom to make a fool of the one who is wise in wickedness. In this he fulfilled the prophecy of noble Job, which says, “You will draw out the dragon with a hook.” Job also says, “You have walked in the place of the abyss,” meaning Christ ran through the regions under the earth and set free the captives there. And again he says, “The gates of death will open to you in fear, and the gatekeepers of Hades cowered when they saw you.”
QUESTION 135. So are you calling Christ a mocker, who defeated the devil by trickery?

There is nothing unfitting in that. Before he appeared as God and man, he appeared to Moses, who revealed sacred things, and said to him, “Do you see how I have made sport of the Egyptians?” In the same way, after he took flesh he made sport of the spiritual Pharaoh and the whole army of his Egyptian demons. He scourged him invisibly and drowned him in the sea by saying, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” O cup that wounds the devil, drives out demons, winnows away sins, atones for sinners, and works eternal life! God the Word truly became man, without change, and went through all human experiences in truth, except unholy wickedness. So at the time of his passion he also begs to be spared the cup. He was not afraid of what he already willed; he was teaching that we should not rush into dangers, but should meet them firmly and bravely when they come. So while the cross was still being plotted, he declined it as part of his saving plan. But once it was decreed, he took it on his shoulders like a victor and went to it willingly, freely going to be nailed to it. All of us together should cry out what the inspired David sang: “How great are your works, O Lord! In wisdom you have made them all.” And the lofty Apostle cries out plainly: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” What folly! The inspired are at a loss over the very things ordinary people try to search out. So let all quarrelsomeness
and every stirring of argument fall silent, for God rejoices to be honored with simple faith.

QUESTION 136. Now that everything has been clearly explained to us, we ask, finally, to learn about our own nature. David belittles man and makes him small. In the eighth psalm he says, “Lord, what is man, that you are mindful of him?” In the thirty-eighth psalm he says, “Surely every man is vanity.” And in the hundred and forty-third psalm: “Lord, what is man, that you have made yourself known to him, or the son of man, that you take account of him? Man is like vanity.” But his son Solomon magnifies man and exalts him, saying, “Man is a great and precious thing.” If Solomon disagrees with his father, how can the rest of the prophets agree?

In none of these can the words of those who revealed God be shown to disagree, so long as they are studied with a love of learning and contemplated soberly, apart from a coarse way of life. For practice is the step that leads to contemplation. The one presents our nature; the other presents the honor we received from the God of all, since we were made by divine hands, unlike all the rest of creation. Open the first book of Moses and you will learn both: that God took dust from the earth and formed man, and breathed the breath of life into his face. The words “he took and formed” show the honor, for they are said of no other created thing but of man alone. From the dust taken from the earth we learn how lowly our nature is: we are earth and dust, worth nothing and easily broken down.
QUESTION 137. How, then, can man be a great and precious thing if he is lowly and easily broken down, subject to countless passions and needs?

Do not look only at the nature; consider the honor along with it. I attributed easy dissolution and a short life to our nature, but these crept in on us through the transgression, after we were turned away from our former blessed life in paradise. For after that ruinous eating, the wretched man heard the sentence, “You are earth, and to earth you shall return,” since he had [obeyed?] the enemy rather than God…
QUESTION 138. What does David mean when he says to God, “Your hands made me and formed me”? Does forming mean one thing and making another? And from this…

I think that "making" should be understood of the soul, and "fashioning" of the body's many-sided moulding. By the hands of God the Father I mean the Son and the Spirit, to whom he also says, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness." The narrative also says that God took dust from the earth and fashioned man. In saying this it uses what is visible and familiar to point to an operation that is invisible. For the whole was the work of his will, and the making was not a moulding by hands. Still, it is called the moulding of his hands to honour our nature. In the same way, "according to the image of God" does not mean that we copy his nature, for no one can even say how far short of it we fall. It means that we bear the stamp of his rule and freedom.
QUESTION 139. Why then do you describe the Divine as having limbs, after our image and likeness, and so suggest that he has ears, arms and legs?

It is right to pause briefly over these matters and set them out in order, point by point, so that a muddled question does not make us stumble in the answer. Let us climb straight up the ladder of reasoning to the very source of our own origin. Man is a great and precious thing, yet both long ago and now he takes his origin from humble stuff. God could have made a mortal out of bronze, or iron [?], or adamant, or stone. Instead, long ago he fashioned him from dust, and today he makes him from a fainter, flowing secretion. This shows that his creative wisdom is incomprehensible and beyond understanding. But do not let the sharp mind of your love mock me or laugh at me if, for the sake of accuracy, I touch lightly on the natural mysteries of our generation. Divine Scripture does not disdain to mention such things. It does so in the case of Judah's son sleeping with Tamar, and in the purifications of the law it mentions the man with a discharge . . . [?] . . . sitting, and the purification of the woman who has just given birth. The lofty Apostle too, writing to the Romans, mentions men who corrupt males and women raving with lust. So the male casts a kind of cold emission into the female. This mixes with the blood the woman casts in return and is curdled by the man's colder secretion. Job says as much, the man God himself attested to be blameless and true. Struck in his body, he speaks with God: "Did you not milk me out like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh and knit me together with bones and sinews; you set life and mercy with me." Here he presents both our nature and its self-determination and free will. "You set life and mercy with me," he says, as if to say: "You set it in me

to live and to have mercy on myself by obeying and keeping your commandments, or else to destroy myself by disobedience and to receive no mercy, being justly punished for siding with the enemy rather than the Creator." This is what our forefather did. He had no mercy on himself and took the deadly counsel to himself like a sword. It slew him, and he passed away, made mortal instead of immortal. So when all the sense organs and senses of both persons close together, and in their union the bodies are, as it were, mixed and kneaded into one another, the ineffable deposit becomes an impression of the person whose seed is given first and is stronger. That is why the child's features are stamped to match [?] and resemble the father or the mother. The male's deposit is cold and bone-like, so it is turned into strong bones and sinews and hardens to suit its source. The blood the woman gives in return during intercourse is hot by nature, and once the cold has congealed it, it turns into flesh. The flesh then comes alive, because a life-giving power is breathed into it by God. "For I am the one who made the earth and man upon it, and who gives the breath of life to all who walk on it," says God. An argument from outside writers: Nature lies within the seed. When the power in the seed begins to move, it is called "nature" (physis), because it brings forth (phyein) and begets. It is nourished by the food in the body, since there is no food without matter. It moves by digesting the food into itself, and by its own action it also carries out the distribution of nourishment. Nature has three powers. The generative power holds in advance the seminal principles. The power of growth moves over time. The nutritive power works up the food. The nutritive power and the power of growth run through the whole body, but the generative power is found only in the seminal vessels that hold the seed. Nature busies itself first of all with food and breath. A warm breath, moving of itself according to the seminal principles, begets man and brings him to completion over time and in size

We say that the soul is present together with the deposit from the man, and that the deposit is living and ensouled. The beginnings of our nature come from a living, ensouled body, and they are like cuttings from trees, which each contain their tree's seed and the life-giving power of the tree they were taken from. For if the blood is warm and the seed from the man is living, then even if it is not in every way like the blood, they have life

[?] . . . and insignificant. On the first day the soul cannot fully display its own operations, because the deposit is so slight. But as the deposit grows in the womb and turns into flesh, and from there turns into an infant, the soul grows along with it. It then fully displays its own operations and appears together with the body as the body reaches completion.

Away with the idea that souls coexist with the seed! How could we suppose that the soul came into being together with Adam's body, when he was made without any intercourse or sowing? If we granted that the soul is secreted from the man along with the seed, it would certainly follow that the soul of the incarnate God and Word, united to his body, must also be supposed to come from seed. That is the height of folly and blasphemy, and it carries endless punishment. This drunken raving would also mean that those who flee fornication, who fight nobly against it, and who make themselves eunuchs through self-control for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, as the Lord says, will pay penalties instead of receiving prizes and crowns. On this view they stifle souls within themselves and put them to death along with their earthly members, so that by their chastity and purity they turn out worse than the lustful and the pleasure-lovers. Will even Paul, so lofty in mind, then go unrewarded and be called to account for bringing punishment and soul-murder upon us? By deed and word he taught, and wrote to the whole world, that we should flee fornication and not touch a woman if possible. And why did he punish the Corinthian fornicator, who was releasing to life a soul that would otherwise have been stifled within him? Why did the law command the man with a discharge to be purified and washed with water, if a soul pent up in his loins had come forth? And from what plants or fruits did God take cuttings or seed when he adorned the earth in the beginning? How was it that Sarah slept with Abraham from her youth until she was a hundred years old and received the same deposit, yet never found it ensouled until God commanded it, so that Isaac was born, the only child of parents a hundred years old? How was it that Hannah lay with Elkanah for many years, yet never received a deposit that was ensouled in her womb until she went to the temple and begged the Divine for a child? The Divine accepted her supplication. For many years the deposit had been cast into her and never brought to life. Then, when it was cast in the usual way at their next lying together as lifeless matter, God ensouled it and formed the lofty and holy Samuel. As an infant still at the breast he was taken from her, and his mother wrapped him in a little cloak and brought him to the temple that had granted her the holy child, dedicating him to God from his swaddling clothes. And how was it with good old Elizabeth? She slept with Zechariah, a man of her own age, from her tender, blooming youth. They reached grey old age and never

gave up the laws of marriage, yet they never achieved a living mixture until the angel's voice ensouled the matter lying in the loins. This matter was deposited by both and congealed into flesh. It was like a stone that a quarryman's hand tears from a mountain or a quarry and carves by daily chiselling until it reaches the intended shape of the statue. In the same way, by an ineffable art, matter that had long been lifeless and unsightly in the old couple was carved into John, and . . . [?] the Baptist and Forerunner. So let this fable that souls coexist in the male's frothing emission be silenced. How can the incorruptible and immortal coexist with what is corruptible and unsightly?
