How could the soul, which is of a better and higher nature, owe its entry into life to what is lesser and worse? And is it not absurd to suppose that the soul is sown in corruption, when the Apostle says of the body, "It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption; it is sown a soulish body"? He does not say it is sown a soul. "Soulish" here stands for the soul's own instrument. Let the nonsense of the soul's later existence fall silent too. The moment God conceives what each being is to be, the matter is present as well, and the [?] of each one's existence are present together with God's effective will. Divine Scripture teaches neither the pre-existence nor the post-existence of souls, so that man may not think himself both older and younger than himself. As soon as it says, "And God took dust from the earth and formed man," it promptly adds, "And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." So neither the soul by itself nor the body by itself is man. Moses, the writer of divine things, declared that a mortal is made complete by the joining and union of both. But let us go back to the point from which our discourse departed. The blood, congealed by the cold, is turned into flesh. This flesh grows as the qualities of food settle into it little by little, given by him who gives food to all flesh, as David the singer of divine things says. It is like the flesh of sea creatures nourished inside the shells of oysters and scallops as if in a womb. They have a life-giving power from God, so they leap and throb, though they have no mouth, hearing, teeth or organs of taste and are not formed into limbs. They are fed only by the moisture of the waters seeping into them. But they stay in the same shape forever, because the divine command gave them that kind of nature. The starting point of our generation, by contrast, is small at the first mixing of the seeds. Little by little the qualities of the food taken in are added, and it is woven around and swells. In an ineffable way it is shaped by the spiritual and invisible divine hand of the one who formed our forefather from dust. Then, over the span of nine months, the infant is brought to completion by divine strength, and by the strength

of the womb that carries it, it is pushed out of its sack. The Creator of all could have formed us complete and perfect all at once, as he did Adam, either from that faint starting point deposited in the womb or even without it, just as he brought all things out of nothing. He does not need the nine months for embryos because he lacks the power. Rather, the belly is like a hide or membrane, and it has to be swollen gradually as what lies within takes shape, and stretched by the one leaping inside. The female organs could not have held a child placed in them fully formed all at once. People who try to fit more into a very small, dry bag sensibly do the same: by softening and stretching it they make it strong and able to hold more [?]. As it seems to me, then, whatever is bony and sinewy hardens from the male's secretion, and whatever is bloody and fleshy is formed from the female's contribution. The divine word and deed follow upon this again. "Increase and multiply and fill the earth," God says to our first parents. In saying it he also brings it about [?]: we grow to the bodily size he has fixed, multiply through our offspring, and fill the earth. From the first-formed themselves we learn what each contributes to the bearing of children. A bone was taken from Adam's rib, and the divine hand fashioned it into a woman. This shows both the joining and union of our nature and what each partner contributes to procreation. From this let it be understood that there is present in us a share of what is regarded as elemental . . . [?]: the hot and the cold, and the other pair, the moist and the dry. The earth, from which the Creator brought us forth, seems to me to be mixed with all of them. It is itself called dry, yet it floats on the moist. Fire lies hidden in rocks, iron and wood, and air runs right through the earth and warms it. Once the infant has been articulated in the womb, and the shapeless, waterless [?] matter has been carved into complete articulation, each limb is nourished from then on and grows by the quality of what enters the belly of the mother who carries it. It is like what happens in farming, when rain from the clouds or water flowing in channels soaks the soil. Suppose, for the sake of argument, a garden that nourishes countless kinds of plants within itself, different in appearance and shape, yet all in one and the same company. The water that makes them thrive is likewise of one nature, but the particular character of each plant changes the moisture into different qualities. The same water turns bitter in wormwood and becomes a deadly juice in hemlock. The one thing becomes something different in saffron, in balsam, in the poppy. In one it is heated, in another it is cooled, and in another it has a middle quality. In laurel, rush and similar aromatic plants it becomes fragrance; in the fig [?]

and the pear it turns sweet; through the vine it changes into the grape cluster and wine; in the apple it becomes juice; in the lily it turns white; in the violet, deep blue. Something like this is wondrously worked by nature in the living garden of our body, or rather by the Master of nature. Bones, cartilage, veins, arteries, sinews, ligaments, flesh, skin, fat, hair, glands, nails, eyes, nostrils, ears and countless other parts differ from one another, yet a single kind of food nourishes them all, each in keeping with its own nature. When the food reaches any part, it is changed to suit that part and becomes proper and natural to its particular character. If it comes to the eye, it is blended with the part that sees and coats the membrane of the eye. Settling into the parts that hear, it is shaped along with the hearing. Moistening the lips, it keeps them from drying out and withering like hides. In bone it hardens, and in marrow it softens. In sinew it is made taut, and over the surface of the body it is stretched out. It passes into the nails, and through the corresponding vapours it is finely worked into the growth of hair. If the moisture is breathed out through crooked pores, it produces curlier, twisting locks. If it passes through straight, softer pores, the hair is straight and like thread, as the moisture seeping from the food is turned into hair by the vapours. But if the exhalations from the heart and liver rise to the head through hotter channels, they naturally produce baldness. When the cold fails and the heat prevails, the hair is parched and falls out. But truly this is the right moment for us to honour our Master and Ruler. It is a sweet thing, admirable and worthy of every word, to join the divine David in singing, "How great are your works, O Lord! In wisdom you have made them all." "Who will tell of the mighty acts of the Lord, or who will recount them?" What words could ever describe it? From substances different and unlike, he fashioned our single nature, and neither part escapes its fellowship and union with the other before the limits you have set to each one's life. The immortal soul pervades the mortal body freely to its farthest limits. Then again it bids a long farewell to the body it was joined to, obeying the command to separate. Who will not be amazed to see so many limbs and parts of the body made from dust? There are various bones that fit together, joined by turns and sockets, to support the flesh and allow every kind of movement. As if drawn by a single line, they keep every proportion: limb balances limb, the right hand is as long as the left, finger matches finger, sole matches sole, foot matches foot, and so on, part by part. But it is fitting that our discourse should run up to the summit of our making and from there make its way down to the feet and the sandals. Or rather, from

the soul itself, if possible, let us begin. Pay attention to yourself, then, and you will have no need to trace the Creator from the structure of the universe. In yourself, as in a small world, you will see the inexpressible wisdom of God. First of all, learn from your own incorporeal soul to think of the Divine as incorporeal, contained by no place. After all, our own mind is not in the first instance confined to a place; it comes to be in a place only through its union with the body. Confess that God is invisible, judging from his own image, the soul. It does not submit to the eyes of the flesh. It cannot be pictured by colour, shape or any other bodily feature, and it is known by its operation alone. So do not seek to grasp God's nature with the eyes either. Do not go beyond a faint condescension, and even that only behind some veil. Not even the Cherubim see him as he is by nature: they shade their sight with the covering of their wings, because that nature cannot be contained. Entrust the understanding of him to your mind and to faith, and you will see God to the extent that you have left the material life and entered on the spiritual. Marvel at his wisdom: how he joins the soul to the body, extending it to the body's farthest limits, and brings limbs that are far apart into one harmony and fellowship. Consider what strength passes from the soul into the flesh, and what feeling is reflected back from the flesh to the soul. The body draws its life from the incorporeal soul, and the incorporeal soul takes on the imprint of the body's pains. When the body is tormented, the soul cries out; when the soul is happy, the body flourishes and blooms. O beautiful joining! O wondrous union! O the wisdom of the one who united them! Who can say what storerooms and treasuries of learning the soul has built for itself? Old knowledge is not darkened by what is newly brought in, nor shut off by some partition from what is heard each day. Today it can report a saying heard fifty years ago. It keeps its memories of what it was taught distinct and unconfused, as if carved in rock. And when it slips toward the passions of the flesh, its own beauty fades. But when virtue cleanses it of the disgrace of vice, it runs back toward the likeness of its Creator. He himself says in the Gospels, "Amen, I say to you, if two on earth agree about the same thing." By this he means the soul and the body, the mistress and the servant. If they agree about the same thing, the flesh serves and the soul advances in virtue. Then the servant is not worn down by excessive harshness and does not refuse its labours, nor is the mistress dragged down by the servant into passions and love of pleasure. Instead, in harmony and by the even rule of virtue, they run side by side and keep each other company. "For if they agree . . ." [?]

…these two, the soul and the body: whatever they ask for, it will be done for them, says the Lord. If we ask of him, we will clearly ask for good things, and it will be done. But if we go over to the devil by a careless and passion-ridden life, then crooked and grievous ways will surely be our lot. In my view, becoming subject to him is itself a kind of request. Let us then, if you will, also touch on the structure and articulation of the body, marveling at God, the wise architect of the universe. That supreme craftsman built a fitting dwelling for the rational soul. Alone of all living creatures under heaven he made man upright, teaching us by our very shape that we have our life from our kinship with what is above. All the irrational animals are bent downward toward the belly. Mortals alone have a natural and ready upward gaze toward heaven, so that one should not be a lover of pleasure or stoop down to the passions, but should stand erect, look toward the things above and have one's motion directed there. Next, he set the head as if on a hilltop of the body and established in it the precious senses. People think that the brain, if emptied out, would not fill even a cup. Yet it has been entrusted with wisdom and understanding by the Creator, who fashioned all things by God's will and understanding. That the brain is of the greatest importance for life is plainly shown by what happens in the opposite case. If the membrane that surrounds it is wounded or torn, death follows hard on the heels of the wound, for nature cannot hold out against the injury for even an instant. It is like vaulted buildings or the roofs of baths: what holds the whole structure together is a single crowning stone fixed into the dome, which builders call the keystone, and if it is shattered or knocked out, the whole thing immediately collapses. The greatest of the luminaries, the Sun and the Moon, toil as they run through the regions above the heavens in the course of a day and a night. But our mind, in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, ranges at once over the lower creation and the things beyond the world. It runs an unwearied course around them, unseen itself, unseen as it surveys unseen things. The locks of hair seem slight and feeble, yet they too have grown on the skin of the skull as an adornment. With their breezes they drive away the tiny creatures that plague the bald, who are always moving their hands [?]. Moreover, the hairs hold out against the frost of winter and the blaze of the sun. Like a grove or a thicket, they shade what lies beneath them and catch the rain. The eyes have been allotted the highest lookout, and though there are only two of them, they see the whole ordered world, so that nothing of the body's [?] blocks their view. They sit beneath the slight projection of the brows, which reach out from the eminence above toward the [?]. With their lashes, as with points or needles, they shake off tiny creatures, and by the constant movement of the eyelids they keep the pupils

safe, fanning away the blaze of the sun. These same lids are like curtains for them [?], and they turn aside the death that comes through licentiousness. Jeremiah, the prophet of many perils, bears witness to it when he says, "Death has come up through the windows." Not only must the body be kept untouched, but the glances of the eyes must also be kept virgin. They must never be allowed to dart shamelessly and flit about the beauty of others, lest from the sight we rush on to the act. For according to the divine word, "Whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." The pupils of the eyes, then, must be kept virgin, since they have been honored with the same name as virgins, for the word for both is "maiden." Often the maiden who dwells in virginity within the eyelids, as they open and she turns about, has become an outright signal and thought of fornication. The ear is the most stunted of all our members, yet it too adorns the shell that surrounds it, and alone of all creation it is entrusted with the mysteries of God. It is turned in a spiral throughout, so that speech does not enter too quickly. Instead, over a longer time, as the speech is worn down by the winding on its way to the depths, it leaves the stuff of falsehood behind on the banks, together with the refuse of slander. It is the virtue of the speaker not to speak falsely, and of the hearer to test what is reported, to see whether any partisan feeling is mixed into it. The one does not see sharply; the other does not see at all. If the word has been corrupted by either defect, we must punish it at the tribunal of the mind within us and scrape it clean of evil, with truth as the executioner. This is what the story of Job, that divine and most valiant contender, teaches when it says, "The mind and the ear discern words, as the palate tastes food." In agreement with this, David, the singer of divine songs, says, "Whoever slandered his neighbor in secret, him I drove away." And the God of all, setting his seal on the words of his servants, says in the Gospels, "Be approved money-changers, telling the counterfeit from the genuine." This does not mean that we should strike the coin and accept it by its ring, as money-changers do. It means that we should weigh the statements of those who speak with us and the outcomes of what is done, and so tip the scales toward the just side. Great is the danger from ears and tongues. The tongue is a small member, yet it is a workshop of falsehood and truth, or rather of salvation and destruction. "My tongue is the pen of a swift scribe," and "My tongue will speak of righteousness," says the singer of divine songs. And again the same singer says, "With their tongues they have practiced deceit; their tongue is like a serpent's; the venom of asps is under their lips." In agreement with his father, Solomon, wise in divine things, says, "For life and

death are in the hand of the tongue." It is as if he presented a murderer, with speech in place of a hand and deceit in place of a sword. And God has assigned the murderer and the deceiver to one and the same portion, as he says through the great David: "The Lord abhors a man of blood and deceit." Whoever is abhorrent to God is surely also liable to punishment. Iron thrown aside is eaten away by rust. Wood or a garment that is filthy and abhorrent to its owner is ruined by the filth in it. A house abandoned by its occupant falls to ruin little by little. In much the same way, it seems to me, a mortal who is abhorrent to God is punished when God turns away from him, afflicted by the evils mingled within him. Then the sentence "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire" falls on those who will hear it, in proportion to their sins. Then the fire falls on some like a live coal among chaff, scouring and burning them forever. It neither destroys nor is itself destroyed, because we rise from our tombs incorruptible. The righteous will remain incorruptible forever, in security and rest and complete freedom. Sinners, punished eternally, will not be destroyed but will live on in the places set apart for them: chafing, helpless, distraught, aching, lamenting, wasting away, wailing, gnawed, torn, shrieking, beating themselves, and able to do nothing more. They thrust aside the present time for repentance. They shut their own compassion against those in need, and so shut God's compassion against themselves. "For judgment is merciless to one who has shown no mercy," says the divine voice. For others, the judge's sentence becomes darkness, driving them into the outer places, scourging the guilty and casting them out. The history of Egypt teaches this: the divine sentence was one, yet it was fitted to the disposition of those who heard it. It punished the Egyptians in Pharaoh and saved the Israelites through Moses. For the one people it turned the Nile red as blood, to punish them with thirst; for the other it kept the water's nature unharmed. For the one it turned the light of day into darkness that could be felt; for the other it kept the light within their borders. For the one it made the Red Sea dry land to cross over; for the other it closed the sea again and left them gone, destroyed beneath the waters. Likewise with the Babylonian furnace, a single sentence was at work. The three Hebrew youths skipped about in the flame singing hymns, as if in the midst of dew. Those who fed the flame by throwing in fuel and raised it to forty-nine cubits were swiftly burned by it to ashes. In the same way we know that the dry land obeyed the divine command. It split open and swallowed Dathan and Abiram as their punishment, yet it bore up the innocent as it naturally does, in the same place, on the same day and at the same hour. So also with the wretched Cain: the divine sentence fell on his ears and punished him, saying,

"You will be groaning and trembling on the earth." At once experience followed the word. It punished Cain, the first murderer in the world, the slayer of his brother, racking him with ceaseless shaking and mournful groaning from the heart and to the fingertips. Yet it did not kill him, though he longed to die and cried out, "It will be that whoever finds me will kill me." To him God declares, "Not so; for I have set a sign on you, so that no one who finds you will kill you." Let us then fear the punishing fire, the worm and the darkness, which do not spare even the holy if they defile themselves in their lives. For God says through Ezekiel, "Pass through and strike [?], and begin from my holy ones." "If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?" says Solomon, wise in divine things, rousing us from our negligence. So let us not neglect ourselves by relying on baptism and on our share in the divine mysteries, imagining that our punishment will then be lighter. They will do us no good there if here they are insulted and partaken of fearlessly and unworthily. "For whoever eats and drinks unworthily" of the mingled cup of God the Word "eats and drinks judgment upon himself," says the sublime Apostle. And again he says, "Circumcision is of value if you keep the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision" for the one who has not lived worthily of it. And again he says, "It is not the hearers of the law but the doers of the law who will be justified before God." It is clear to everyone with any education at all that saving baptism is the counterpart of circumcision. Likewise, in place of the law the venerable Gospels have been given to us, the faithful. The Lord confirms this in the Gospels when he says, "Truly I tell you, not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but those who do my will. For many will say to me on that day, 'Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name and heal diseases?' And I will say to them, 'I do not know you. Depart from me, you cursed, you workers of lawlessness, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.'" It seems to me that the mass of the faithful are Christians of this kind. Judas the apostle would surely be among them, for he worked signs and healed the sick before he committed his outrage against Christ, the God of all. So would Simon, whom Peter and Paul struck down, and a great many of the Galatians. They worked signs, wonders and healings and were counted worthy of prophetic gifts, yet they slipped back into error and returned to their former wickedness. The sublime teacher of all under the sun writes to them and says,

"O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you? You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?" As I said before, such people seem to me to gain nothing from baptism, even if they should say to Christ as their judge, "Lord, in your name we did mighty works and cast out demons and healed the sick." To them Christ gave a stunning and bitter sentence, full of wailing. In his mercy he leads all of us away from that sentence, for his blameless saints entreat him on our behalf. "For the ungodly will not rise in judgment," says David, the singer of divine songs. In agreement with him the sublime prophet Isaiah says, "Let the ungodly be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord." Confirming this, the holy Paul says, "For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law." What he means is God's utter abandonment of them and his turning away from them, and punishment for endless ages. The prophets make the same thing plain: when the ungodly rise, they will not stand trial but will be led away at once to condemnation along with their leader, the devil. Not even today's laws, when they summon a manifest murderer or adulterer from prison, try him with long speeches in sight of the awestruck crowd; through him they bring that crowd to its senses. When one member of the body is cut or burned, the whole body shudders and suffers along with that part. Often, when one servant is flogged, the whole rank of servants cowers and resolves in mind to mend their ways and not to touch the forbidden things for which he was torn with pain, dragged to justice by heaven-sent wrath. Understand that God arranges this in a city of ten thousand men. One household is punished, paying here the penalty for its sins, so that the rest of its fellow citizens and all cities may be sobered and corrected. "For when the ungodly fall, the righteous become fearful," says Solomon, wise in divine things. At that unswerving and incorruptible judgment, holy baptism will be of no benefit to those who outrage it here by a wicked way of life and live unworthy of the name of Christ. The sublime Apostle teaches us this even more clearly than the passages just quoted, for he cries out plainly: "Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse a punishment will be deserved by the one who has trampled on the Son of God and counted the blood of the covenant as common?" The one who tramples on God's Son, the Word who is God, is the one who receives his mystical mingled cup fearlessly, with grasping hands raised against his neighbor, and treats as ordinary bread and wine what the faithful behold with the eyes of the mind as God. "For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and body, of joints

and marrow, and able to discern thoughts and intentions," as he himself says through Paul. He was cut off from neither, though the one was nailed and the other flowed. Nor again is he used up. Like the air he is shared by all, and he remains the same God, undiminished. The Lord sets his seal on Paul's words in the Gospels. There he shows that those who are Christians in name but wicked in deed, who behave like drunkards and neglect their own salvation, will be punished just like the unbelievers. He says, "But if that servant says in his heart, 'My master is delaying his coming,' and begins to beat his fellow servants and to eat and drink with drunken fellow servants, truly I tell you, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in two and assign his portion with the unbelievers." Let us not take the cutting in two of the servant in a bodily sense, for that would be ignorant and laughable. Rather, let us understand that the Lord cuts in two those of us who are to be judged by taking away our spiritual gifts, our baptism and our freedom to speak boldly before him. Those who have enlisted with Christ have been marked like soldiers with his seal and girded with the belt of his army. They cannot be punished until they have first been stripped [?] of these. In the same way, today's laws teach that soldiers who are guilty are not punished until they have been stripped of the belt, the emblem of military service. Once it is taken away, they are flayed by the executioner like civilians. I will use a still clearer image to show what the divine cutting in two means. When one of the ordained members of the company has fallen into some lapse, the high priests who govern the lofty throne of Christ do not hand him over to justice until they have first severed him from the divine rite and stripped him of its emblems. Once deposed in this way, he is reckoned as one of the laity. By this removal, the cutting in two we spoke of is made plain, and by his enrollment among the common herd, his portion with the unbelievers. David, the singer of divine songs, foreshadowed this when he testified, "Make vows and pay them to the Lord your God (94); all who are around him will bring gifts to the one who is fearsome and takes away the spirits of rulers." Let no one think the song is about taking away souls. He himself surely puts in and takes away the spirits that animate the soul, not of rulers only, but of subjects, masters and servants alike. Rather, it is surely about the gifts of the soul, or rather the spiritual gifts, and about baptism. It seems to me that the faithful are rulers and masters over the unbelievers. From the Word, who was God in the beginning, they have received rule over them and over the demons (95). For the unbelievers will differ in no way from the demons, since they are of one mind with them in opposing God and making war on Christians. The God-bearing David prayed in advance that the faithful would rule over them and trample on them, and he asked God this: "You will make them rulers over all the earth.

They will remember your name in every generation and generation." God the Word heard the prophet. He became man from among them and came into the world for their sake. Speaking as God in the Gospels, he says to us, "Take courage; I have conquered the world," and, "Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy." That power is every heresy (96). In every generation and generation we remember the name of Christ, for through baptism and the Holy Spirit given to us in it, he has made us rulers and masters over our adversaries. Let us strive to honor these gifts by living virtuously and bring no stain or blemish on them by an impure way of life. Otherwise Jesus, when he judges, may cut us in two, sever us from the spiritual gift and from baptism, and destroy us in the eternal fire together with the unbelievers who are ruled. One of the myth-makers (96b), who charms the ears but does not nourish souls, has held that the punishment of sinners will come to an end. His reason is that the Lord called the punishing fire only "eternal," and not "eternal for ages of ages." He is wrong. The prophet says, "Forever, O Lord, your word abides in heaven." Let us not conclude from this that God the Word remains in heaven only up to a certain point, and after that age leaves the heavens. And again the same prophet says, "And the truth of the Lord abides forever." Will the Lord, then, cease to be true after some lapse of time, as the drunken ravings of the man named after wrath would have it? The judge himself says to his divine apostles in the Gospels, "And I am with you until the end of the age." Are we then to suppose that he will be with the saints only for a time, rather than everlastingly and without end? Surely it is the height of madness to suppose that the age has an end. It is madness to think that the devil, punished until then together with the wicked men driven away with him, will then be freed from his torments and punished no longer. If that were so, the opposite would surely happen to the righteous. Having lived in bliss and security until some age, they would die again or suffer some harm when their age came to an end. For the judge declared that the one group goes into eternal life and the other into eternal punishment. If the punishment of the wicked ends, the life of the righteous must also end. So say those who are deprived of true life. They weaken the hands of those who practice self-control and buoy sinners up with hopes of an end to punishment. Carried along by the rush of the discourse, we have strayed far from what we set out to say about the tongue, so let us hurry back to it. Great is the danger from ears and tongues. That is why he keeps it guarded behind two lips… (96b) "As one of the myth-makers has thought." The author

[?] the Deity wisely arranged, binding it within the bulwark of the teeth, so that, with the fortress secure, its glibness might be kept in check. For it lies in moisture: at one time, when it reviles, it stirs up a stench; at another, when it blesses, it pours out hymns and offers them up to God. So with the divine David we ought to sing: “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door to enclose my lips.” For the tongue is soft and nimble, so it turns its voice more easily to every sound, and it surpasses every other voice. The swallow chatters and never stops; the turtledove is sweet-voiced and loves solitude; the cicada pipes briefly; the crane clangs; the dove murmurs; the bear groans, withdrawn and treacherous; the bull bellows like a trumpet; the lion roars and shakes the desert; the heifer lows and draws her calf to her; ravens let out cries like a rioting mob; the night-raven's song is a lament. The flute sounds for weddings, the trumpet for slaughter, the harp for dancing, and the drum also for the chorus. Yet all of them together fall short of the sweet voice of mortals. For where among them is the clear meaning of our tongue, its distinctness, its melody, its rhythm and its great sweetness? Swallows do not understand the cooing of doves, nor cranes the cry of geese, nor the owl that of the seleucis, the halcyon or the peacock; nor do the other irrational creatures understand the voices of other kinds. And we are not able to interpret or explain theirs either. For who will know what the lion means when it roars, or the bull when it bellows, or the sheep when they bleat among the kids? Yet all of them recognize the clear meaning of articulate speech. When the shepherds call, the sheep come near; when they threaten, the sheep draw back again. When the goatherd shouts, the goats leap away from the crops and turn aside from the fields. In the same way the horse, the mule, the ox and every beast of burden are taught by the human tongue when to go right and when to go left. Dogs that spring out barking cower when they hear the voice of someone calling, and are quickly brought to quiet. Look too at a sow that has wandered off, and see how she runs back from her straying at the voice of the swineherd. A dog chasing a gazelle has often run far from the huntsman; but when it hears his whistle it answers with a bark, calling for help from the one who sent it out. Observe also the flocks of doves: when they hear the whistle of the one calling them, they swoop down like a cloud upon the [?]. And every musical instrument is struck by the hand and guided to echo our tongue. It is truly wonderful how the tongue, small and soft as it is, has a twofold activity: it tastes, and it discerns, both by nature and by training. By the wisdom of its Maker it is sufficient both for every movement of speech and for taste. “Whoever does not sin with it is a great man, able to bridle the whole body as well,” says the divine James, writing to the whole world under the sun. The teeth also work together with the tongue to produce

articulate speech, giving it firm resistance so that it can speak, as if the tongue struck against them like a plectrum on the strings of a lyre. At the same time the teeth serve our food, some cutting it and others grinding it fine. The front teeth cut, and the inner ones are fittingly called millstones, because they grind and smooth what is brought to them. The nose sits between the cheeks. It draws in the air and gives it back, and it drains off the fluid from the skull, drawing in what is fragrant and loathing the opposite. Down shades the cheeks when we exchange the restless age of youth for settled manhood and begin to look about for our livelihood. By this, I think, nature shows that we grow only until then, and that from then on we take up our labours. It is fitting, then, for us to sing with David: “How great are your works, O Lord! In wisdom you have made them all.” For in so small a head he has placed all our more precious senses: sight, hearing, taste and smell. He built them close to one another as neighbours, and none of them obscures the work of the one beside it. Besides these we have no other senses, except touch through the hands. The neck is [?] and well proportioned, and because of it man looks up to heaven; the image [?] is the upright face. The head rests on the neck as on a pillar, bending and rising as needed with the neck's help. We have five fingers on the right hand and as many on the left. With them we cut the dry land, mine the mountains, draw water from springs and redirect rivers. Through them, with ropes and timber, we sail across the deep, hoist the ship's sails to suit the wind and steer with the rudders. We capture and tame wild beasts. We net sea monsters as big as hills and mountains and fearful to look at. We harvest the air, catching birds with limed reeds. Fire is fierce in its onrush, fearful to touch, destructive and violent in its movement, yet we force it to serve our purpose and to change at each person's will. With our hands we also raise cities and surround them with battlements and walls, arming them with slings, bows and other defences. The heart is a small organ, round and without joints. Yet in it, together with the brain, we deliberate about God, angels and archangels, heaven, earth, sea and the whole creation. It is like a storehouse or fortress of the cause of life within us and of the strength of the spirit around the heart. We have held that the heart is, after God, a kind of spring and source of our life. From it pipe-like channels branch out in many ways, one through another, through the whole body, and spread the hot and fiery spirit everywhere. But the heat must surely also

be accompanied by some nourishment supplied by nature, for the fire within us cannot last by itself unless it is fed with what suits it. Therefore channels of blood start out from the liver as from a spring and travel through the whole body alongside the hot spirit. In this way neither one is left isolated from the other, and neither becomes a disorder that destroys our nature. The Deity has no need of anything, but poor mortals need things brought in from outside to sustain them. For if the liver is the source of the blood, a supply of food is necessary, since what food brings into us makes the blood well up from the liver. It is like the snow on a mountain, which fills the springs below at the foothills with its own moisture, pressing its water secretly through the depths into the veins below. The spirit in the heart is brought in through the neighbouring organ, called the lung, which is a receptacle for air. The lung draws in the air from outside by breathing, through the windpipe that is set in it and reaches up to the mouth. Enclosed in the middle of the lung, the heart is always in motion, much like the nature of fire, as you may see in the bellows of a forge. It draws air to itself from the lung beside it, filling its cavities as it expands, and it supplies its fiery part to the arteries next to it, breathing out without ceasing. As it expands it draws the outside air into its own cavities, and as it contracts it sends its own air out into the arteries. As in a smelting furnace, it melts and digests the material by its natural heat, and pours it, as through a funnel, into the channels that follow. Having separated the thick from the thin, it pushed the coarse matter out into the intestines, and passed the thin, pure part to the gates of the liver. Boiling the moisture with its heat, it stores it up, reddening the moisture into blood, since blood is akin to fire. What has been united to the body by another power, through a kind of mixing and blending, it nourishes through the blood, and through vapours it sustains the brain. From the brain, in turn, the exhalation is refined to a purer state and anoints the membrane that encloses the brain. This membrane stretches down like a pipe from above into the depths, carrying itself and the marrow inside it through the successive vertebrae, and ends, by way of the lower back, at the private parts. Like a charioteer, it gives every junction of bones and joints, and the origins of the muscles, their movement and rest, each in its turn. But let us return to our subject. The heart is the most sovereign and necessary part of our life. Therefore, more than any of our organs, the Creator has secured it, fortifying and fencing it with firmer parts all around. Behind, he set the spine and the shoulder blades; on each side he wrapped it in the ribs, making the middle hard to injure. In front he placed the breastbone and the pair

of collarbones, guarding it safely on every side from harm from outside. Let us also say a few words specifically about the nature of the lung. It is attached to the chest, and it is spongy [?], soft, very porous and unsightly. All its hollows open together into the base of the windpipe. When it draws together and collapses, it is forced to squeeze out the air left in its pockets. When it relaxes and opens, it pulls in the air forcibly, drawing it toward the moving part. With its constant motion it swings about the heart and, by fanning it, beats back its flaming, fiery heat. For just as a flame that cannot breathe is quenched by its own smoke, so an animal that does not breathe through its lung quenches the fire around its heart. Therefore the lung, moving about the heart and soothing it with gentle breezes, keeps the animal flourishing and strong. For it seems to me that the cause of life is seated in the heart, and in it alone. The liver is also hot, for the digestion of what is taken in and its conversion into blood, and it is attached on the right side. When it is chilled, the face changes, and spasms and partial weakness follow. The spleen is set on the left side; it draws off and separates the coarse dregs of the blood. When it is sweetened [?], it swells and becomes inflamed, going beyond its bounds and walling off digestion. It makes a person look fleshy, but brings on pallor and partial weakness. The coils and windings of the intestines lie around the belly, so that by their winding course the food may be held in the entrails for some time. Otherwise, if the passage were straight, the food would be quickly discharged again and would stir the animal back to appetite, so that, like the irrational creatures, it would never be free of that occupation. The Creator contrived membranous chambers for the flow of liquids, with invisible channels that draw off the moisture little by little. In this way the animal is not ambushed by thirst through being flooded all at once and then dried out, but what it has drawn in is husbanded bit by bit for a time. Our legs are jointed with hinges and fitted into sockets. Like columns bearing a load, they support the whole body, with the knee for a capital and the ankle for a base. They are nimble and ready for every movement: for prayer and supplication, for running and leaping. Our feet were made tougher than all the body above them, since they were to strike the ground constantly, and in walking they are helped by the toes, which act like hooks. If we lose our toes through frost or some injury, we walk with difficulty. What words could set forth the wisdom and power of the Creator within us? The perforations and membranous tubes, the interweaving of fibres, the tension of the sinews and the solidity of the bones, and the hidden roads and paths that manage what is taken in, all through the single harmony of the body: the drawing of breath,

the conveying of blood, the dwelling of heat, the onset of cold, and all that medicine has studied. The account of these I shall leave to those who have devoted themselves to it [?]. “It must be known…” etc. These words are not Caesarius's, as

flowing, as the efficient cause, while the menstrual fluid supplies a kind of material for children, like bronze for the sculptor. For the woman emits no seed, only a useless fluid that occurs in those parts. The male seed acts like a craftsman and supplies a principle of motion, as we see with rennet, which curdles milk. So too the seed, falling into the moist matter, is mixed with the purer part of the female's residue. He says that what is formed in the womb also shares in soul, not the complete soul but the nutritive one. For just as plants live in the earth, so the embryo lives, using the navel as a root to draw its nourishment from the womb. When it comes forth it also acquires the sensitive soul, and as it grows, the rational and intellectual activity of the soul grows along with it. For in the seed there is a part of the soul called the vital heat, which corresponds to the heat of the sun, since the sun's heat has a life-giving power and engenders life. The heart is formed first, and it is also the last to perish. Likewise the other internal organs are articulated before the external ones, especially those above the diaphragm. A human being is shaped in the womb with the nose between the knees and the eyes on the knees. The embryo begins to grow strong when the menses are held back and changed into milk in the breasts. At once the nausea and vomiting of women stop. A male is produced if the male's seed is well concocted. That is why the young and the old mostly beget females. Excess or deficiency in certain parts comes from a deficiency or excess of material. The seed is discharged from the regions around the head, as is clear from the hollow eyes of those who have intercourse most often. The womb is moved along with the mind, as is the male member, sometimes even involuntarily. Twins arise when the seed splits in the womb: if it is well concocted, two males; if not, the opposite. They also arise through a second conception, which is why there is often a male and a female. Nourishing milk is thick and yellowish, as is clear from cheeses. A woman often gives birth after seven months, mostly after nine, often after ten when extra time is added, and only rarely in the eleventh. Either the child lives, or she will bear what is called a mole, which is hard flesh, or she will be in danger. At around fourteen years, males and females change their constitutions, the healthy becoming sickly and the reverse. Then females begin their monthly periods and males produce seed, and the voice deepens; the breasts and the private parts grow. A woman has a poor complexion if she is going to conceive a female. By the same Gregory of Nyssa. The union of the mind with the body is joined in a way that cannot be described or understood. The mind is neither inside the body

(for the incorporeal is not held fast by a body), nor does it surround the body from outside (for the incorporeal is not contained by bodies). Rather, the mind approaches nature and touches it in some inexplicable and inconceivable way, and it is seen both in it and around it, but in a way that can be neither spoken nor conceived. We can only say that when nature proceeds well in its proper order, the mind too is active; but if some fault befalls nature, the movement of thought limps to the same degree. We must understand why, on earth, the sprouting of what grows from the earth comes first, then the irrational animals, and after them man. It is not only because grass is useful to the animals, and the cattle exist for man's sake, since they are to serve him. It is also because Moses is handing down the philosophy of the soul. The argument is divided as follows. Of the things that exist, some are intelligible and some are bodily. Let the intelligible be set aside for now. Of the bodily, some share in vital activity, while others have no part in life at all. Again, of living bodies, some have sensation and some do not; and of those with sensation, some are rational and some irrational. Nature makes its ascent from the lesser to the perfect. That is why the lawgiver says that, after lifeless matter, as a kind of foundation for the form of living things [?], this natural life came into being. It came first in the sprouting of plants, namely the life of nourishment and growth. Then he brings in the sensitive life of the animals, which also shares in the life that came before it. For things that live through flesh can exist even without the intellectual nature, but the rational cannot exist unless it is blended with the sensitive. That is why man comes last. For the rational animal is compounded of every form of what are called, by the same name, souls. He is nourished by the plant-like form of the soul. The sensitive power grows onto the power of growth, and then the activity of the intellectual substance shone out upon the sensitive. Hence the soul that pervades them all is properly called rational and intellectual. For in the rational it has embraced the rest as well, and in the sensitive the vegetative is certainly present, but the vegetative [?] only in what is material. Yet these too, because of their vital activity, are called souls in a loose sense. It must be known that the organs made simply for us to live are the brain, the heart and lung, the liver and the stomach. For if any of these is injured, the animal necessarily dies. But the eyes, hands and feet were made for us to live well, for if they are injured, the animal lives, but not well. Still other organs exist for the succession of those who come after. Man was brought forth by God last, after the rest of creation. This was not because he was cast aside and thrown in at the end, as something worthless. It was fitting that the ruler should not appear before his subjects,

nor that the guest should be brought in before the feast was prepared. Human nature proves more honourable than all creation. For creation was made by God offhand, coming into being at the moment of his command. But in the making of man, counsel goes first, and the Word considers everything about him beforehand. For God said, “Let us make man,” and the words about him that follow, so that man received his dignity before he came into being. That is why God prepared beforehand the material from which he would be made, and considered after what archetype he would bear a likeness. So God, the supreme craftsman, fashioned human nature as an instrument fit for kingship [...], both through the advantages of the soul and through the very shape of the body. For the soul shows its royalty in being masterless and free to choose. As the image of God, it shares in the archetype. Instead of royal robes it is clothed in the splendour of the virtues, and it has no part in the lowliness of a commoner. There is one power that grasps things: the mind itself, set within man. It passes through each of the senses and lays hold of the things that are. It is like an impress of the one essence of God, and it brings about many different works. Let those be silenced who say that the Son or the Holy Spirit is unlike the Father in essence. For he who said, “Let us make,” and pointed to the Holy Trinity by using the plural, would not have spoken of the image in the singular if it were unlike its archetype. It is impossible for one image to resemble different forms; if the natures had been different, they would have set up different images as well. Man is naked of the weapons and coverings that nature provides. He is not armed with horns or sharp claws or fangs, or a venomous sting; he has no coat of hair or wings; he is not swift of foot or massive in bulk. Yet he was to rule, so he ought to have been fenced about with weapons of his own. But this was reasonable. For if he had been so equipped, he would have been savage and dangerous to meet, and he would have neglected his rule over the other creatures, since he would not need their help. As it is, what looks like a lack in his nature gives him the opportunity to master those placed under his hand. For this reason he brought the ox under the yoke and tamed the horse; he tends sheep for what they yield, and he has yoked the beasts of burden. The dog, with the grip of its teeth, has given him the means to overpower some of the animals. Iron, stronger than horns and claws, was devised. Birds serve him too, and so do their feathers. The hides of animals protect our feet, which are easily chafed. Man's upright posture and his hands show how his dignity differs from that of the other animals, which stoop forward with feet in front

…limbs, and because they need something to support them. The hands assist in every need, in war and in peace, in the use of speech, and in writing. For we fit our sounds to the letters they form, so that the hands are a special property of the rational nature. If man had no hands, his face would have been built like that of the four-footed beasts, to meet the need for food: its shape would be long and the nostrils narrowed [?], so that he would of necessity also have a strange voice. But the body was built as an instrument for the use of speech. Since the mind is something intellectual and incorporeal, it needed such a structure, so that by some contrivance it might make its movement visible, touching the parts that produce the voice like a plectrum. The activity connected with this instrument is twofold: one part makes sound, the other hears. The one is always sending something out, the hearing is continually taking things in, and it is a wonder that no confusion arises among the words and thoughts brought in through it. The same thing happens with the activity of sight. For through these too the mind lays hold of what is outside the body. The mind examines each thing brought in and stores it in the appropriate places of knowledge, often building a single piece of knowledge out of different senses, and again grasping many things through a single sense. Someone who hears the name of honey, and sees it, smells it, touches it and tastes it, has come to know one thing through all the senses. But through hearing alone he has recognized many different sounds, and through sight he has taken in views of different kinds of things: white, black and grey. The mind is something other than the senses. If it were the same as a sense, being simple, it would be akin to only one of them. As it is, it is spread out through the many parts of the senses and acts through each: it is variety in singleness and singleness in variety. That is why its nature escapes our knowledge, and by its own unknowability it reflects the incomprehensible nature of the one who made it in his own image. The body has been crafted like a musical instrument. A man who knows how to make music cannot display his art when the instrument is unusable. In the same way the mind, pervading the whole instrument with its intellectual activities and touching each of the members, performs its proper work in those that are in their natural condition, but is inactive in those that are sick; for it does not touch one part and stand apart from another. Just as the mind is adorned by its likeness to the archetypal divine beauty, like a mirror shaped by the image that appears in it, so too the nature governed by the mind is adorned; and in turn the material element of the underlying substance, in which the nature is observed, is held together by that nature. And just as the mind, darkened by the formlessness of the passions, becomes unable to receive the

divine beauty unless it is cleansed, so too the nature observed in the underlying substance, when it suffers some harm, cannot receive the activity of the mind unless it returns to its former health. This also shows that the mind is bound up with nature. When nature is sound and awake, the mind acts and moves; but when nature is relaxed in sleep, it remains motionless. The images we see in sleep we regard as certain phantoms of the mind's activity. For a person often seems to be in absurd and impossible situations, which would not happen when he is awake. Dreams also arise in some people from the state of their character: the phantoms of the brave differ from those of the coward, those of the licentious from those of the self-controlled, those of the generous from those of the greedy. For the echoes of our daily pursuits remain in the soul's memory. Dreams often arise in accordance with particular conditions of the body as well: the thirsty man seems to be at springs, and the man who needs food at banquets. In short, the vision of dreams takes many forms, but it is empty. For the mind, veiled by the inactivity of the senses during sleep, can neither shine out through them nor is it entirely extinguished. And if Pharaoh of Egypt and Nebuchadnezzar were guided by dreams to the knowledge of future things, God arranged this for another purpose, so that the hidden [?] of the saints might be revealed [?]…
It must be understood that the communion of the intelligible with the bodily involves a union that cannot be expressed or conceived. This too has been written above.

Question 141. Now that the questions about man have been settled for us so well, where do you think paradise is: in heaven or on earth? For some say that it is heavenly and intelligible, others that it is earthly and sensible [?]…
To me it seems to be sensible and on earth, since divine Scripture proclaims this clearly, plainly and expressly.

Question 142. What then does Paul mean when he says, "I know a man who fourteen years ago, whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows, and I know that such a man was caught up into paradise and heard unutterable words, which it is not lawful for a man [to speak]"? From this it is shown that paradise is in the heavens. For he did not say, "caught up into the third heaven, and having come down from there into paradise", but in the catching up of both [?]…
But he did not declare heaven and paradise together in one brief statement. For he says, "I saw a man caught up as far as the third heaven", and again,

"into paradise". I must therefore turn your own words against you, and then proceed to examine the phrase. You say that he did not say "having come down" but "caught up into paradise", and by this, it seems, you shake off the teachings of the celebrated fathers. Since he did not say "having gone up" but "caught up", does that mean he did not go up? But if, when he was caught up, he went up, then clearly, when he was caught up into paradise, he also came down. For he says, "And I know such a man caught up into the…"
But the heaven that we see above us shows that he made an ascent and came to be above it, and that is where we understand paradise to be.

Why then did he not put it together and say, "And I know such a man caught up into heaven and paradise"? Instead, by inserting the phrase, he separated the places, saying, "And I know such a man caught up as far as the third heaven", and again, "caught up into paradise". The words "and again" transfer him to some other place. Picture a mountain surrounded by a sloping plain. Someone who wants to be on the plain reaches it easily by traveling across the plain; but if he wants first to climb the mountain and after that to reach the plain, he must of necessity come down from the height onto the slope. In the same way I think the holy Apostle first visited the heavens and from there went down into paradise. And a trustworthy witness before Paul is Solomon, wise in divine things, who shows that paradise is sensible and on earth. For he says, "My kinsman went down into his garden." With these words he signifies both the Lord's divine-human coming and foreshadows Paul's descent into it from the heavens, after he had been caught up from the earth above them. For Christ, who came down into his own world, is the brother of Solomon and Paul according to the flesh. And the other, too, is their brother: both were nursed by the synagogue, both endured the knife of circumcision and the yoke of the law.

Question 143. What then? Do you think that Christ the Saviour, while he was being crucified, committed his soul not in the heavens but on earth, when he said, "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit", and to the thief, "Today you will be with me in paradise"? If, then, the God and Father of Christ is in heaven, paradise is surely there too, the place into which Christ promised to bring the thief crucified with him.

It seems to me blasphemous and utterly senseless to think that the Divine is only in heaven or in paradise and not everywhere. For it is present in all things and encompasses all things, in heaven, on earth and under the earth. And so even when the soul of the incarnate God and Word went down into Hades,

we say that it was in the Father's hands. Christ, by his divinity, was in paradise and brought the thief's soul there with him, and so we confess that he dwells in the palms of the one who begot him. For "our God is in heaven and on earth, in the seas and in all the deeps", says David, the singer of divine things; and again, "For in his hand are the ends of the earth"; and again the same writer says, "If I go up to heaven, you are there; if I go down to Hades, you are present." If heaven is higher than all things and Hades deeper than all, and the Divine is in them, and at the same time the inspired writers cry out that it encompasses all things, then clearly Christ too, being everywhere present with the Father by his divinity, commits his soul into his hands. For if "the souls of the righteous are in the hand of the Lord", as the prophet says, how much more is the soul of the God and Word. From him we are taught that paradise is earthly and sensible; for does he not say to the thief hanging beside him on the wood, "Today you will be with me in paradise"? So the one who banished Adam the thief now brings into paradise in his place the hostile thief, on whom he has had mercy.

Question 144. What then does Isaiah mean when he says in the person of God, "I have painted your walls on my hands"? We understand this to be said about paradise. And the Apostle shows this when he writes, "But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us [all?]", and we think that she is none other than paradise.

You seem to me to be arguing on my side rather than against me, when you bring forward a city and walls instead of a paradise of plants and guarded fruit [?]. What do paradise and Jerusalem have in common besides a name, or heaven and Eden? Moses shows that paradise was made by God in Eden, saying, "And God planted a paradise in Eden toward the east", not "in heaven toward the east". "And a spring", he says, "comes up out of Eden to water the paradise", not "comes down from heaven". "And a river goes out of Eden", not "comes down from the heavens". "This", he says, "is divided into four heads", not "flows down into four heads". Where in heaven are the fig trees, palms, pomegranates and the rest that make paradise dense and cause it to flourish? Where in the heavens are a spring and rivers and the tree of transgression? Listen, then, to the writer as he names the four rivers flowing from a single spring, as though pointing to each with his finger by naming it: "And the name of the one is Pishon." This river, he says, passes through Ethiopia and India and is called the Ganges by the people there; by the Greeks it is called the Ister and Indus [?]; by the Illyrians and the Rhipians [?] who live along the Ister, the Danubius; by the Goths, the Dunautis. Encircling the whole land of Havilah, the second Ethiopia,
and the regions of the Elymaeans, and running through the first Ethiopia, it then flows out toward the south [?] the west inside Gades, and discharges into the famous Ocean.

The second is the Gihon, which the Egyptians call the Nile. Each year it gently floods and waters all of Egypt. It is traveled by ships [?] … [?] and between the sails [?] it then lends itself to being worked by the plough, and to water creatures herding with land creatures, some grazing on grass, others eating flesh. Running past the greatest Ethiopia, it flows through the lesser, [?] and Blemmyia and Axum and the regions of the Thebaid and Egypt, and then discharges into this sea of ours. Jeremiah, who suffered much among the prophets, holding back frenzied Israel from running back to Egypt, cries out plainly, "What have you to do with Egypt, to drink muddy water?" The water of the Nile is muddy. — We ask you not to begrudge us a little time, but to tell us briefly about the third stream as well: where it begins and where it ends.

The one that follows the second from the same source [?] is called the Tigris by divine Scripture. It runs opposite the Syrians and passes through the regions of the East; it sinks beneath the dry land of the mainland [?], bubbles up again in Armenia, and cuts its way through the land of the Assyrians.

The fourth, born from the same womb, is the famous Euphrates. It too carries along in its stream certain Indian [?] products of paradise's autumn and leaf-fall and brings them to us. Like its sister river from the same spring, it runs underground for a long stretch, gushes up again in Armenia, and from there flows through Babylon. Each of these rivers is navigated by great cargo ships, after their underground course, to the lands beyond [?]. By sinking underground they in a sense cut off access to paradise and make it unapproachable for those who try to trace the way to it, whether by sailing upstream or by traveling over dry land along the banks. Among these, some Egyptians, who drank only water and ate seeds, having lived from infancy apart from our heavy diet, provisioned themselves with various kinds of seed and filled enough ships. They had the stream that carried them as a ready supply of drink, and they soaked their pulses in its water [?], making them easy to eat.

Sailing up the Gihon, which flows past them and which they call the Nile, and guided by the stream, they tried to find paradise, which no one has seen since Adam. After sailing upstream for a very long time, they passed beyond the inhabited world and were helplessly scorched by the fire of the sun. The stream there was boiling, so that they could no longer touch the water even with their fingertips or their lips. So they turned their rudders toward the place they had set out from and were carried back to their native land, bringing none of their provisions with them, since these had been used up over the long time, as some Egyptians have recorded. These sailors, who missed that blessed sight, were clearly taught the words of the wise Solomon: "Do not search into things too deep for you, and do not examine things too high for you; think about what you have been commanded." But if, as the utterly impious Origen holds, paradise is not on earth, how did Egypt send men to search it out? And how does Moses, the first writer of divine things, say, "And the Lord went down into paradise", and not "went up"? And, "The Lord brought Adam into paradise", and not "brought him up"? If, as that teller of myths holds, paradise is not on earth, and neither is the spring that divides into four, where then do the Gihon, Pishon, Tigris and Euphrates pour out from? Where in the heavens is there a fig tree or a vine, with whose leaves the transgressors covered themselves? If the place is not sensible and here among us, then there is no fig tree at all; and if the tree does not exist, our first parents did not eat; if they did not eat, they did not transgress; and then Adam does not exist, nor Eve from him, nor we from both of them, nor anyone else like us.
Question 148. What then? Do you not think that the devil fell from heaven? For as with him, so too with man we speak of a fall, clearly a fall from heaven.

We say without any doubt that the demon who was the author of evil was hurled down from the realms above the world, for Ezekiel [sic], who saw the Cherubim, laments over him and says, "How has the Morning Star fallen from heaven?" And in agreement with his servant the Lord says in the Gospels, "I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven." But about Adam this will be found nowhere in divine Scripture. Even if common usage says that man "fell", and speaks of Adam's fall, the heavens are not attached to his fall as they are with Belial. We also call it a fall when someone is driven from wealth and distinction into poverty, when someone slides back from virtue to worse, when someone turns from virginity to lust, and when the body comes to its end. Have these people, then, fallen from the heavens? By no

means. But I thought it necessary to use divine Scripture as my helper and to furnish proofs from Moses, the sacred writer. He says, "And God set the man to work and to guard paradise." From what, then, was he supposed to guard it, if in the heavens angels do not steal [?]? A bear that devours [?], or a pig, or a wild boar does not exist in the heavens, nor a grass-eating coney, nor a fox that digs into beehives, breaks up their [?] and devours the honeycombs; no bloodthirsty lion, no ravening wolf, no eagle or griffin, nor any other of the creatures we have here exists in heaven. These, dreading even Adam's rebuke alone, were afraid to touch or invade paradise, for before the transgression they all trembled at his voice. But after he transgressed, Scripture says, "And he drove them out of paradise", not "cast them down". "And he settled them", it says, not below paradise but opposite it; "and he set the Cherubim and the flaming sword that turns, to guard" not the way up but the way in to the tree of life. It calls the sword "turning" because it terrifies from afar those who would venture in, whether irrational animals or demons. Farmers usually do something similar: with shouting they keep birds and four-footed beasts out of the vineyards and cucumber beds, and by whirling the sword in their hands, and with the flash of it, they terrify men still coming from far off to steal the fruit; and often, by whirling a sling, they frighten off an approaching thief from far away with the stone flung from it.

Question 146. What do you think the garments of skin are, which the Lord put on Adam and Eve after the fall? For we have heard someone say, and say well, that man was a rational mind, an incorporeal rational living being; but after he sinned by disobeying God, the mind, having grown cold, was separated off, and for this reason was called "soul" (psyche): because the warmth of the mind had cooled (psygen), it could no longer remain above and join in the service of the beings there. Instead it was clothed with this body, which Scripture calls a garment of skin, put on the sinner as a punishment, serving as his chastisement and his prison. That is why the saints begged God that they might die and be set free from this punishment. David says, "Bring my soul out of prison"; Paul says, "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?"; and Job prayed for death without ceasing, no longer able to bear the chastisement of being in the body, the garment of skin.

I already perceived it earlier and said that you hold the poisonous and corrupting doctrines of Origen, which trip up the simpler people. For souls did not sin in heaven and then get condemned to be punished in a body, no longer able to share in the worship that goes on above the world. If they were shut up in these bodies for correction and sobriety, how is it that in this

state they sin more gravely? A man being punished in prison cannot sin even if he wants to. And why, then, did God not likewise secure the demons, who together with the devil are minds and incorporeal, and who sinned and were hurled down from the heavens, by joining them to bodies like ours for their sobriety and correction? And when Moses prayed that the people might become a thousand times more numerous, countless as the sand of the sea, did he want so many powers in heaven to sin and be cast down into bodies to swell the numbers of those on earth? And when the godly-minded Hannah begged the Divine for a child, was she asking that an intellectual and incorporeal power should fall from the heavens so that she might give birth to a mortal? Or again, when David, the singer of divine things, prayed for the virtuous, "And may you see your children's children", did he long for the race of the righteous to be multiplied by the fall of the powers above the world? And if God bound souls that had sinned in heaven to our bodies as a punishment, why did he condemn in the same way souls that had not sinned at all, punishing them in bodies just as he did the others? For see, he himself testifies about the great Job, before Job's courage against the devil, saying, "There is no man among those on earth like my servant Job, righteous, true, blameless, God-fearing, keeping away from every evil deed." Question 150. But look at what you said God said: "There is no man among those on earth." This shows that there are other, intelligible men in heaven, and that Job, being one of them, sinned and was bound to a body as a punishment; and that, having been purified through virtue, he is declared by God before his affliction to be more righteous than the men on earth, but not than those in heaven.

Sight and touch seem to me more trustworthy than hearing. So let us leave aside what is said rashly and without proof [?], and rather handle what can be seen. You cannot prove from the divine words about Job that, besides those on earth, there are intelligible men in heaven. Look, then, and handle what I am clearly handing on to you from divine Scripture. In past ages there was the righteous Abel, then after him Enoch, Noah, then Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. All these had fallen asleep and were under the earth, so that in those times Job was the only righteous man among mortals on earth, just as Lot, the only one living virtuously in the Pentapolis of Sodom, was rightly spared the death of its people. Since the righteous who had fallen asleep before him were under the earth, Job was the only righteous man on earth. And that he did not sin in heaven, get condemned and joined to a body, and then press on toward righteousness, we learn from what follows. For what virtue did he display

[?] the divine Jeremiah, before he came out of the womb, attested by God? And what had John done, while still carried in the womb, toward the Son and Word who was likewise carried in the belly of the Ever-Virgin, that he found the boldness he showed by leaping? And again, if, as you say, they were sinless in the heavens, why were they clothed in bodies like those of the condemned? Away, O Christ, with those who babble about the pre-existence of souls, so that they dare to call the soul a mind that has cooled!

[?] the Word and God became mortal through an ineffable conception. So bodies do not exist for the sake of souls, and neither is older than the other. God created both ineffably, in an instant, out of his goodness. And when they had turned away from the good and been stripped of divinity, again out of goodness he clothed them in skins, protecting the tenderness of the body as with a covering [?], since it had just left the delights of paradise and its divine garment, and was just beginning to know toil and to experience a laborious life and sweat. It is therefore not holy to teach pre-existence, co-existence or post-existence. Otherwise we might be deceived into thinking that souls fall from the heavens and are inserted into bodies, or we might blaspheme virgins, the continent and those who suffer a discharge of seed as soul-murderers who choke the souls in their loins and their seed. Keep far away [?] also from those who babble about post-existence; for no one is both older and younger than himself.

Of Saint Maximus. God's original purpose was that we should not come into being through marriage and corruption. But the transgression brought in marriage, and so all who descend from Adam fall under the condemnation of our forefather and are conceived in iniquities. As for 'In sins my mother conceived me,' this is because our foremother Eve was the first to conceive a craving for pleasure. That is why we too say that we are conceived in sins: we fall under her condemnation.

QUESTION 152. What then? Must we think of God as a tanner or a slaughterer of animals, so that he could clothe Adam in the garments of skin? Answer. Let me ask you in turn, most contentious one: which is easier and less laborious? To make the heaven firm out of the waters, found the earth upon the abyss, drive the boundless water into one gathering, and adorn each with what suits it, studding the heaven with stars, embroidering the dry land with plants and making the sea teem with swimming creatures? Or to stitch together a skin and clothe the one who had been stripped naked? To fashion the living being, or to clothe it? To turn the sea into dry land by a command and bring six hundred thousand men, with women and children, across with dry feet, or to clothe the needy with tunics by a command? To split the sheer rock and make water gush out, and to cut off the stream of the Jordan and lead a people across, or to cover the naked? To take up [?] dust and give it sinews and a soul, or to clothe the rational being made from it?
Tell us, then, who did the sacrificing, what animal was sacrificed to provide the skins, and who sewed them? If you can give an account of these things, we must no longer doubt what you say.

Then you too show us the slaughterer and the slaughtered animals, and their number, by which the much-celebrated Nile was reddened, when so great a river was suddenly turned into blood in obedience to God through Moses. Where is the meat from that countless slaughter of cattle by which the navigable stream was changed into blood? And how was the holy, self-subsistent, living God and Word, who bore flesh [?] and rose from the tomb for our sake, not seen naked, though he left the grave-clothes [?] in it? Who supplied his garment, who sewed it, who clothed the one who encompasses the universe? But if these things came into being by his divine will, let us be persuaded that our forefathers too were clothed with the skins in this way. For it is not true, as the idle babbler says, that our bodies are the skins which souls put on after eating what was forbidden. The fashioning of the bodies is recorded before the eating and the transgression, and indeed Adam had his rib taken to make the woman before the transgression; and it is absurd to imagine a rib in a bodiless [?] being. And what need would they have had to cover themselves with fig leaves if they were bodi[less] [?]
QUESTION 154. We learn from the great David that souls exist before bodies. For he says to God, 'Your hands made me' (meaning the soul) 'and fashioned me' (meaning, clearly, the body).

The great Job was not inferior to David in righteousness or in the extent of his power. He too was a famous king, and God testified that he was equal [?] in righteousness and truth. And he says to God, 'Your hands made me,' and again, 'Remember that you fashioned me from clay.' Since the fashioning is placed first, shall we then say that the body exists before the soul? Or again, since the fashioning alone [?] is mentioned and the making is not added, shall we say that he was soulless, or something else? Moses, the divine writer of the creation, says, 'And God took dust from the earth and fashioned the man,' and does not add that he completed him whole at once, in an indivisible instant. Shall we then conclude that the crown of the head existed first, the eyes second, the neck third, and the ankles and feet afterwards? Away with such nonsense! For how could we know that God, the supreme craftsman and all-wise, did not begin our creation from the soles of the feet or from the tongue? QUESTION 155. In what do you think man possesses the image of God? In the soul, since it is spirit and invisible [?], or in the body with its many parts [?]?
In neither, except in the immortality of the soul and in his ruling over all things. But not even in these does he preserve exact equality and [?]

likeness to the Divine. For both are created, the soul and the body, and they are composite through their union and communion with each other. Separation and division inevitably follow from composition, but the Divine is uncompounded, indivisible and without form, abiding in itself and always the same. Nor again does man preserve likeness to the archetype of the image in his ruling. For the one who receives is not equal [?] to the one who entrusts.
