The giver has no need whatever of what he has given, while the receiver needs everything that is given. And man was appointed by God to rule his fellow servants, whereas God was appointed by no one, for he is sovereign and almighty. QUESTION 156. But consider each by itself, the soul on its own and the body on its own, and tell us in which you think the image of God lies.

Neither, separated from the other, is a mortal man. The one is spirit, not man; the other is clay, irrational and without sensation; but from both one mortal is formed. The soul is subject to alteration and change. It forgets some things and remembers others. It exults and grows haughty [?] when it has abundance, and laments and grows gloomy when in want. Now it thinks holy thoughts, now licentious ones; now it chooses what is just, now what is unjust; now it becomes humane, now inhumane; it is angered in an instant and calmed in a moment, yielding to divisions and changes. As the lofty Apostle expressly cries out, 'For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, and discerning the thoughts and intentions.' How then can the soul be an image of the unchangeable God, when it falls under divisions and has its thoughts and intentions discerned, and is often examined to its depths not only by God but also by his prophets? But who can grasp the counsel or thought of God, when the holy Apostle cries, 'Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?' If then the soul, the more important part of the human compound, falls short of the divine image and likeness, how much further from it will the comparison with the body prove to be? For the Divine [?] is incorruptible, but the body corruptible; the one is without magnitude or quantity, the other small and circumscribed; the one is incomprehensible and intangible, the other tangible and fluid; the one is incorporeal and immaterial, raised above and beyond every height, the other small and material, earthbound and lowly, rolling about among things below. The one does not grow, does not cease, does not slacken, does not diminish. Do not then be persuaded by things below, and do not picture the Divine with limbs when you hear God saying, 'I will lift up my hand to heaven, and swear by my right hand, and say,' and again, 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool

of my feet'; or when the prophet says, 'He who measured the heaven with a span and the earth with a handful'; or when it says elsewhere that he engraved stone tablets with his finger and handed them to Moses, who saw God. Nor, because David, the singer of divine things, says, 'Incline your ear, O Lord, and hear me,' and 'Look upon me and have mercy on me,' should you give the Divine a shape, depicting it with limbs and organs. For if the wind blows and is present everywhere, and the air encompasses all things, how much more is this true of the one who commanded the wind to blow and gathers it as it blows? A throne contains the one seated on it, but the Divine cannot be contained. And if he has the earth as his footstool, how is it that when we walk or plough, or race from east to west riding horses at royal command and jostling one another, we do not bump into his feet? And how, if he measured the heaven with a span and sits above, does he say that he lifts his hand to heaven? And how with such fingers did he hew tablets without an axe and engrave them without a stylus, and write the law on them and give it to the lawgiver? So come to your senses, even if late, and see with the eye of the mind that these are figures of thought, not shapes. And consider with me a simple, brief comparison with respect to the Divine. The sea surpasses all the elements in size; yet compared with the ocean of the Divine, the whole universe is like a drop from a bucket and a drop of drizzle, as the prophet says. Nevertheless, though the sea is something simple and without shape, it roars without a mouth and runs without feet. It leaps and mocks as it swells, though it has no legs. It holds sailors fast though it has no hands. It rises to a height without wings. It drowns many without soles [?], fingers or arms. It froths and spits though it has no lips. It dashes against the rocks without arms, lifting ships of great burden. Without teeth it gnaws and wears away the neighboring land. If the sea, simple and fluid by nature, is accustomed to do these things, how much more can he who bridled its unbearable violence and tyranny with the tiniest sand and hemmed it in as with an iron wall? For when it rushes with its waves upon the land beyond, it is struck back by the sand as by a bridle, dissolves its onrush into foam, and returns into itself. Likewise the breath of the wind, though simple, whistles as it blows without lips. It pulls down roofs without arms. It harvests the fruits, shaking the trees without hands. It heaves up the abyss and makes it boil like a cauldron, and brings what lies on the bottom to the surface, without using a winnowing shovel or a mattock. It contends against ships of countless burden and, opposing them, keeps them from their course, though it has no chest or shoulders. Others, with white sails, it drives over the sea like sheep across a meadow or plain, striking them with no goad or staff. It reddens

the very pale faces of seafarers, though it daubs them with no rouge. Sea and wind surpass all their fellow servants in size, yet compared with the Divine they hold the rank of a gnat or a mosquito or a mustard seed, or of something even smaller. If, then, though they have no hands and no shapes, they roar, run swiftly, mock, overpower, block the way forward, do good, punish, enrich, drown, lead on and lead away, why do you give a shape to the Divine, my dear friend, and picture with limbs what is simple, uncompounded and without shape, when you hear 'Incline your ear, O Lord,' and again 'Look upon me,' and again 'Send forth your hand from on high, O Lord, deliver me and rescue me,' and all such sayings? Away, then, with defining mortals as being in God's image in soul or in body! For how can it be reasonable to compare what is easily overpowered and changeable with the Divine, which cries through the prophet, 'I am, and I have not changed'? The divine word does not lie when it says that man was made in the image of God. Yet the pitiable wretchedness of human nature has not been made like the blessedness of the impassible Godhead; for if they were alike, either the Divine would have to be passible or the human impassible. We must therefore examine how the human has been called like the Divine. Scripture says, 'And God made man; in the image of God he made him.' Then it continues: 'Male and female he made them.' This is foreign to God, and so the image does not possess the likeness of the prototype. The solution to this is as follows. The constitution of our nature is twofold. One part is intellectual; since it participates in all good things, it is said to have been made in the image of God. The other is divided by the distinction of male and female. Only the Divine is unchangeable, whereas our nature is changeable, for it began from non-being. So he who knows all things before they come to be, foreknowing which way the self-determining movement of human choice would incline, devised for the image the distinction of male and female. And when the word says that God made man, by the universal name and the indefiniteness of its meaning it embraced the whole of humanity. For Adam was not yet named along with the creature, as he is later; it was man in general. Therefore being made in the image of God is to be seen not in Adam alone but in every human being, for the first one ever formed and the last of all who will be born are alike in this. He, then, who had comprehended the whole of humanity by his foreknowing activity, and honored it with a lot equal to the angels, foresaw that human choice would not go straight toward the good. So that the multitude of human souls might not be cut short by falling away from the mode by which the angels increased in number, he devised a means of increase suited to those who had slipped into sins:

in place of the angelic way of life, he implanted in humanity the beastly and irrational mode of succession from one another. As David says, 'And man, being in honor, did not understand.' Hence our kinship with the beasts often covers over the better with the worse, whenever someone drags the mind down toward the passions. For whoever gives the mind's cooperation to passion produces an abundant brood of absurdities; but if passion does not have reason as its ally, it is quickly dissolved. In the blessed nature, however, there is no distinction of male and female. That is why, when God made what is according to the image, he did not then give man the power to increase and multiply. Only when he divided humanity by the distinction of male and female did he say, 'Increase and multiply,' and so on, words that God had spoken earlier to the irrational creatures. For if these words had been spoken when he made what is according to the image, we would not have needed animal generation. For this reason too he took into account, in our constitution, the measured span of time for human beings, so that it would be completed together with the passing of the predestined souls. Then both would come to a halt, and so would come the re-forming of the universe and the change of the human from the earthly to the impassible and everlasting. It must be understood that the image of God, which is in all humanity, has been brought to completion; for Scripture said, 'God made man,' not 'Adam.' Only after adding the properties of human nature, that is, male and female, did it name him Adam, which in Hebrew means 'earthly creature,' just as Paul, writing in Greek, calls him 'of dust.'

QUESTION 157. The mind and the soul seem to us to be the same. For what the eye is in the body, that exactly is the mind in the invisible soul, being itself invisible too. That is why we asked whether the mind is in the image of God.

[?] the mind and the soul, by my definition at least, are [?] the same. And even if the argument shows the mind to be something other than the soul, not even so will it be an image of God, since it is subject to corruption and change. As the lofty Apostle says, 'I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the mind,' defining the spirit as the soul, and the mind as its leader and president. When the soul yields to the mind and refers the counsels of the heart to that lofty leader enthroned in the head, as to a king, it becomes hard for the many to capture. It sets counter-reasoning against reasoning, and understanding against madness. For 'out of the heart come evil thoughts [?],' says the Lord. If, then, when the reasoning from the heart besieges us, we set against it the counter-reasoning from the mind, like a law sent down

from a king, the passion quickly subsides. And if we bring understanding to bear against madness, the swelling of arrogance is broken again, and the seething of anger, boiling up about the wretched body, is lulled to rest. For madness (aponoia) is the absence (apousia) of the mind (nous), when the soul rejects its guidance in what it must do and goes over to the one who whispers suggestions. Understanding (epinoia) is the visitation and bringing in of the mind. And admonition (nouthetēsis) is the placing (thesis) of mind, which teachers place in their pupils when they admonish them.
QUESTION 158. What then? Do those who have learned nothing not have a mind?

They have one, but they are like people in filthy or ragged clothes: they are dressed in a garment, but it is torn and shameful. I demonstrated above, using the Apostle as a trustworthy witness, that the mind is something other than the soul. But if perhaps you are waiting for a clearer proof, look at the mad and the senseless. They have souls but do not have a mind, which is precisely what madness is: their mind has slipped away from them, pushed aside by something troublesome. Look also at infants at the breast. They have souls but no mind, since admonition has not yet come to them from God, because their nature is immature and not yet able to receive it. Because their mind is absent, they often put their mouths to a blade or to glass, or swallow something harmful as if it were good, and quickly meet a most pitiable death, torn violently from life by the [?]

QUESTION 159. Then, if the mind is the leader of the soul, and we are saved by its presence but not at all in its absence, surely what is 'in the image of God' lies in this, since it is what saves us.

Although I called the mind the leader of the soul, I also said in the proper place that not even the mind is in the image of God. For how can what is corruptible and easily overpowered, the captive of the strong one, be an image of the incorruptible, who remains always the same and unchangeable? Whatever is pushed aside [?], or does not alone have authority over what it chooses, but yields or falls together with the worse, cannot be an image of the one who is unswerving and unconquerable. And the mind gave way to these things in paradise: either it yielded to the counsel of the serpent, or it was thrust away by the soul, or it fell together with it. The lofty-minded Apostle shows this when he says, 'I fear that the serpent may come again and deceive some of you, and your thoughts be corrupted.' And elsewhere, mocking those already caught, he says, 'Men corrupted in the [?]'
[?] image of the two [?] sets up in the midst of it, their glory [?]; so too God [?]

[?] the angels, ruling powers [?], and the sun [?] and the moon to rule the day [and] the night [?]; but they are not on that account said to be in the image of God. Again, when [the Apostle] [?] says, 'The man is in the image of God, but the woman is the glory of the man,' [?] this shows that the woman was made equal in honor to the man, but that her share of honor was curtailed after the transgression. And 'according to the likeness' was perhaps said as a synonymous parallel, like 'Look down [?] and [?]' and 'Blessed is he who considers the poor and needy.'

QUESTION 161. [?] appointed to rule the fish [?] the birds, and then the cattle and wild beasts, birds and creeping things? Answer. So that he would first venture against the weaker [?] and then, having taken courage, master the stronger [?].

Now we want to hear why we do not also rule heaven and earth, sea and rivers, sun and moon and clouds, if we are in the image of God. For God is the ruler of all.

QUESTION [?]. [?] "our [image and likeness]": the "according to the image"

he gave, but about the "according to the likeness" he was silent. For Scripture says, "And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them"; and it is not added "according to the likeness".

The Divine did not want us to pass our lives idle and lazy, like pigs or wild boars or sheep and the other irrational beasts of the wild, nor again to honour us undeservedly, without our earning a reward. So it left it in our own power to become like it, by imitating it and by achieving and displaying the virtues, so that through care for our neighbour we may become like it, as far as mortal nature can vie with God. "Be as a father to orphans, and as a husband to their mother," says Solomon, wise in divine things. And the Lord himself says in the Gospels, "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy"; and again, "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God"; and again, "Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls." Let us then be kind to others and merciful. Since we ourselves need mercy, let us have pity on whoever needs kindness. For God does this when we do good to those in need, if we do what we wish to have done to us; for God does to us whatever we do.

QUESTION 163. But God did not say, "Let us make man who will become like us through virtue"; on the contrary, he created him perfect and complete from the start. Did he then say one thing and do another?

None of this charges God with a change of plan. Rather, he left in us a spark of love for himself, so that by imitation we might vie with his great torch. Moreover, there did not yet exist anyone else who would need to receive kindness from the one being created; and the future he rightly assigned to those who would descend from him. But let us also consider "image" and "likeness" in another way. We set aside none of what has been said, but are supplying proofs in abundance. God says, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," knowing the future as though it were already present, and foreknowing the outcome of each thing before anything was done. So it was with Esau and Jacob: before they were conceived in their mother's womb, or had even issued from their father's loins, he said through Malachi, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." So it was with Jeremiah, to whom he said, "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb I sanctified you." So it was with Judas: he revealed his betrayal beforehand, when not even Judas' parents yet existed, saying through the inspired David, "He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me." So it was with Peter, the chief of the apostles, through the inspired David: "And those who

praised me swore against me." And of the flight of them all together: "My friends and my neighbours drew near and stood against me, and my nearest kin stood far off." Yet these had not yet issued from the loins or been formed into flesh; they did not even have parents or ancestors yet. He also foretold his own saving cross as though it had already been set up and he had already been nailed to it: "They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones", meaning where they would pierce him through with the nails. In short, in many places in divine Scripture we hear the Divine speaking about future things as though they were already present, or already past and done, since by predestination they will certainly come to pass. As the lofty Apostle says, "For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers." He clearly knew that our first parents would be led astray and would slip into disobedience. He also knew that at the end of the ages the only-begotten Child of God would of his own will become mortal, for the sake of mortals who were in danger of being separated from him; this he had predestined. That, it seems to me, is what he declares by saying, "Let us make man in our image and likeness." It is as if he said: "Even if it is late, I shall become like him for his sake, taking a body without seed from an ever-virgin who knew no marriage. I shall be laid in a manger of dumb beasts, to call him back from his senselessness. For I must become what he is, and make him what I am. I must dwell in the dark cave and his lightless life, so that he may dwell in heaven; I must be bound in swaddling clothes, so that he may be loosed from the bonds of death; I must grow in body, so that he may grow in divinity. I must be baptized, and wash the one who was defiled; I must be tempted, and conquer the adversary, and subject him to the one he had defeated. I who feed all things shall hunger for the one who ate wrongly; I who give the rain and walk on the deep in the flesh shall thirst for the condemned. I shall be bound willingly, and release the one bound against his will. I shall be mocked and reviled, so that the woman who transgressed may be freed from the reproach of men. I, the Maker, shall be spat upon in the face of my flesh, so that I may wipe clean the face of the one I formed. I, the Lord of the angels, shall be struck by a servant, so that I may free the one enslaved to sin; for masters free their servants with a slap, releasing them from slavery in the very act of striking them. I who planted paradise shall be crowned with thorns, so that the thorns of mortals may be rooted out. I shall be fed gall and given vinegar to drink, by taking it on myself sucking out all the bitterness of mortal nature. I who gave manna to Israel shall go to the altar and the cross, I the bodiless, to have the body nailed. Having put on this body for the sake of mortals, in it I, who cannot be held, shall be seized by the Jews; in it I, the immortal, shall be put to death, a death to death;

in it I shall be buried for the sake of those who are in Hades; with it, as with a rock, I shall strike Hades' gates, "leading out those bound in fetters with might," as David my servant says; in it I shall ascend into heaven, though I need no ascent, for I fill all things; in it I shall sit at the right hand of the formless Father, being formless like him. This is what I have been pleased to do at the end of the times: to come to be in the image and likeness of the one I made, having predetermined for myself what my creation would become." If, then, this account of the image and likeness seems sound to you, let there be no further inquiry about it.

QUESTION 167. What then? Did the Trinity become flesh and become man? For God did not say, "Let [me] make man in image and likeness," but "Let us make man in image and likeness", not "mine" but "ours".

If we are willing to follow the passage further, the divine word will certainly explain itself. It says, "And God made man in the image of God": "made", not "they made"; "God", not "the gods"; "of God", not "of gods". So "Let us make" signifies the three persons of the Godhead, while "made" signifies the oneness of the nature, of the will and of the act. We know this from our own creation too. "And God made man": here it presents the single nature of all mortals. "Male and female he made them": here it indicates persons. Elsewhere it says, "I will blot out from the earth the man whom I made," though there were countless thousands of people drowned in Noah's time, even if the word is singular. Elsewhere again, the divine song of Miriam, lamenting the drowning of Pharaoh's whole army, says, "Let us sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea." It sang of the mass of cavalry in the singular, and likewise of the army, though all of them were swallowed up in the Red Sea together with their wretched king. And to Moses it says, "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." By the "I" the divine Trinity indicates its oneness and identity; by uttering "God" three times (5) it presents its three hypostases and persons. It speaks "I" once but "God" three times. And the divine-human manifestation in the flesh from the ever-virgin Mary, which is beyond all speech and utterance, one might say came about through the Father willing it, the Son becoming flesh and the Spirit working with them. This was not because one was too weak for the deed. Rather, because of the agreement of all, and the unity and identity of the one will, authority and kingship in the Trinity, Scripture is accustomed to divide many of God's works in three. [?] (5) "Three ... uttering": perhaps read "three times ... having uttered" or "uttering"? Ed.

QUESTION 168. But God did not say, "Let us make man in an image and likeness which I shall one day become"; he presents it as already established and complete, when Moses says, "And God made man; in the image of God he made him."

If people do not wish to be contentious and do not set themselves stubbornly against what has been said, it seems to me reasonable that the matter of the image depends on the Word's divine appearing in our form. In many places the company of the prophets bears me out. Many ages beforehand they proclaimed the Word's life in the flesh, which was to come after their time, as though it were already present. Isaiah, the loftiest of the prophets, cries out plainly, "A child has been born to us, and given, and his name is called Mighty God", when his mother according to the flesh, the ever-virgin, had not yet even been brought into being. Another, more than five hundred years before the divine-human appearance of the Word, asked him as though he had already been crucified, had risen from the tomb and was standing before him, "What are these wounds between your hands?" And the Divine, not yet incarnate, but confirming the words of the [?] as already accomplished, says to him, "These are the wounds with which I was wounded in the house of my beloved." And David, the singer of divine things, a full thousand years before, sang of the ascent into heaven of the one who had taken a body as though it were present or past: "God has gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of the trumpet."
QUESTION 169. How is it that earlier you condemned those who describe the Divine as having limbs and call it man-shaped, and yet now you yourself answer that it exists in our form?

I did not say that it "exists" in our form, but that it "becomes" so, united to our soul and body. For the holy Word himself, having become like us and living among us, while remaining what he was and being seen as what he was not, said to the company of the apostles as he broke the bread, "Take, eat of it, all of you; this is my body", though he had not yet been sacrificed in the flesh. And he said, "Take, drink; this is my blood", though his side had not yet been pierced by a spear on the cross. And today we see that holy bread set forth on the spotless table, on the bloodless altar, at the time of the divine and mystical rite. Yet it does not resemble the form of the saving body of God the Word. Nor does the cup of wine set forth with the bread resemble the blood mingled with that body. It resembles it neither in the articulation of the limbs, nor in the quality of flesh and blood, nor in the invisible and imperceptibly united, form-

less divinity. For the body has blood, a soul and sinews; it is red and jointed, [?] with various arteries and veins. The creating Word is interwoven with all of these, down to the hairs and nails, for I call the hair of Christ God's hair, and likewise his feet and nails, and his blood and water. For the Word has been united with what is mine for my sake. And the body is upright and jointed, able to walk and act. The bread, by contrast, is round, without joints, without soul, without blood and without motion. It resembles neither: neither the visible body nor the invisible divinity. Nevertheless we believe the divine word. We believe that what is consecrated on the divine table is not something similar or equal to the divine body, but properly and firmly the divine body itself. It is distributed to the congregation wholly without being cut, and partaken of without ever running out. For the sun does not cease supplying its light to those who need it. Nor does the sea shrink in its bulk because its salt is shared out. Nor does fire wither or diminish when it lights countless lamps, so long as someone is there to stir it and raise the flame. Nor again is the air lessened by the breathing of all living things. And again he says, "He who does not believe in me is already judged", though he had not yet judged anyone. "But he who believes in me has eternal life", although believers have not yet received it, and will not until they are released from this passion-ridden, material life; for from this life we pass over to that one. But because we believe the divine word and hold the future securely, we are disposed as though already established in it. We understand the account of the image in the same way. It is fulfilled by the predestination of the Word's taking form, being born and living as we do, but without our unholy wickedness.

They would have been blameless had they not been told beforehand, through the law and the prophets, to refrain from the killing of God in Christ, and not to transgress by senselessly destroying the Word through the flesh. And those who told them were not foreigners, but their own kinsmen of the same blood, who had studied the teaching of the law alongside them. They gained nothing from their idle chatter, since they used the law lawlessly. For though they were devoted to the law and instructed in it from childhood, they grew grey in ignorance, or rather in perdition, and rejected him. But the lawless nations, who were neither brought up in the law nor instructed in it, kept the law well. They became a law to themselves and admired their Maker, believing him to be God from his works alone.
[?]: "But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal."

But just because the argument has shown that what we sought is beyond our grasp, let us not neglect the virtue that is within reach. The divine word says plainly, "Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." It is certainly not commanding us to stretch ourselves to match the incomparable divine nature, which is beyond reason and thought, for that is impossible. It is commanding us to imitate that nature's love for humanity, its approachability and its perfect goodness, by showing every compassion to our neighbour, even if he is an enemy and a schemer. For the Divine helps everyone in everything and pours forth like a spring without stint. Let us anticipate with gifts the requests for what is needed, even if no one honours us as we deserve. Let us then pursue virtue as far as we can, leaping toward it with light and frequent bounds, even if it is impossible to reach the summit. In the finest things, even if one cannot attain the whole, to attain a part is no ordinary gain. Since we cannot drink up the whole spring or the whole jar, should we not relieve the burning of our thirst with what share we can take? Or, because it is impossible to draw in the whole air, should we therefore not breathe at all? Or, because we do not know the whole art of logic, should we not speak at all? We must therefore show every effort not to fall wholly short of the perfection that is within reach, but to embrace it as far as we can, and even beyond our strength; for to have more of it is praiseworthy. So the perfection of virtue seems to me to be always striving to have the larger share of the good, and to outweigh injustice with justice. For in the divine judgment, what each person has lived is weighed and measured against each other in an instant, in a way beyond words. We shall receive our recompense according to which prevails, the good or the worse, and we shall be assigned to those who are like us, to be honoured or punished along with them.

QUESTION 170. What are the kinds of virtue, and how many are there? And is it possible to succeed through just one of them? For not everyone is able to achieve them all. Perhaps someone cannot offer hospitality because of poverty, but can practise self-control and chastity, or endure in temptations, or teach the things of godliness. Another gives the poor what they need to live; another serves without pay. What then? Can a person not be delivered from eternal judgment through one of these?
Every virtue is eagerly sought by those whose reason has not been darkened by matter, and by those who are truly sound of mind. Every vice is abominable,

since it stands as the adversary of what is better and fights against our nature. Some, then, have named four kinds of virtue: courage, prudence, temperance and justice. These are good, but they crawl along the ground and swim on dry land, lying below the vault of heaven. For by courage they meant what fights against matter; by temperance, mastery and victory over the passions; by prudence, the rule of the best in cities; and by justice, the glorious share in life. In this way they thought they were laying down a kind of order by law, bridling excess in either direction. But they could neither conceive nor express anything loftier. As far as it lay with them, they confined virtue to visible things alone, supposing that it had nothing lofty about it, nothing to rival the beautiful order of the heavens. We, however, have as our guide the lofty Apostle. He lists many kinds of virtue, but three that surpass them all: faith, hope and love. Of these, faith grants mortals what is beyond nature, enrolling among the spiritual beings one who is still clothed in matter's passion-laden garment. For what the orders of angels and the other bodiless beings did not know, faith teaches to mortals who walk the ground and roll about on the earth. It reveals it to them, bringing the mind to the royal and formless throne. It flashes upon them the exact radiance of the nature that has no beginning and is unmixed, and with the lightning from there it drives away the fog of the senses. Having expelled from the mind whatever is gross and deathly [?] in things here below, it becomes the mind's companion and enables it to believe that nothing absurd has been done. In the bath of baptism it gives the mind forgetfulness of former things and sobriety to drink, and makes it appear ever-virgin and blameless.

QUESTION 174. What does the Lord mean when he says, "From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it"? We know that the violent man deserves every judgment and curse. How then are we to understand the [?]

[?] When John first announced to mortals that the kingdom of heaven had come that very day, and the Saviour quickly appeared, those who believed firmly and sincerely did violence to themselves. Through the strictest asceticism and hardship they overstepped the bounds of nature. While still in the body they passed over into freedom from passion, soaring above the hindrances that come from the body and putting to death its desires. They walked by the virtues along the narrow and more toilsome road, pressing on toward the prize of the upward call, as the holy Apostle says.
QUESTION 175. What does the Lord mean when he says about his own John [?]
[?]: "And if you are willing to accept it, this is Elijah who is to come"? But we know that Herod beheaded John; so how is this man in turn Elijah himself?

Since John was sent ahead of him, in the spirit and power of Elijah, at his coming as God-made-man, the Lord fittingly calls him Elijah, because their grace was equal and their roles in the divine plan were alike. For John became the end of one Testament and the beginning of the other: the end of the law and the beginning of the Gospels, that is, the guide to a way of life and conduct different from that of the law. In the same way we expect Elijah to come a little before Christ's second coming as God-made-man, to be the end of the present way of life and the beginning of the one to come. Like John, he too will be murdered by a spiritual Herod for the sake of the truth.

Question [?]. How is John the Baptist greater than anyone born of women? And if he was a prophet, what did he have beyond a prophet? For this is what the Lord says in the Gospels. And why, then, when the Savior had testified that he was greater than all, did his own father Zacharias…

This question seems to me to have more than one explanation. First of all, you yourselves acknowledge that the Lord testifies that John is greater than all mortals and higher than the prophets. We have no word higher than the living Word, and it is he who testifies to the voice crying in the wilderness, "Prepare the ways of the Lord, and make his paths straight." So I will take my starting points about the Voice from the Word, and give an account of each point. It will not be what either deserves, but it will be the best I can do. John, then, is greater than anyone born of women because, while still in his mother's womb and before he had touched our life at all, he prophesied, using his mother's tongue as his instrument. Though hidden in darkness, he did not fail to recognize the Light that was taking flesh in the womb of Mary, ever-virgin. The young woman who carried God embraced and kissed his mother, and through the mouth of the woman carrying him, as through an opening, he drew in that flash of lightning. Lifted up, he cried out with his mother's tongue, "Why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" The grateful servant recognized his Master. Leaping as if to spring out of the womb, he hurried to serve the Word, to reach the Jordan first and prepare the bath that would be taken in the flesh for our sake. He surpasses the prophets because he saw with his own eyes, in the flesh, the one they had prophesied, and touched that head before which all things tremble. All the patriarchs and prophets saw him only in imagination, through dreams or riddles, because they departed this life before the Word appeared as God-made-man. As for Zacharias being struck dumb when the birth of his child was announced to him, I say it was not out of astonishment

at the angel who appeared to him (for he was accustomed to seeing angels, since he lived purely according to the law). Rather, the silence of the law follows from the figure of his silence. When the child was born, the father's tongue was restored, showing that the voice is born out of silence, disability [?] and old age. That is, it is born out of the law, which had grown old and aged and barren because of the unfruitfulness of the Jews who received it. They gained nothing from the prophetic predictions. They did not understand that the birth of God the Word among us, from the Jews, had come to pass, or that his mother according to the flesh came from them.
Question 177. And how is it that Christ testifies that John is greater than all, and then says himself, "But the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he"?

The meaning of this too has more than one sense [?]. In fact the saying shows us three. First, the Lord himself is younger than John according to the flesh. Six months after John's conception, the Lord came to dwell in the Ever-Virgin and put on the body taken from her, in a union that cannot be divided and is free of mixture. We learn this from the great Gabriel when he brought the good news to the Theotokos. For he says, "Behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has herself also conceived a son in her old age, and this is her sixth month." Seen as a mortal, Christ is younger than John; understood as God, he is greater. Second, the angels are superior to John. Whichever angel seems last of all in rank and lesser in nature in the kingdom of heaven is still greater than John by nature and by birth. For a contemptible Herod beheaded John, but a single angel, even the very least of all, could strike down and destroy ten thousand Herods in an instant. In the days of Isaiah and Hezekiah, one angel went out from the camp and in a moment mowed down and slew a hundred and eighty-five thousand of the enemy. And whom does the third sense present to us as lesser in the kingdom of heaven but greater than John? Surely the one whom the Lord renamed "Son of Thunder," John the Theologian. For the Baptist, in great fear, did not dare to touch the head of the Word who bore flesh, even when he was commanded to. But the Theologian surpassed everyone in boldness. At the divine supper he reclined in the Lord's bosom, and shortly afterwards he leaned back onto the holy breast of the God-man, as the Gospel teaches, to ask who was going to betray him; for Peter had signaled to him to find out who it was that would hand him over. Not the mother who bore him, not Joseph, who was called his father but was not, not John the Baptist, not an angel, not an archangel, nor anyone else [?]—none of them, where God

and the Word had become man, dared to touch that awe-inspiring breast. Yet this John reclined on it, melting with affection like a father over his son. From there he drew his word about the Word, and he thundered to all under heaven: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The Baptist saw the divine and all-holy Spirit only in the form of a dove, flying down from heaven upon the Word when he was baptized in the flesh. The Theologian received the Spirit on his own head in the form of a tongue of fire, together with his fellow disciples, on the day of Pentecost, as the great Luke recorded when he wrote the Acts of the Apostles. The Baptist was beheaded because of a licentious harlot who had committed incest with her brother-in-law: Herod's wife, who had been his brother's wife. The Theologian was condemned for the Lord's sake to live in [?] the tomb, and died later. The Baptist only baptized those who came to him and could not give the divine Spirit to anyone. That is why the Theologian and the other apostles rebaptized those whom the Baptist had baptized, to make them perfect, and by laying hands on the faithful they gave them a share in the Holy Spirit, for the display of signs and wonders. The Baptist was declared by the Greater One to be the greatest of those born of women. The Theologian was called the light of the world by the true, unbegotten and eternally existing great Light, who is God. The Baptist departed this life without doing a single sign or working any miracle at all, as the Gospel says of him, and without hearing anything of what awaited him in the next life. To the Theologian, together with the Twelve, Christ, speaking as God, promised that he would sit with Christ and judge the tribes of Israel at his command. The Baptist is nowhere called blessed, great as he was among mortals. The Theologian received proof that he was greater from our blessed God and Savior Jesus Christ, who says to them: "Truly I tell you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear." And we all believe that John the Baptist was a prophet and a righteous man. When the mother of the one who had no father here on earth drew near to the Baptist's own mother, he was afraid. He leapt as if to spring out of the womb, putting the woman who carried him in danger, because he could not bear the approach of the woman who carried the fire. But the Theologian is commended and entrusted to his own mother by the one who is motherless in his essence and fatherless in the divine plan. At the time of the saving passion, as they stood by the cross, he looked at John and said to the unwed mother, "Behold your son," and in turn to John, "Behold your mother." So he commended each to the other in his own place, and before that God-fighting crowd he publicly declared that the virgin was undiminished and untouched by either [?]. To put it briefly, Christ is the kingdom of heaven. So John the Baptist, perfect and exact according to the law, seems to me to be less than those who have been baptized into the death of the

Lord. For the law perfected nothing, as the Apostle says, who was great in the law and lofty in the Gospels, and experienced in everything. So in his own generation and in his own times John was greater than all. Otherwise the divine word would contradict itself, since it says to Solomon, "There has been no one like you before you, and after you no one like you will arise," while it says about John that "there has not arisen among those born of women anyone greater than he." So according to the law he was greater and more exact than all, but the apostles are better. For the Lord does not say, "No one greater than he will arise," but, "No one greater has arisen" [?] in his own times. And before both of these, God says to the devil, "Have you set your mind on my servant Job? For there is no man on earth like him." And to Moses he says, "I have known you above all men, and you have found favor before me." Enoch was great in his own times, and so he was taken up. Noah was righteous in his own generation, and so he was saved in the ark as the eighth person when the world was flooded. Lot was great, and so he alone was saved when Sodom and the five cities were burned. In the same way John was greater than all according to the law in his own times.

Question [?]. About whom does the Lord say, "Truly I tell you, there are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his glory"? For some say he said this about John the Theologian, meaning that he will not die until Christ's second coming.

Answer. He had already taught the disciples who followed him to despise death and to strip like brave fighters for the dangers they would face for his sake. But when he examined their secret thoughts, he found them still limping and wavering this way and that. So he tries to make them somehow cast off what they were dreading. He rouses them and anoints them like athletes with the promise of long life, so that for his sake they might meet death with a great spirit [?]. For he saw that they were as changeable as a tidal strait, like reeds shaken by the wind. Indeed, before there was any constraint, persecution or torture, Judas Iscariot, afraid of what was coming and greedy for money, was taken captive by the assault of the spirit of self-love and sold the Lord. And at that same time of the passion the chief of the apostles cowered before the maid Ballila and denied the Lord three times with an oath, though afterwards he found healing through his tears. To put it briefly, when he went to the stake of the cross, the spirit of cowardice burst upon them and made them all run away. And he [did not?] allow them to be killed before they had preached about him. That is why he also says to those who arrested him, "If you are looking for me, let" (8) Pros hapantas: read para pantas (conjecture).

these men go." Since he knew in advance that they would run away and waver, he supports them with the promise. He unveils it in part, assuring them of the whole through a dim glimpse. They could not take it in. They were overcome at that moment and almost melted away on the ground. For after six days he took Peter, James and John up onto a high mountain peak and was transfigured before them, "and his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became like the light," says the divine Matthew. Here, then, before they tasted death, they saw the Son of Man in his glory, as he had promised them earlier. Yet even though the Godhead appeared not naked but united to our nature, the unbearable sight threw them to the ground. He was teaching them that if Christ chose to appear as he is by nature, everything would be utterly melted down before a sight it could not contain, dissolving like wax near a fire. He also brought Moses and Elijah to stand beside him and talk with him, the two lofty summits among the righteous. In this he showed that he is master not only of those on earth but already of those beneath the earth too. He showed that by his command he can bring before himself, alive and strong, not only those four days dead, like Lazarus, or dead that same day, like the widow's son, but also those who have been dead a thousand years (9), who perished ages ago and have dissolved into dust. He does these things before his passion and resurrection, showing that it was not through these, as if through endurance and courage, [?] that he has unlimited power over all things, and that he himself is sovereign. This is why he brings to himself men who departed this life in different ways, showing, even before his tomb and resurrection, that he is Lord of the living and the dead. Moses had already been led out of life by the death that is common to all. Elijah had been carried off in a fiery four-horse chariot, as if to heaven, to an unseen place on the earth. He brought the one from the regions beneath the earth and summoned the other from the land of the living that had received him, and in the twinkling of an eye he set them beside himself. "While he was still speaking with them," says the great Matthew, "suddenly a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came from the cloud, saying, 'This is my beloved Son; listen to him.'" When the Father gave this charge through the cloud, the divine men quickly departed, and the disciples fell down, shutting their eyes at the unbearable voice. So the one who stood there in his form appeared alone as the true Son, beloved and consubstantial, talking boldly with the Father. For at a divine and imperial silentium the attendants withdraw, and those who remain [?] stay and keep silent out of respect for the silentium. So the Lord's disciples did not taste death until they had seen the Son of Man in his glory. They saw it not as it is but as far as they could take it in, and only three of them, the most clear-sighted and best of the company. For the Lord says, "There are some of those standing here"—not all of them—"who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God." When they saw it dimly, (9) Chiliōntōtas: so in the text, for chilieteis or chiliétas. Eutr.

they almost broke away from life. So John, and all the apostles and prophets, have departed this life, except Enoch and Elijah. These two alone are said to be still in the flesh, and a little later they too will be put to death.

Question [?]. Then how does the Lord say to Peter about John the evangelist, "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?" This seems to show that he is alive.

John himself made this clear near the end of his own Gospel, where he says: "And after saying this, he says to him"—that is, to Peter—"'Follow me.' Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who had also leaned back on his breast at the supper and said, 'Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?' When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, 'Lord, what about this man?' Jesus said to him, 'If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?'" He had found them fishing and ordered Peter to follow him. Peter wanted his fellow disciple to come with them too, and so he said to Jesus, "Lord, what about this man?" Jesus had ordered John to stay at the fishing, and so he says, "If I want him to remain until I come, what
Dialogue 1. We would like to learn how the parable of the leaven should be understood. For yesterday we had no small debate about it

The parable seems to me to be understood in two ways. But let us first quote it, and then go on to examine it. "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a wise woman took and hid in three measures of flour until all of it was leavened." The Lord seems to me to compare the leaven to teaching and to faith in him, and the woman to his Church, which he also loved, as the holy Apostle says. The three measures of flour are Noah's three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth. From them alone, after the flood, came all the nations that are now being gathered into the Church. In the Church the instruction of the preaching, and faith, kneaded in like leaven, leavened the whole flour of the nations, which came from Noah's three rational measures, and raised it to godliness. But if you think the words should also be heard another way, let the leaven be understood as the venerable and divine body of God

the Word. He formed it for himself in the womb of the Ever-Virgin, weaving it around himself without seed, and was united with soul and body. Moreover, the wise woman may fittingly be understood as the holy and living God the Word himself, who exists in his own person, because the title is feminine; for "Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God," says the divine Apostle. The three measures of flour are, first, the whole nature of mortals; second, death; and after that, Hades. The divine body was hidden in Hades through burial, and it kneaded everything into resurrection and life. Understand the three measures in another way too: baptism, the Gospels, the mysteries. And understand them in yet another way: apostles, prophets, teachers. And in another way again: past, present, future. For the Word made flesh did not help only those who were living at that time. He also raised those who had already fallen asleep in death, and he gave hope of resurrection and life to us who came after. When he rose from the dead, he raised some of these together with himself. He himself went up to heaven, but he settled them in the land of the living, where Enoch and Elijah are, never to die again.

Question 181 [?]. Since we never have our fill of interpretations of divine Scripture but always long to hear more, explain to us the parable of the dragnet. You will gain a great reward for yourself and benefit for us. For the Lord says, "Blessed is the one who does and teaches one of these commandments," and again, he did not leave unpunished the man who buried in silence the talent of the word that he had received from him.

What this parable says also seems to me akin to what has already been said. "For the kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it up onto the shore, sat down, and collected the good into baskets, but threw the bad away," says the Lord. He seems to me to liken the order of the gospel to a dragnet. The Lord said to the divine apostles, "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men" (for most of them had been catchers of fish, which lack reason). After this the apostles wove and strung that net together from both the Old and the New Testament and let it down into the sea of this present life, netting rational beings instead of fish. For the time being they gather from every kind, wicked and good, righteous and sinners, enclosing them in the divine dragnet of the preaching. For now these divine men fish the sea without discrimination, by letter and by spirit, since in body they are absent from most people. Isaiah, the loftiest of the prophets, had already cried this out five hundred years before: "The wolf shall feed with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; the ox and the donkey shall eat chaff together, and the calf and the lion shall graze together; and a little child shall lead them." The

…showing that the spiritual gathering makes no distinction. For in it we all share in divine things together: robbers and murderers, the gentle and the savage, led by a little child. Elsewhere the same prophet says of him: “A child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us, and his name is called Mighty God, Ruler.” But when the time of the end arrives, they will haul the net up onto the shore. At Christ’s nod, together with the angels, they will sort out what is in it and set the wicked apart from the righteous.

QUESTION 182. What does the Lord mean when he commands Peter to go and cast a hook, to open the mouth of the first fish that comes up, and to give the stater found there for himself and for Peter to those collecting the census tax and the double drachma?

I think this passage too has a double meaning. Peter was ordered to take the stater with a hook from the deep, inside the fish. I take that stater to be our form, covered by the passions as if in the deep of this life and tossed underwater by the waves of sin. Or if not this, it is our captivity in Hades, which came about through death. The Lord calls this back in himself to its original pattern when he orders the stater to be given for himself and for Peter. For he became a mortal like us, subject to our passions and liable to tribute, yet he remained unyielding to unholy wickedness and never leaned toward evil. In providing the stater for himself and for Peter, he willingly suffers for the Church. For he says to Peter, “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church,” and he teaches the Church through himself. The teaching of divine things is the building of souls, and its cornerstone is Christ, the leader of all. Of him the singer of divine things says: “The stone which the builders rejected” (the Jews, through the law) “has become the head of the corner.” Again, speaking in the person of that stone, the same singer said: “At the head of the book it is written of me.” John unveils this and cries out: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” This Word, united to flesh and teaching it through himself, shows by what was said about the fish and the stater that we should not oppose a king or ruler who gives commands that do no harm, but should pay tribute with good grace. By the same events he also shows himself to be God. If he were a mere mortal, as the drunken raving of those who fight against God claims, how could he know that a fish in the deep had a stater in its mouth, and that it was in its mouth and not in its flesh? And how could he know that this fish would be the first one drawn up by the hook? If the fish came to the hook of its own accord, even so it took God to foretell the capture of the creature that had swallowed the stater. But if, as is truer, he drew it to the hook by the invisible strength of his divinity, then he was truly the one who commanded the sea monster to swallow

Jonah, to keep him unharmed in the deep for three days, and then to cast him out again onto dry land, safe and sound. If the fish took the stater [?] in the deep and was swimming toward the [?], and was itself the first, then the one who foretold it is God. For what does he say? “This fish will be caught first of all its kind.” But it may be, as is more fitting, that at the very moment of need the one who brought all things into being out of nothing made the stater, placed it in the fish, and drove the fish to the fisherman. Then he is clearly the one who ordered Peter to cast the hook into the sea. Of him the king who was also the singer of divine things says: “But our God, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and in all the deeps, has done whatever he willed.”
QUESTION 183. What was the Lord’s purpose in withering the fig tree and cursing it, so that it would never bear fruit again? For he did not do this without some meaning.

Let no one think that he cursed and withered the plant for no reason. Through it he wants to teach the God-fighting synagogue of the Jews that he is able to punish, but because he is good he does not wish to. Since they never saw him take vengeance on anyone, they supposed he could only do good and could not also punish. So through inanimate nature he convinces the God-hated synagogue that he will punish in due time, though for now he is patient. He withers the lifeless fig tree in order to curse the godless synagogue […], seeing its barrenness and the desolation within it, so that not one stone will be left on another there. The fig tree did not yield what its nature should produce, and the synagogue did not yield what the law required. So the lifeless tree is punished, so that the godless synagogue may bear the fruit of faith. Who does not know that a fig tree has no fruit in winter? Even someone who has lived in palaces from the womb and from tender childhood, with no experience of farming, knows that. But, as I said, he used the plant as an image for many reasons. First, he shows that he is able to punish the wicked even now, but for the time being holds back his power and gives each person room to repent. As the divine tragedian says: “God is a righteous judge, strong and patient, and does not bring wrath every day. If you do not turn back, he will polish his sword,” meaning his power to punish. For it is truly God’s work to dry up [?] a green tree with a word and to make a dry tree flourish, as Ezekiel, who beheld the cherubim, says. The one who withered the fig tree by his command is the same who, a thousand years before his birth among us, suddenly brought to life as a serpent the dry, lifeless staff that Moses held in his hand. The inspired man was stunned at the sight of it leaping at him and tried to flee, until the one who had given it life turned it back into a rod. For the one who asked where Lazarus was buried says to him:

“What is this in your hand?” He answered, “A rod.” And again the divine voice said, “Throw it on the ground.” When he threw it down, it became a serpent and leapt at the one who had thrown it. When he fled [?], God said to him, “Stretch out your hand and take hold of its tail.” When he did so, the creature was restored to what it had been before it turned into a beast. In the same way, the one who said of the bound [?] Lazarus, “Unbind him and let him go,” reshaped the man [?] who had decayed and begun to stink into what he had been before he tasted death. Likewise he made the dry, sapless rod of Aaron sprout leaves and nuts in a single night, effortlessly, without moisture or the enfolding of the earth, and so gave Aaron proof of his priesthood. The same one who made the rod sprout without planting took a body [?] himself without marital union. “For a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse,” and Jesse was a mortal, the father of the great David. So we must understand that from a living root the rod also is living. The lofty Isaiah says this about it, and the God-bearing Apostle unveils it and cries out plainly: “We have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens.” Not long afterward this same one went to Jerusalem to undergo the cross for us of his own free will. With a bare word he suddenly withered the plant. He showed that he is the one who also commanded it to grow, and that he could command the wood of the cross to strike with lightning those who were nailing him to it. But as God he bore being nailed [?] in the flesh. “As they were going to Jerusalem, Jesus became hungry on the way, and seeing a fig tree he went to it looking for fruit, and found none,” as the divine evangelist says. Let the way be understood figuratively as this present life. The living and holy Word, having become like us, walks it in the body and moves from place to place, though as God he is present everywhere. Hungering spiritually for the salvation of all, and above all of the Jews, he came to the fig tree, that is, to the synagogue. He sought from it fruit, not figs that can be seen but spiritual fruit: the sweet harvest of the law and the prophets. Just as seeds lie within a fig, the divine commandments lie within the synagogue, and the soul that shares in them is sweetened. But Jesus found no fruit on it, only leaves: the books of the law and the prophets. And even these were like fig leaves, trampled without fear through the transgression of divine things by Jews who had turned to folly. For the Lord-killing synagogue is a beast of burden that carries books. She killed the king but honors the soldier, and she has often been taken captive by him and made a servant and a tributary. She reads and does not understand. She holds on to the letter and is ignorant of the substance. She has the covenant and stays far from its good order. Christ alone could be called her husband, but he does not wish to be called the husband of one who plays the harlot [?], and so he says through Hosea the pro- [?]

-phet: “She is not my wife, and I am not her husband.” Another of the inspired prophets gives the reason and cries out: “They did not remain in the covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord Almighty.” So the fruitless fig tree, or rather the synagogue, is disinherited. The Word of piety rejects her for adultery and also bars her from the inheritance.

QUESTION 184. Since we never tire of your eloquence, we ask to learn also the parable of the women grinding and the mill, and of the field and the two who are in it. For the Lord says in the Gospels: “Then two will be in the field: one is taken and one is left. Two women will be grinding at the mill: one is taken and one is left.”

Both sayings show that the same things will happen at the time of the resurrection and of the second coming. He compares the world to a field, as he says elsewhere: “The field is the world, and the reapers are the angels.” He likens the mill to the unstable round of life and the constant turning of the things done in it. Like a mill, life runs around us in endless, restless motion and exchanges one thing for another among us before the grinding is done [?]. By those who grind in it, or rather are ground by it, some taken and some left, he means us, who have been grinding from Adam until today. Some are carried off by death. Others are left for the time being and are changed to incorruption in a moment, in an instant, as the lofty herald, the Apostle, says: “Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.” So those who die are taken, as it were, from the mill, and those who remain are left. At that moment the divine trumpet will sound and at once raise those who have slept since the beginning of time. Then the unswerving and incorruptible judge will take his seat, repaying each according to the worth of the life he has lived, as the divine Apostle says: “To those who by patience in good work…,” and so on.
In many places divine Scripture calls the Godhead an immaterial fire. So the choirs of angels and the souls of the righteous, set aflame by their nearness to God through purity, are fittingly called

burning coals. They shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life. We know that fire acts in two ways: it burns and it gives light. To those who approach it properly it gives light. To those who approach it with contempt and without fear it burns and purifies. Too much nearness burns, while a moderate distance gives light. Physicians, for their part, are accustomed to check most hard-to-cure diseases with the cautery. In the same way the Godhead does not destroy but recasts and cleanses away the shame of what a person has done, if the one gripped [?] by the passion turns toward healing through repentance. But if he departs this fleeting [?] present life still sick, he burns without being consumed, punished forever by the divine fire, in a body now immortal and incorruptible. For “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality,” so that “each may receive according to what he has done through the body,” as the lofty Apostle says. Here, then, is the time for healing, there the time for giving account; here for health, there for punishment; here for God’s patience, there for his unswerving righteous judgment. QUESTION 186. How should we understand the axe in the Gospels that cuts down the fruitless trees?

John saw the fruitless disposition of the Jews and likened them to fruitless plants. He declared that the axe lies at their root. The axe is the swift, sharpened division made by the living Word, by which “every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.” The divine Apostle refers to this again when he says, “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword.” By this he means the cutting power of the preaching.

QUESTION 187. What does the Lord mean when he says, “His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor, and he will gather the wheat into the storehouse, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire”?

The winnowing fork seems to me to be God’s impartial judgment, which by God’s law, as it were, sorts each person into the place that matches the life he has lived. Understand the threshing floor as the universal Church throughout the world, and as the resurrection of all humankind from the dead. There the divine verdict acts like a winnowing fork. Some are like chaff: fickle, blown about by every wind of sin, light and fruitless. These it flings into the fire for eternal burning. Others, like wheat, have become nourishment for their neighbors and have kept a straight course in virtue. These it gathers into a fitting storehouse, which he also calls a dwelling of salvation. For there truly is our dwelling, since the present life is not a dwelling [?]

QUESTION 188. Taking occasion from this answer, we ask you to explain why we often see churches and pious people fall and perish through earthquake, thunder or some other threat, as though they were sinners.

Divine Scripture teaches us about these things. The Lord did not spare even the divine ark, but handed it over to foreigners together with its priests, who had acted lawlessly. He razed the holy city of Jerusalem. He took down the cherubim of glory from the mercy seat and tore the sacred robe apart. He handed over to the nations, to be trampled and plundered, the divine gifts: prophecy and manifestation, the ephod and the oracle, the plate of pure gold bearing ineffable letters, and the rest of the sacred rites. He did this to condemn those who had transgressed at that time. If so, he does not spare his own palaces today either, nor the ineffable and spotless mysteries kept in them. In this way he strikes fear into those who stumble, so that they expect a harsher punishment if they persist in wickedness. “Let the pine wail, for the cedar has fallen,” says Jeremiah. That is, when the strong and holy are shattered, let the weaker things on earth take the lesson. Solomon, wise in divine things, says the same in reverse: “When the ungodly fall, the righteous become afraid.” Spear points, helmet, breastplate and greaves will not give the wicked a safe life, those who rob travelers and lie in ambush on the highways. For many who thought themselves hard to capture were pitiably torn from life. In our records there are Oreb and Zeeb, Zalmunna, Abimelech, Goliath, Absalom and others like them. Among outsiders there are men like Hector and Ajax, and the Spartans themselves, so puffed up over their strength. They fell because justice did not go hand in hand with their might. So before God hands us over to our enemies for our wickedness, or shakes the churches down on us sinners, let us make war on our own injustice, and against the mob of sin let us arm an army of piety.
QUESTION 189. What does the Lord mean when he tells us to be well disposed toward our adversary while we are on the way with him? For our fellow travelers are not always our adversaries.

Goodwill of the simple, ready sort is indeed good: not holding a grudge and not hurrying to retaliate against someone who has wronged us. For he himself says, “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who curse you,” and, “Repay no one evil for evil,” and other such sayings. But it also has [?]
The Lord wants us to be wise like the serpent, protecting the head in every danger or temptation. The head is Christ, as

the Apostle says. When a serpent is caught by a mortal’s strength, it gives up its whole body to the one striking it, but it contrives to keep its head unwounded. When it settles down to sleep, it coils itself up and secures its head in the middle of its whole body, as though fortifying it with the wall of its trailing coils. It also wisely strips off its old skin by squeezing through some narrow passage, and so lays aside its old age. So he wants us too to squeeze through the narrow and toilsome way, strip off the old man, and put on instead the new man, who is renewed according to his image. He also wants us to imitate the serpent’s cunning for a better purpose. As it used flattery to lead us into a fall and into transgression, so we too should approach our neighbors shrewdly, sow the seeds of the faith in them, lead them back again and unite them to God. So let us give up the body to be torn by those who torment us for Christ’s sake, but guard the head unwounded with all our strength, and the head is our faith in Christ. Nor, when the community is settled and at peace, should we neglect the strenuous work of the virtues. We should not think that a cloak, a beard and a staff are enough to fulfill the angelic way of life, and parade [?] the trappings of the teacher’s life while shunning the wrestling and the battle. It is from that battle that victory comes to the obedient person who has put on the breastplate of the word of faith.
You have explained the matter of the serpent well for us. We ask to hear about the dove too: why did he set it beside the serpent, showing that it is pure and innocent?

The serpent was wise, but not for good. So the Lord joins the dove’s innocence and purity to wisdom. In this way he presents true prudence: to be wise, but purely and innocently. We are not to creep and grovel on the ground like the serpent, but to be heavenly and fly up to God. “Be wise,” says the Lord, “as the serpent”: as it schemes against you, so you also be shrewd against it. As it drove you out of the blessed life, so you drive it out of your own way of life. “And be pure and innocent” toward your neighbors “as the dove,” repaying no mortal with evil. For they say that the dove is more innocent than any bird or any other creature of the air, and that it does not even have a gall bladder. To put it another way, in these two creatures we find the beginnings of virtue and vice, each choosing [?] an instrument suited to it. Vice, being heavy, groveling and creeping, appeared in a creature like itself. Virtue, being divine and heavenly, appeared in the bird that travels the sky and proclaimed God’s kindness. For it is clear that the virtues are worked in mortals through the divine Spirit. This was shown again in the dove sent out by Noah from the divine ark [?]

[?] …of the dove that was sent out [?] returned to the divine man, carrying a twig of olive with leaves: by the twig it signified the dry wood of the Law, and by the rich leaf the evergreen teaching of the Gospels. For Noah's ark, which held every kind of creature, was an image of our Church of all nations. It floats on the sea of this flowing and unstable life, and our Church is drenched on every side by the surge of temptations. Through the serpent we fell out of paradise; through the dove of the Spirit we have been led up to heaven. For in the form of this bird the divine Spirit, the crown of the virtues, flew down upon Jesus at the Jordan. It showed him to be the natural Son of God and not an adopted one, and it brings to us innocence and guilelessness. So let us not be wise like the serpent only to deceive mortals, but let us be wise in the right way, to do good. (For the prudent and wise Apostle says, not only "to think highly" but "to think soberly"; and the same Apostle says again, "I want you to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil.") Let us not be puffed up and swollen by praise, nor be struck down and distraught by blame. For a man wounded by words and wailing about it, and carried away into unrestrained anger, cannot become a worker in the Lord's vineyard. The one who is struck on one cheek and offers the other is the one the Lord appoints to bear nobly the burden of the day of this present age and the scorching heat of its temptations, since he has eagerly fulfilled all the laborious work of the commandment. For the Lord himself, at the very time of his voluntary passion, did not retaliate when a servant struck him, though myriads of angels served him. Emulating him, [Paul] received from the Jews five times forty lashes less one and bore them gently. He taught a long-suffering equal to God's, a virtue aptly named, since whoever shares in it becomes far from anger. And since God is perfect virtue, he is fittingly called long-suffering, as being far from anger. Even those of the learning outside honored this virtue. Socrates, the lawgiver of Attic doctrines, did not retaliate when he was struck. Antisthenes, when some insolent man battered his face, said nothing and went away, only writing the name of the man who had struck him on his forehead, so that onlookers would not suspect him of being possessed or drunk. And Epictetus's leg, maimed by his wicked master, became for many philosophers a school of silence in danger. For by his philosophy he proved to be the master of his master. So let us not be changed when we are insulted. Let us walk in the footsteps of the Creator of ourselves and of all things, and even if the one who strikes us is someone else's servant, let us too say to him the divine words: "If I have spoken wrongly, testify to the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?" For in this way your opponent will be wounded by your magnanimity as if by an arrow. Called back from his rash tongue and mind, he will be grateful to you as the cause of his change, having been taught not to wail, and

[?] … not reaching for great rewards in return for lesser labors, but content to accept greater labors too, since he will not receive the denarius any other way unless he is attested by the completeness of his toils. "The sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed," says the lofty Apostle, who suffered a great deal for Christ and counted all present things as refuse for his sake. Question [?]. What does the Lord mean when he says, "A sower went out to sow; some seeds fell along the path, some on rocky ground, and others among the thorns. The birds of the sky came and devoured those along the path; those on rocky ground had no depth of soil, and when they sprang up [?] they withered; and those under the thorns were choked"? And what of everything else the passage relates about them?

"A sower went out to sow": Christ, God before the ages, went out from the Father. For he is the sower of our salvation. His seed is the divine and life-giving word; the field is all humanity; the oxen are the apostles; the plough is the cross; the yoke is concord; and the yoke-bands are the sweet love that binds together the necks of these divine men and bows them down. The sower went out to sow, not wheat or barley or any other earthly thing that serves the belly, but faith in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, hope of resurrection, and unfeigned love for God and neighbor. Christ the sower went out with ten yoke of oxen, as the lofty Isaiah says: "For where [?] ten yoke of oxen [work], they will make one jar." The ten yoke of rational oxen signify the company of the apostles: twelve before the passion; seven, those with Stephen, appointed by the twelve after the divine resurrection; and the twentieth, the one who heard from heaven, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" He went over to the side of the one he was persecuting, against his own kin Israel, and took up arms against them in the war. These twenty rational oxen of the sower dug up the field of mortal souls and, through Christ, sowed faith in him throughout the world under the sun. They made our whole earthen lump into one jar that can receive the divine outpourings [?], and the blood and water poured out on the cross when the spear pierced the jar of the divine body. For Christ himself is the sower, and he himself is the potter of our clay. Before the incarnation he created us from nothing. When we had been defiled and had become receptive of what is worse, he crushed us through death and shapes us anew, so that from then on we may remain unreceptive of evil. For he himself is blended with what he fashioned, without mixture and without confusion, and he has made us to be immortal forever by union

with what is ours and in an appearance like ours. And he himself is the jar made from our earthenware according to the flesh, holding the living and springing [?] water of his own divinity. It was as if carrying this jar that John cried out in his preaching of baptism, when he saw Jesus: "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" — by the cross and the outpouring [?] of blood and water.
