Concerning this jar, again, when the disciples asked Jesus where they should prepare the Passover of the Law for him, he said to them: "Go into such-and-such a city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Say to him, 'The Teacher says, I am keeping the Passover at your house with my disciples,' and he will show you a large upper room, furnished; prepare it there." Let these words be taken literally, but let them also be understood figuratively. The man carrying the jar of water is John the Baptist, who preached a baptism of repentance and baptized. The city is the Jerusalem above, whose citizens are John and the rest of the company of the righteous and [?]. The upper room furnished with bright mosaic is heaven, which is shaped into various [?] figures by the variety of the stars, like a royal floor among us laid with many-colored mosaic. That the prophet likened the apostles to oxen is made plain by Paul, the chosen one of the divine twenty yoke, who says, "It is written, 'You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain,'" and then adds, "Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Surely he speaks for our sake; it was written for our sake." But let us go back to the lofty Isaiah and follow his prophecy: "For where ten yoke of oxen work, they will make one jar," and he adds, "And whoever sows six artabas will reap three measures." Are we to suppose that such a [?] ever happened, that someone sowing six artabas would yield only three measures? For he does not say he will produce three artabas, but three measures, which are something small. But if we slip in behind the inner veil of the letter, we shall find [?] what these words point to. With six artabas, then, the rational field of the Church is sown: four are the tablets of divine speech, the fifth is the Acts of the divine apostles, and the sixth is the single volume of the lofty Paul, made up of fourteen [epistles]. From these and through these, by the instruction of its leaders, the congregation bears fruit as the divine seed is sown in it: three measures, that is, faith in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. For the sower went out to sow, not wheat for making bread, but life-giving faith; but [?]

[?] … the divine and Holy Spirit of the Trinity. So too the singer of divine things shows that all things are the work of the Trinity when he says: "By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host." The Lord is the Father, the Word is the Son, and the Spirit is the Holy Spirit, who completes the divine Trinity. The Lord showed the Spirit's authority when, having risen from the dead, he said to his disciples: "Receive the Holy Spirit; if you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven" — that is, by the authority of the Spirit whom you receive, who divinely grants you the power to forgive sins. So let us not slide down along with the heretics, who are to be condemned by the queen of the South [?] 1 Cor. 1:4.

because of their indifference to what is better. For she, merely on hearing of wisdom, was urged to fly from the ends of the earth to Solomon; but these, though Christ cried out to them daily, he did not persuade to sober up and look to what is good for them. Words and reports gave her wings toward salvation; but these were in no way improved by seeing God the Word made flesh and witnessing his deeds. QUESTION [?]. Are Peter's question and the Lord's answer to be understood only according to the letter, or do they also have another, deeper meaning? Peter asked, "How often, if my brother sins against me, shall I forgive him? Up to seven times?" and the Lord answered generously, "Truly I tell you, not only up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven."

The answer is good and ready to hand, and it benefits both the one who sins and the one who is wronged: the one who asks pardon for his stumbling, and the one who grants it, since he too is subject to the same failings. For nothing is free from falling and unconquered except the [?] and uncompounded nature of the divine Trinity in unity. For the God-inspired oracle says: "Who will boast of having a pure heart? Or who will dare to say he is clean from sin?" And before these, the divine Job — the unshaken tower, unyielding to the devil who struck him and to his sufferings, the adamantine [?] — cries out plainly: "No one is clean from sin, even if his life on earth is but one day." Now the life of a mortal is not his coming out of the womb into life, but rather, after the body has grown and the understanding has matured, the beginning of his reflection on life. Peter was about to be entrusted with the keys of the kingdom of heaven and with the community of the Church. (By "key," understand the authority to forgive sins. For instead of a key he had his tongue, which opens heaven and shuts it. This belongs to us too: with the tongue we open heaven for ourselves or shut it, the one happening to those who utter things worthy of God, the other to those who utter things unworthy of him.) Expecting, then, to receive the authority to forgive sins, he asks the Lord: "How often, if my brother sins against me, shall I forgive him? Up to seven times?" And why does he not ask about four times, or ten times or more, but "up to seven times"? It seems to me that he secretly longed to learn about the murderer: whether the one who fell into the seven sins is granted pardon through baptism and repentance. That was Cain, the first in the world to commit murder, who was condemned to as many punishments, corresponding to the sins that go along with murder. For Cain was the first among men to act with guile; the first to murder; the first to lie to God when God asked about the man he had killed; the first to bring grief and wailing on parents by killing his brother; the first to conceive envy and jealousy; the first to offer the firstfruits of his produce with an evil intent; and the first to defile the earth with blood and so become the cause of a curse upon it. And for these seven sins in the murderous deed, an equal number of [?]

are imposed by the divine voice: the barrenness and unfruitfulness of the earth, which no longer welcomes the murderer, and the groaning and trembling of his whole body. But I thought I should try to set out the punishments by number as well. "Cursed is the ground because of you": that is one punishment. "You shall till the ground": that is the second, for God bound him to an unspeakable necessity that drove him to labor wretchedly and toil at the earth. "And it will no longer yield its strength to you": the third punishment, to toil and reap no fruit from his toil. "You will be groaning and trembling on the earth": to the three, the divine sentence adds two more punishments, unceasing groaning and endless trembling, so that he could not even bring food or drink to his mouth. His murderous right hand was unsteady, because it had wickedly used its former strength against his brother and bought weakness with its vigor. The sixth punishment was that he lost his freedom to speak before God. For God's turning away is a terrible and most heavy punishment, which contains every penalty. Lamenting it, the one who experienced it begs for death, knowing that this would be better for him than to live cast away from God. And he says: "If you drive me out from the land" — that is, if I am no longer to enjoy its produce — "and I am hidden from your face" — if I am deprived of what the earth provides to live on, and cannot show myself to you while you are angry — "then," he says, "whoever finds me will kill me"; for it is better for me to die than to live in wretched punishment. To him the Lord says: "Not so; for I have set a sign on you, so that no one who finds you should kill you." This is the seventh punishment: not to be granted death, which brings an end to all shame and glory, but to remain under punishment, publicly branded by the sign as the originator of evils among mortals.

[?] … to slip from some snare, let us not despair of cleansing or of forgiveness. And once we have been called back, let us not grow slack, but let us leap away from the worse all the more quickly and lay hold [?] of the virtues. Let us wash our garments and our senses; let us flee matter, since it chokes us; let us [?] toward the lofty way of life of old; let us bend our ear to divine teachings; let us forget what clings to the ground; let us acquire love, the citadel of the virtues; and let us engrave the divine law on the tablets of the heart, a tablet [?] … [?]. Why then did Saint Peter, who had himself stumbled so badly and been forgiven, not also forgive Ananias and Sapphira, but in a single hour put them both to death with a word? And yet there was no [sin?] … [?] comparable to his denial with an oath [?] … [?] … and the gold they hid was their own, not someone else's. And even if it had been someone else's [?], it is not the same thing to hide a little of one's own and to deny Jesus. Answer. [?] The fear that the chief of the apostles struck into the guilty did not come from folly, but from a foreseeing discipline that heals very many of the passions of mortals. Since [Ananias], wounded by sacrilege, embezzled the gold dedicated to God and denied it when asked, then [?] … [?] … the gospel seeds being sown, and seeing the tares springing up alongside them, he wisely [?] … [?] quickly cut them back, lest they grow up together and ruin the [?]. For [he saw] him in the bond of bitterness [?]

to be like Simon, and incapable from then on of changing for the better. For he would have asked that the crime be forgiven while his heart did not agree with his lips, as the singer of divine things says about Israel: "They loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him; but their heart was not right with him, nor were they faithful to his covenant." Physicians are accustomed to act in the same way: when one of the extremities of the body is seized by an incurable disease, they immediately cut off the finger of the hand or the toe of the foot, before the corruption spreads to the rest of the limbs. Likewise the divine Moses, contemplating the matters of the Law from the very beginning, and being urged on, ordered that a man gathering wood on the Sabbath be stoned for a small sin, and he wrote that God had pronounced this. For transgression is judged in great and moderate matters alike, as the Lord says: "If anyone fulfills the whole law but stumbles in one point, he has become guilty of all." This does not mean that all his virtue is wiped out (for that would rightly seem unjust even to those who understand only a little about God's just judgment). Rather, he seems to me to become guilty of all because there is subtracted [?] … the acquisition of one crime, and he is held liable to a counter-reckoning against them all, so that either something is cut away from the substance of those very virtues or something is subtracted from their number. So the one who has not wholly despaired of himself and given himself over entirely to what is worse, but offers virtue to God even if only rarely and has pity on his neighbor, owed God for the times he stumbled, but is owed by him for the good he has done. When the counter-reckoning is subtracted, then, he is assigned to the side of whichever is greater. We have often known this to happen among ourselves too: we owe a hundred denarii while thirty are owed to us. Just as a debtor of money is liable for the whole to the lender until the debt is repaid, so the one to whom God owes for a thousand good deeds, but who owes for one transgression, is liable for all until the reckoning of each person's account is made. For transgression is judged in small and greater matters, and the difference lies in the comparison. So let us hasten to have the greater share in what is good, outweighing injustice with righteousness. If the end of the world and the coming of Christ cannot be escaped, how can he himself say, "Then let those in Judea flee to the mountains; let the one on the housetop not come down to take anything out of his house, and let the one in the field not turn back to take his cloak"? And again he says, "But pray that your flight may not be on a Sabbath or in winter; and woe to those who are pregnant and those who are nursing in those days." If the end happens to come in summer, on a Sunday or a Monday, can we escape notice, or flee? And why, when there was such a great crowd and population at that time, did he call only the pregnant and the nursing wretched, out of everyone, and lament over them?

The Lord was foretelling to the Jews the flight that awaited them, and he urges them to escape to the mountains. For after Vespasian, Titus took command and utterly razed and laid waste Jerusalem. He destroyed the Jews miserably: he cut down the men with the sword, dashed the newborn infants against the ground, and ripped open the pregnant women, and so wiped out the God-fighting race with every kind of destruction and annihilation. The city was taken on a Sabbath, when everyone was at leisure at home because of the Sabbath rest, and it was winter too, so none of them could escape the capture and the slaughter [?]. The one on the housetop tried to escape notice, not wishing to take anything from below, since he considered staying alive more precious than possessions. The one in the field not only stayed where he was without turning back home, but hurried to get farther away, seeing the burning and capture of the city. But if you rightly wish the passage to be applied anagogically to our own affairs: "Let those in Judea flee to the mountains" means that those who are firm in piety (for this is what "Judea" is interpreted to mean) should look to Christ, the lofty refuge, guarded by their own confession of faith. "Let the one on the housetop not come down to take anything out of his house" means that the one who has despised this shadowy present life, trampled underfoot the whole tent of this world, become lofty in his way of life, and sent away the passions that dwelt within him, should not draw any of them back: not fear, not despondency, not vainglory, not desire for wealth, which are a descent from the height. "Let the one in the field not turn back to take his cloak" means that the one who has stripped off the old man and renounced the things of the flesh should wear the new man, who has renewed him into the newness of God and cleansed him of the mire; for in this he will be unconquerable against every scheme. So let no disturbance, or sympathy for kinsfolk, tear him away from the love of Christ. For Christ himself, when his mother and brothers were looking for him, did not answer their call, since he had begun giving saving teachings to his hearers; and so he taught that spiritual things are to be preferred to fleshly ones. In the same way his disciples left the care of the tables and devoted themselves instead to the word of piety, not only teaching wisdom in words but instructing by their deeds. For to speak well is like a lyre or a cymbal; but to act kindly [is like] the angels [?]

But they will be called back again at the end of the world. When all those from the nations have believed, then at last those from Judea too will turn. For the Lord says in the Gospels, "I have other sheep too, which are not of this fold; I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd." And the Apostle, with regard to this,
agreeing, he says: “But when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved.”

I will never be persuaded that the Jews are to be called back. Neither the Lord nor the lofty Apostle teaches this in the words they spoke, which were rightly said by them but wrongly understood and expressed by you. For the Lord said, “I have other sheep” (clearly meaning us) “which are not of this fold” (that is, the Jewish one). The first part of that fold was the Lord’s [?]; then came the divine apostles, and with them and through them the believers from Judea. For before the saving Passion the flock from the Gentiles did not yet exist, because the gospel had not yet been preached to us and we had not been baptized. After the resurrection Christ did this through his apostles and brought us into the believing flock from the Jews. So all of us believers are one flock under one shepherd, tended and guarded by Christ, the high priest and chief shepherd. “For there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism,” says the lofty Apostle, the disciple of the chief shepherd and the teacher of the whole world under heaven. He also says, “When the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, all Israel will be saved.” By this he does not mean that the Jews will be saved and called back at the end of the age. He means those who see God through purity of mind and through faith. For “Israel” is interpreted by everyone, the Jews included, as “a mind that sees God.” “For not all who are from Judea are children; but in Isaac your seed shall be called. That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God,” says the same Apostle. And again the Lord says in the Gospels, “Many are called” (that is, Israelites and Christians), “but few are chosen” (that is, those who are saved). So when the fullness of the Gentiles, that is, the Church of all peoples, has come in (clearly meaning, come in to judgment), then all Israel (the mind that sees God) will be saved. That means every mortal who has knowledge of God through faith and piety.
